He danced for her — a courtship dance, his feet stamping the hard-packed floor, his arms spreading like wings. She smiled. She agreed to marry him.

She went to the Kachina kiva, where many different Kachinas gathered — Crow Mother, the Parrot Kachinas, the warrior Kachinas — all preparing for the spring dances. She cooked their food while they wove her bridal costume: a robe of white turkey feathers, a belt of turquoise beads, moccasins of soft deerskin.

They had two children, both Circle Kachinas — small, round-faced beings who danced in the plazas with their father.

But the Hotóto Kachina — a being of great charm and questionable intentions — seduced the wife away to Shongópavi, another village on Second Mesa. The Circle Kachina followed her tracks across the mesa, carrying his children on his back.

At the kiva in Shongópavi, the Flute priests played for four days. The music was so beautiful that the water spirits wept, and their tears formed a pool at the kiva's entrance. On the fourth day, the wife emerged from the water in her bridal costume, restored.

The Flute priests declared: "You shall always follow each other this way."

The two ran westward. They are still running. They became the stars that chase each other across the sky — Nangö'sohu — one constantly overtaking and then falling behind the other. In the Hopi sky, you can see them every night: two points of light, forever pursuing, forever separated, forever connected.

title: The Toad and the Snow Kachinas
summary: In Oraibi, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. North of the village at Katcínavala lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy often went to listen to the Kachinas sing. On the dance day, the Toad Boy painted his face and wore a wildcat robe. Children laughed at him and took him to an anthill because he liked ants. He ate the ants and returned to the plaza to enjoy the dance. When the children gave him red piki (paper bread) from the Kachinas, he brought it home to his mother. She was happy, and they ate it together. This story teaches about the inclusion of even the lowliest creatures in Kachina celebrations and demonstrates the Hopi value of kindness to those who are different.
source: H.R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905); told by Kwáyeshva of Oraíbi
full_text:
In Oraibi, on Third Mesa, the Snow Kachinas were practicing for a dance in the Chórzhovi kiva. Their masks were white as the first frost, and their songs were the songs of winter — slow, deep, resonant with the weight of snow.

North of the village, at a place called Katcínavala, lived Toad Woman with her son. The boy was small and strange — his skin bumpy, his eyes too large, his manner quiet. He liked ants. He would sit for hours watching them carry seeds across the sand, marveling at their industry.

Every day, the boy crept to the kiva and pressed his ear against the stone wall, listening to the Kachinas sing. The music moved him in ways he could not explain. His feet tapped. His hands waved. He wanted to dance.

On the day of the dance, the Toad Boy painted his face with red ochre and wore a wildcat robe over his small, bumpy body. He walked to the plaza and stood among the children.

The children laughed at him. "Look at the Toad Boy!" they cried. "He thinks he can dance!" They grabbed him and carried him to an anthill, dumping him on top of it because he liked ants.

The boy sat on the anthill and ate the ants, one by one, while the dance continued. When the Kachinas finished, they gave the children red piki — thin, paper-like bread made from blue corn. The Toad Boy received a piece. He carried it home to his mother.

She was happy. They ate it together in their small lodge, the sweet, thin bread dissolving on their tongues.

This story teaches a Hopi value that runs deeper than it appears: inclusion. Even the lowliest creature — a toad boy who eats ants — has a place in the Kachina celebrations. The dance is not for the beautiful or the strong. It is for everyone. And the gift of piki, that thin red bread, is the gift of community itself.

title: Coyote Helps Decorate the Night
summary: In this Hopi story about the origins of the night sky, the animals were decorating the darkness. Various animals placed stars and patterns in the sky, but Coyote, growing impatient with the slow, careful work, grabbed a handful of stars and threw them carelessly across the sky. This explains why some stars are scattered randomly while others form orderly patterns. Another version tells that Coyote was given the task of placing the stars but became distracted or deliberately did a poor job, resulting in the Milky Way and the chaotic scattering of stars. The story warns against impatience and the consequences of rushing sacred work.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
In the time before the stars were placed, the sky was a blank canvas of darkness, and the animals were given the task of decorating it.

The Beaver went first. He was careful and methodical, placing each star in a straight line, like the logs of a dam. The Deer followed, arranging stars in gentle arcs that mirrored the paths she walked through the forest. The Eagle placed the brightest stars in patterns that resembled wings spread against the night.

Coyote watched. He had been given the task of placing the scattered stars — the ones that did not fit into any pattern, the ones that were too small or too dim for the important constellations.

The work was slow. Each animal placed a star, then stepped back to admire it, then placed another. The night was cold and the work was tedious. Coyote grew impatient.

"This is taking too long," he said. "Let me help."

The other animals were wary, but they gave him a blanket full of stars — hundreds of them, glowing faintly like embers. Coyote grabbed the blanket and flung it into the sky.

Stars scattered in every direction. Some landed in neat rows. Others landed in clumps. Some landed alone, isolated in vast dark spaces. The careful patterns the other animals had created were disrupted, overlaid with Coyote's chaotic scatter.

The animals were angry. "You've ruined it!" the Beaver cried.

But the Creator looked at the sky and saw something the animals did not. The orderly patterns — the Big Dipper, the Hunter, the Pleiades — told stories and marked seasons. But Coyote's scattered stars filled the spaces between, creating the Milky Way and the countless faint lights that make the night sky feel infinite.

"Both are necessary," the Creator said. "Order without chaos is a cage. Chaos without order is a flood. Together, they are the sky."

And so the night remains: partly patterned, partly scattered, partly deliberate, partly accidental — like the world itself.

title: The Boy Who Crossed the Great Water and Returned
summary: A Hopi tale of a boy who journeyed across the great waters and returned with knowledge and power. The boy's curiosity led him to leave his village and travel east toward the rising sun. He encountered various supernatural beings and overcame trials, including crossing a body of water that no Hopi had crossed before. Guided by Spider Grandmother, he learned sacred songs and ceremonies from the spirits on the other side. When he returned to his people, he brought new ceremonies, dance forms, and agricultural knowledge that benefited the Hopi. The story reflects the Hopi belief that spiritual power and knowledge can be gained through journeys to sacred places and that those who venture forth with pure hearts return to enrich the community.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
The boy's name has been lost, which is fitting, because the story is not about who he was but about what he found. He lived in a village on the mesas, a quiet boy with restless feet and a mind that wandered beyond the horizon.

One morning, he left. He told no one where he was going. He walked east, toward the rising sun, carrying nothing but a water gourd and a piece of dried corn.

He walked for many days. The mesas gave way to valleys, the valleys to plains, the plains to mountains he had never seen. He crossed rivers too wide to see the other side and climbed passes where the air was thin enough to make him dizzy.

Guided by Spider Grandmother — who appeared to him as an old woman sitting by a fire — he found his way to a body of water so vast it might have been the edge of the world. On the other side, he could see mountains glowing with a light that was not sunlight.

Spider Grandmother taught him to build a boat from reeds and to navigate by the stars. He crossed the water and found a land where spirits lived in houses of cloud and spoke in songs. They taught him sacred ceremonies — dances that brought rain, songs that healed the sick, prayers that opened the way between the living and the dead.

He stayed for one year, learning everything the spirits could teach. When he returned to his people, he brought new dances, new songs, and new knowledge of agriculture — how to read the stars to know when to plant, how to read the clouds to know when rain was coming.

The people benefited from his journey. The corn grew taller. The children grew stronger. The ceremonies became richer.

The boy — for he was still a boy, though his eyes were old — never spoke about where he had been. But sometimes, at night, he would sit outside his lodge and look east, toward the water he had crossed, and the people knew that the knowledge he carried had come from a place beyond the ordinary world.

title: Two Friends: Coyote and Bull Snake Exchange Visits
summary: Coyote and Bull Snake were friends who decided to visit each other's homes. Coyote visited Bull Snake first and found his burrow beautiful and comfortable. Bull Snake then visited Coyote's den. During the visit, Coyote played a trick on Bull Snake, or vice versa, depending on the version. The story humorously explores the nature of friendship across differences, the expectations of hospitality, and the consequences of deception between friends. It also incorporates elements of Hopi social values, including proper guest behavior and the responsibilities of hosts. The story ends with the two friends parting ways, each having learned something about trust and respect for different ways of living.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
Coyote and Bull Snake were friends — an unlikely pair, for Coyote was loud and restless while Bull Snake was quiet and still. But friendship, like rain, falls where it will.

Coyote visited Bull Snake first. He found the burrow beautiful — cool and dark, with walls that glowed faintly with embedded crystals. Bull Snake offered Coyote the best sleeping spot, the one near the back where the air was warmest.

"Now you must visit my den," Coyote said.

Bull Snake agreed and traveled to Coyote's home — a hollow under a rock, messy with old bones and scattered fur. Bull Snake was polite, though the smell was terrible.

During the visit, Coyote decided to play a trick. He told Bull Snake that the greatest honor in his den was to sleep in the deepest corner, where the air was thinnest. Bull Snake, trusting his friend, slithered into the deepest part of the den — and found himself stuck, his thick body wedged between two rocks.

Coyote laughed. "I've caught a snake!" he cried.

But Bull Snake did not laugh. He spoke quietly: "A friend who tricks his guest is no friend at all."

Coyote's laughter died. He helped Bull Snake out of the crevice, cleaning the dirt from his scales with his own paws. "I am sorry," he said, and for once, he meant it.

Bull Snake returned to his own burrow, and Coyote did not visit for a long time. When he finally did, he brought a gift — a fine piece of turquoise, smoothed by the river. Bull Snake accepted it, and the friendship resumed, though it was changed.

The story teaches Hopi values about hospitality and the responsibilities of hosts. A guest must be treated with respect, and a host who betrays that trust loses something that cannot be easily regained.

title: Why the Salt is Far Away
summary: A Hopi legend explaining why the Hopi must travel long distances to obtain salt. Long ago, salt was close to the Hopi villages. But a woman or a group of people violated a taboo involving salt — either by being wasteful, disrespectful, or by using salt improperly during a ceremony. The Salt Woman (or salt spirits) became angry and moved the salt deposits far away, to the Grand Canyon and other distant locations. Ever since, the Hopi have had to undertake long, dangerous journeys to gather salt, a sacred substance used in ceremonies and daily life. The story teaches respect for natural resources and the consequences of taking blessings for granted.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993); various Hopi oral traditions
full_text:
Salt was once close to the Hopi villages. It lay in deposits along the riverbanks, white and crystalline, easy to gather. The people used it freely — sprinkling it on corn, preserving meat, marking the boundaries of their fields. They did not think about where it came from or how blessed they were to have it.

Salt Woman saw this. She was a spirit — old and powerful, her body made of the same white crystal as the salt itself. She lived in the deposits, and the people's carelessness wounded her. They wasted salt. They used it in ways that were not sacred. They forgot to give thanks.

One night, Salt Woman packed her belongings — which were also salt — and walked away from the villages. She walked south, toward the Grand Canyon, where the river carved through layers of ancient rock. She walked to other places too — to distant salt flats and underground deposits.

When the people went to gather salt the next morning, the riverbanks were bare. The deposits were gone. They searched everywhere and found nothing.

A hunter tracked Salt Woman's footprints to the Grand Canyon. There he found her, sitting on a ledge overlooking the river. "Come back," he begged. "We need the salt."

Salt Woman looked at him with eyes like white stone. "You forgot to give thanks," she said. "You forgot that the salt is a gift, not a right. If you want salt, you will have to come and get it — the long way, the hard way, so that you remember."

The hunter returned to his people with Salt Woman's words. And so the Hopi began their long journeys to gather salt — traveling for days to the Grand Canyon and other distant locations, carrying the salt back on their backs.

The journey itself became sacred. The people sang songs as they walked. They left offerings at every spring and shrine along the way. And when they returned with the white crystals, they gave thanks — not just for the salt, but for the reminder that blessings must never be taken for granted.

title: The Journey to the Land of the Dead
summary: In Hopi tradition, the journey to the land of the dead begins at the sipapu in the Grand Canyon. The spirit travels westward, following the path of the setting sun, to the land of the ancestors. Along the way, the spirit encounters various challenges and must have the proper knowledge, gained through ceremonial instruction during life, to pass safely. The spirit is judged by Masauwu and the Kachinas who determine its fate. Good souls pass into a land of plenty, while those who lived badly face difficulties. The dead eventually become cloud people who can bring rain to their living descendants. The spirits of the dead are associated with the Kachinas and reside at the San Francisco Peaks. This cycle of life, death, and return as rain-giving spirits reinforces the Hopi connection between proper living, ceremonial participation, and the well-being of the community.
source: Harold Courlander, The Fourth World of the Hopis; H.R. Voth, The Traditions of the Hopi (1905)
full_text:
When a Hopi dies, the journey begins at the sipapu — the opening in the Grand Canyon where the people first entered the Fourth World. The spirit descends through this passage, back through the layers of the earth, following the path that the ancestors once climbed.

But the journey is not a straight descent. The spirit travels westward, following the path of the setting sun, moving through a landscape that is both familiar and strange — a shadow version of the living world, where the rivers flow backward and the mountains lean in directions that make no sense.

Along the way, the spirit encounters challenges. There are crossings where the bridge is made of a single hair, and the spirit must be light enough to walk it. There are gates guarded by spirits who ask questions that only the properly instructed can answer. There are tests of character — moments where the spirit must prove that it lived well, that it honored the ceremonies, that it treated others with respect.

The spirit is judged by Masauwu and the Kachinas. Those who lived well pass into a land of plenty — a world like the Fourth World but better, where the corn grows tall and the water flows clear. Those who lived badly face difficulties — not punishment, but the consequences of their choices, a world shaped by their own failures.

The dead eventually become cloud people. They rise from the land of the dead into the sky, where they join the Kachinas at the San Francisco Peaks. From there, they can bring rain to their living descendants. The dead are not gone — they are transformed, becoming part of the forces that sustain the living world.

This is why the Hopi perform ceremonies for the dead. They pray not for the dead to return, but for the dead to find their place among the cloud people, where they can fulfill their final duty: bringing rain to the fields that feed their children and their children's children.

title: Mockingbird Gives Out the Calls
summary: In this Hopi story, Mockingbird was responsible for distributing the languages and calls among all the peoples of the world. During the migrations after the emergence into the Fourth World, the people were all speaking the same language. Mockingbird called the people together and assigned different languages and dialects to different groups, effectively creating the diversity of tribes and nations. He gave various bird species their distinctive calls as well. According to some versions, Mockingbird received this task from Spider Grandmother or the Kachinas, and his imitative ability was used to create the range of human languages. The story explains why Mockingbird can mimic other birds and why there are so many different languages among the peoples of the earth.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
In the time after the emergence, when the people first spread across the Fourth World, they all spoke the same language. Every clan, every village, every family — the words flowed between them like water between connected springs.

Mockingbird saw this and was troubled. "The world is too large for one language," he said. "If everyone speaks the same words, they will never be truly different. They will never have their own songs, their own stories, their own way of seeing the world."

Mockingbird had been given a special gift by the Creator: the ability to imitate any sound, any voice, any song. He could sound like a hawk or a frog, like wind in the pines or water over stones. This gift made him the natural choice for what needed to be done.

He called the people together at the base of a great mesa. They gathered in hundreds, their voices rising in a single chorus of the common tongue. Mockingbird perched on a rock above them and began to sing.

He sang the song of the Hawk, and the people of the north spoke in sharp, clipped tones. He sang the song of the Frog, and the people of the south spoke in deep, resonant voices. He sang the song of the Wind, and the people of the east spoke in words that moved quickly, like grass bending in a breeze. He sang the song of the River, and the people of the west spoke in words that flowed slowly and steadily.

He gave each group its own language, its own dialect, its own way of forming words. The people tried to speak to each other and found they could not understand. They laughed. They wept. They gestured. And slowly, they learned to communicate through other means — through sign language, through shared work, through the universal language of ceremony.

Mockingbird also gave the bird species their distinctive calls. The hawk's cry, the owl's hoot, the sparrow's chirp — all are fragments of the languages Mockingbird distributed.

This is why Mockingbird can still mimic other birds and why there are so many different languages among the peoples of the earth. It is not a curse but a gift — the gift of difference, of perspective, of the understanding that the world is too vast to be spoken in a single voice.

title: Sikakokuh and the Hunting Dog
summary: A Hopi story about a boy named Sikakokuh who had a remarkable hunting dog. The dog was no ordinary animal but possessed spiritual power, able to track game without fail and communicate with its master. Sikakokuh's success as a hunter made others jealous. Through the dog's guidance, Sikakokuh learned the proper rituals for hunting, including prayers and offerings to the spirits of the animals he killed. When enemies or jealous rivals tried to harm the dog, supernatural forces protected both boy and animal. The story teaches the sacred relationship between humans and animals, the importance of gratitude, and the proper conduct of hunters who must respect the spirits of the animals they take.
source: Harold Courlander, People of the Short Blue Corn (1993)
full_text:
Sikakokuh was a boy of the Hopi villages who possessed a hunting dog unlike any other — a creature born with eyes the color of river stones and a spirit that seemed to know things no animal should know. Where other dogs chased rabbits blindly through the mesas, Sikakokuh's dog would pause at the edge of the wash, lift its nose, and point toward exactly where a deer would be standing three valleys away.

The other hunters noticed. They whispered. "How does the boy find game every time?" jealousy poisoned their words like stagnant water. Some began to scheme against the dog, for they believed it carried bad spirits.

But the dog was no ordinary animal. In dreams, it spoke to Sikakokuh in a voice like wind through canyon walls. "When you hunt, you must first offer cornmeal to the earth. You must speak to the spirit of the animal before you draw your bow. If you take without asking, the game will hide from your people forever."

Sikakokuh followed every instruction. He scattered cornmeal at the four directions. He whispered prayers before each hunt. And the deer came willingly, walking toward his arrow as if offering themselves.

One night, a jealous hunter tried to poison the dog with tainted meat. But the spirits of the mountain — the Gahe — intervened. They appeared as masked dancers in the moonlight, their wooden headdresses scraping the stars, and they drove the wicked hunter away into the desert where he wandered for three days without water.

When the hunter returned, broken and repentant, Sikakokuh shared his harvest with him. The dog sat beside them, watching with eyes that held the memory of every hunt, every prayer, every life given so the people might eat.

"The dog is our teacher," Sikakokuh told the village elders. "It shows us that hunting is not conquest. It is conversation."

The story spread through the Hopi villages and became part of the teachings given to young hunters — a reminder that the sacred relationship between human and animal is built on respect, gratitude, and the proper conduct of ceremony.

title: The Iatiku and Nautsiti Creation (Acoma Pueblo)
summary: In the Acoma Pueblo creation myth, two sisters named Iatiku (Life Bringer) and Nautsiti (Full Basket) emerged from the underworld through a sacred place called Shipapu, guided by Tsichtinako (Thought Woman). They were given two baskets containing seeds, animal figurines, and sacred objects. Tsichtinako instructed them to pray to the Sun (Uchtsiti), their father, who had created the world from a clot of his own blood. The sisters created the mountains, directions, plants, and animals. Iatiku created the Corn Mother and the Kachinas. Nautsiti introduced death into the world when she disobeyed a taboo. The sisters became the mothers of the Acoma people, with Iatiku's children becoming the Pueblo clans. The story explains the origins of ceremonies, clans, and the relationship between the people, the land, and the spirits.
source: Edward Proctor Hunt, The Origin Myth of Acoma Pueblo (1928); Peter Nabokov edition (2015)
full_text:
Before the world had shape, there was only Shipapu — a dark opening in the earth through which the first light would eventually shine. From within this darkness, the voice of Tsichtinako — Thought Woman — spoke. She could not be seen, for she was a spirit without a body, a voice without a face. But her words were precise as starlight.

"Two sisters must emerge," she said. "Iatiku — Life Bringer — and Nautsiti — Full Basket. They will carry the seeds of everything that lives."

The sisters climbed upward from the underworld, emerging into a world of blinding light and empty plains. Tsichtinako placed two baskets in their hands: one filled with seeds — corn, beans, squash, sunflower — and one filled with animal figurines of wood and stone, each one carved with the likeness of a creature that did not yet exist.

"Pray to the Sun, your father," Tsichtinako instructed. "He created this world from a clot of his own blood. Without his warmth, nothing will grow."

The sisters knelt and prayed. The Sun — Uchtsiti — looked down from the sky and sent his rays to warm the earth. Where his light touched the soil, it turned from gray to brown to rich, dark loam. The sisters planted the seeds from their baskets, and from the earth rose the mountains, the rivers, the plains.

Iatiku created the Corn Mother — a figure of power and abundance — and the Kachinas, spirits who would bring rain and fertility. Nautsiti, proud and independent, introduced death into the world when she disobeyed a taboo, walking where she was told not to walk and touching what she was told not to touch.

The sisters became the mothers of the Acoma people. Iatiku's children became the clans — the Corn Clan, the Sun Clan, the Kachina Clan — each one carrying a piece of the original gift. The story explains the origins of ceremonies, clans, and the relationship between the people, the land, and the spirits who watch from above.

The baskets that Tsichtinako gave are still represented in Acoma ceremonies, carried by priests who walk the paths the sisters first walked, planting hope in the dry earth.

title: The Pueblo Emergence from the Underworld
summary: A central Pueblo creation theme across multiple Pueblo tribes (Acoma, Zuni, Hopi, Laguna, etc.) involves the emergence of the first people from the underworld through a sacred opening called the sipapu. In the beginning, the people lived in darkness beneath the earth. Guided by spirits, culture heroes, or twin war gods, they climbed up through four underground worlds, each representing a stage of development. They used a giant reed, spruce tree, or ladder to ascend. As they climbed, they transformed from insect-like or unfinished beings into fully formed humans. The last people to emerge were often an old man and woman who became trapped, becoming the rulers of the underworld — establishing that all must return there after death. The sipapu is often identified with the Grand Canyon or a specific location within each Pueblo's traditional territory.
source: Various Pueblo oral traditions; Edward Proctor Hunt, The Origin Myth of Acoma Pueblo; Wikipedia: Pueblo mythology
full_text:
In the beginning, the first people lived in darkness beneath the earth. They dwelt in four underground worlds, each one a layer of development, each one a step closer to the light they had never seen.

In the deepest world, they were barely human — small, blind, their hands and feet webbed, their bodies covered in slime. They could not speak or think. They were more dream than flesh.

But the spirits watched. Culture heroes and twin war gods came to them in the darkness and said, "Climb. There is a world above this one where the light is."

A giant reed grew from the floor of the underworld, pushing upward through layers of rock and soil. The people gathered at its base and began to climb. The reed was hollow, and the climb was long — through the third world, the second world, the first world — each time finding themselves still incomplete.

As they climbed, they changed. In the third world, they gained the ability to see — though the light was painful, and they covered their eyes. In the second world, they gained speech — though their first words were clumsy, like a child learning to walk. In the first world, they gained thought — though their thoughts were simple, like ripples on still water.

The last to emerge were an old man and an old woman who became trapped at the top of the reed. They could not make the final climb. "We will stay here," the old man said. "We will become the rulers of the dead. All who die must pass through our world before they can be reborn."

The sipapu — the opening through which they emerged — is sacred to all Pueblo peoples. It is identified with the Grand Canyon, or with a specific location within each Pueblo's traditional territory. It is the place where the living remember they came from darkness, and where the dead must return.

title: The Pueblo Hero Twins
summary: In Pueblo mythology, the Twin War Gods (Masewi and Oyoyewi in some traditions) are the most important heroic figures. They were born to a virgin mother who conceived from the Sun, much like the Navajo Hero Twins. These twins are credited with creating the world and all living creatures, as well as slaying a giant monster that terrorized the Pueblo people — a beast so large it could eat entire villages in one bite. The twins tracked the monster and killed it with their magical weapons, which included lightning arrows and shields. They established the directions, brought order to the world, and taught the people how to live. After completing their work, they returned to the underworld but continue to watch over the Pueblo people. They are often celebrated in ritual performances and dances, reinforcing their cultural significance as protectors and culture heroes.
full_text:
In Pueblo mythology, the Twin War Gods — Masewi and Oyoyewi — were born to a virgin mother who conceived from the rays of the Sun. They were not merely warriors but creators, beings whose power shaped the world itself.

When they were born, the earth shook. Their mother placed them on a blanket of eagle feathers, and they grew with supernatural speed — from infants to toddlers to young men in the space of a single day. They carried weapons made of lightning: arrows that could split mountains and shields that could stop the wind.

A great monster terrorized the Pueblo people. It was so large it could swallow an entire village in one bite — homes, people, cornfields, all disappearing into its gaping maw. The people tried to fight it with spears and arrows, but their weapons bounced off its hide like rain off a rock.

The Twin War Gods tracked the monster across the desert. They followed its trail of destruction — flattened hills, dried rivers, the bones of those it had consumed. When they found it, it was sleeping in a canyon, its body blocking the sun.

Masewi struck first, his lightning arrow piercing the monster's left eye. Oyoyewi followed, his arrow finding the right eye. The monster thrashed, but the twins were relentless. They shot arrow after arrow until the creature fell, its death creating a new valley where the people would later build their homes.

After their victory, the twins established the four directions, brought order to the world, and taught the people how to live — when to plant, when to harvest, when to dance and pray. When their work was done, they returned to the underworld, but they never left entirely. They watch from below, ready to return if the people need them again.

title: The Ants That Pushed on the Pine Tree
summary: A Pueblo story from Isleta about Kahp-too-óo-yoo (Corn-stalk Young Man), a famous hunter, warrior, and wizard who controlled the clouds and brought rain. After being bewitched by a false friend, he was imprisoned in the top of a giant pine tree that reached the sky. His family and village suffered from drought without his rain powers. The Little Black Ant discovered Kahp-too-óo-yoo in the tree and summoned all the armies of the Little Black Ants and Big Red Ants. They climbed the tree, placed a cup of cornmeal and honey at the top, and then — with the Black Ants pushing from above and the Red Ants pulling from below — drove the giant pine tree deep into the earth, freeing Kahp-too-óo-yoo. He returned home, playing his flute, and the rains returned. The story reflects Pueblo values of community, cooperation, and the power of even the smallest creatures to help.
source: Pueblo Indian Folk-Stories (Sacred Texts Archive); sacred-texts.com
full_text:
Kahp-too-óo-yoo — Corn-stalk Young Man — was the most powerful hunter, warrior, and wizard in Isleta. He could control the clouds. When he sang, rain fell. When he danced, thunder rolled. The people depended on him, and he never failed them.

But he had a friend who was not a friend. The false friend was jealous of Kahp-too-óo-yoo's power and devised a scheme. He invited the wizard to a ceremony, and during the night, he bewitched Kahp-too-óo-yoo and imprisoned him in the top of a giant pine tree that reached the sky.

The tree was enormous — its trunk as wide as a house, its branches lost in the clouds. Kahp-too-óo-yoo was trapped at the very top, where the wind never stopped and the cold never relented. He sang his rain songs, but the wind carried them away before they could reach the sky.

The village suffered. The clouds came but did not rain. The crops withered. The people grew thin. They did not know where Kahp-too-óo-yoo had gone.

But the Little Black Ant knew. She was small enough to climb any tree, and she found Kahp-too-óo-yoo sitting in the top of the great pine, his flute silent, his songs wasted.

The Little Black Ant went to the village and summoned the armies of the Little Black Ants and the Big Red Ants. Thousands of them marched to the base of the tree. They climbed in lines that covered the trunk like a living carpet.

At the top, the ants placed a cup of cornmeal and honey where Kahp-too-óo-yoo could reach it. Then, with the Black Ants pushing from above and the Red Ants pulling from below, they drove the giant pine tree deep into the earth.

The ground shook. The tree sank. And Kahp-too-óo-yoo walked free. He picked up his flute and played a song of rain. The clouds gathered. The rain fell. The crops revived.

He returned to the village playing his flute, and the people danced. The ants had saved them — the smallest creatures in the world, proving that no being is too small to make a difference.

title: Tsichtinako Teaches the Sisters
summary: In the Acoma Pueblo creation story, Tsichtinako (Thought Woman) appeared as a voice guiding the sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti from within the earth. She couldn't be seen because she was a spirit without a human body. Tsichtinako instructed the sisters in all aspects of life: how to plant seeds from their baskets, how to make prayer sticks (pahos), how to conduct ceremonies, and how to organize their society into clans. She explained that Uchtsiti (the Sun, their father) had created the world but it was not yet complete, and the sisters were to complete it. Tsichtinako also taught them language, naming each plant, animal, and feature of the landscape. She established the four sacred directions and the relationship between the people and all beings. Tsichtinako continues to guide the Acoma people invisibly, representing the power of thought and the spiritual foundation of existence.
source: Edward Proctor Hunt, The Origin Myth of Acoma Pueblo (1928)
full_text:
Tsichtinako spoke from within the earth, a voice without a body, a mind without a face. The sisters Iatiku and Nautsiti could not see her, but they heard her as clearly as they heard the wind.

"Take the seeds from your baskets," Tsichtinako said, "and plant them in the earth. Each seed has a purpose. Corn will feed your children. Beans will climb the cornstalks and fix the soil. Squash will spread its leaves to shade the ground and keep the water from evaporating."

The sisters planted. They made prayer sticks — pahos — from reeds and feathers, and placed them at the four corners of their fields. Tsichtinako taught them how to arrange the prayers, how to face each direction, how to speak to the Sun Father and the Earth Mother.

"Name everything," Tsichtinako said. "The naming gives it power. Name the corn and it will grow. Name the rain and it will come. Name the directions — East, South, West, North — and the world will have order."

Iatiku named the plants. Nautsiti named the animals. Together they named the mountains and rivers, the clouds and winds, the stars and the shadows. Each name was a prayer, each prayer a thread connecting the people to the world.

Tsichtinako also taught them to organize their society into clans. The Corn Clan would tend the fields. The Kachina Clan would perform the ceremonies. The Arrow Clan would protect the village. Each clan had its duties, its responsibilities, its place in the web of relationships that held the community together.

Tsichtinako continues to guide the Acoma people invisibly. She is the power of thought itself — the ability to imagine a world that does not yet exist and bring it into being. She is the voice that speaks in the quiet moments, when a farmer looks at the sky and knows it will rain, or a mother holds her child and knows it will grow.

The Acoma people say: "Tsichtinako is always with us. We cannot see her, but we hear her in every thought that brings us closer to the truth."

title: The Kachina Spirits of the Pueblo
summary: Across Pueblo cultures, the Kachinas (Katsinam) are supernatural beings who are the spirits of ancestors, natural forces, and all things in the universe — rocks, stars, animals, and plants. They reside in the San Francisco Peaks (north of Flagstaff, Arizona) and come to the pueblos for six months each year during the winter season. The Kachinas bring rain, fertility, and other blessings through ceremonial dances. Each Kachina has a specific identity, mask, songs, and role in the ceremonial calendar: Crow Mother brings rain, the warrior Kachinas police behavior, and the clown Kachinas expose human pretension through comedy. When a man wears the Kachina mask, he becomes the spirit, not merely a representation. The tihu (Kachina dolls) given to children are teaching objects to help them learn to recognize each Kachina. The Kachinas emerged from the underworld with the people and taught them how to live properly.
source: Various Pueblo oral traditions; Wikipedia: Kachina; Susanne and Jake Page publications
full_text:
Across the mesas and valleys of the Pueblo world, the Kachinas — Katsinam — move in procession through the plazas, their masks painted with the symbols of every living thing. They are the spirits of ancestors, of natural forces, of all things in the universe — rocks, stars, animals, plants.

They reside in the San Francisco Peaks, north of Flagstaff, Arizona, where the snow never fully melts and the pines stand like a cathedral. For six months each year — from winter solstice to July — they leave the peaks and come to the pueblos, bringing rain, fertility, and blessings.

Each Kachina has a specific identity, a mask with its own colors and design, songs that are sung only for it, and a role in the ceremonial calendar. Crow Mother brings rain and protects the children. The warrior Kachinas police behavior, appearing at dances with weapons drawn to discipline those who disrespect the ceremony. The clown Kachinas — the Koyemshi — expose human pretension through comedy, acting outlandish and foolish to remind people not to take themselves too seriously.

When a man wears the Kachina mask, he does not merely represent the spirit — he becomes it. The mask is not a costume but a face. The dancer's identity is subsumed. He speaks with the Kachina's voice. He moves with the Kachina's step. He sees the world through the Kachina's eyes.

The tihu — Kachina dolls — given to children are not toys. They are teaching objects, carved to help children recognize each Kachina and learn its songs and stories. A child who knows the Kachinas is a child who understands the world.

The Kachinas emerged from the underworld with the people. They were there in the beginning, in the darkness, in the climb. They are the oldest friends of the Pueblo people, and their return each winter is as certain as the turning of the earth.

title: The Origin of Corn (Pueblo)
summary: In Pueblo mythology, corn was a gift from the Holy People. The origin story varies between communities but commonly involves a culture hero or deity who obtained corn from the underworld or from supernatural beings. In one version, the Corn Maidens (Blue Corn Maiden, Yellow Corn Maiden, etc.) brought corn to the people. In another, a boy discovered corn growing in a hidden place and brought it to his village. The sacred nature of corn is reflected in its inclusion in nearly every Pueblo ceremony. The different colors of corn (white, yellow, blue, red, black, and speckled) each have spiritual significance and are associated with the six directions. The successful growth of corn depends not only on farming skill but on the proper performance of ceremonies and the people's moral conduct. Corn is understood as a sentient being with which humans have a reciprocal relationship — humans care for corn, and corn nourishes humans.
source: Various Pueblo oral traditions; Frank Cushing, Zuni Folk Tales
full_text:
Corn was not always there. Before the Holy People gave it, the people survived on roots and berries, on whatever the earth offered without being asked. They were hungry, always hungry.

In one tradition, the Corn Maidens brought corn to the people. Blue Corn Maiden was the most beautiful — her body the color of the evening sky, her hair the color of twilight. Yellow Corn Maiden followed, bright as the sun. White Corn Maiden came after, pale as dawn. Red Corn Maiden blushed like sunset. Black Corn Maiden carried the darkness of the deepest earth. And Speckled Corn Maiden, who was different from the others, carried the promise that difference was not deficiency.

They walked among the people, and where their feet touched the ground, corn grew. They taught the women how to grind the kernels into meal, how to make piki bread thin as paper and sweet as honeydew, how to store corn for winter so it would last through the lean months.

In another tradition, a boy discovered corn growing in a hidden place — a cave in the mountains, or a clearing in the forest where the Holy People had planted it. He brought the seeds to his village, and the people planted them in hills, three seeds to a hill, just as the Holy People had instructed.

The different colors of corn each have spiritual significance. White corn belongs to the East and dawn. Yellow to the West and twilight. Blue to the South and midday. Red to the fire. Black to the North and night. Speckled to the center, where all directions meet.

Corn is not merely food. It is a sentient being with which humans have a reciprocal relationship. Humans care for corn — planting, weeding, harvesting — and corn nourishes humans. This reciprocity is reflected in the ceremonies that accompany every stage of corn's life, from the first seed placed in the ground to the last ear stored in the granary.

The successful growth of corn depends not only on farming skill but on the proper performance of ceremonies and the people's moral conduct. A community that fights and lies will find its corn withering. A community that lives in harmony will find its fields heavy with ears.

title: The Jicarilla Apache Creation
summary: In the beginning there was nothing — no earth, no living beings, only darkness, water, and Cyclone the wind. Only the Hactcin (supernatural beings) existed. They made the earth as a woman facing upward and the sky as a man facing downward. Black Hactcin, the most powerful, created the first four-legged animal from clay, then made many animals from its body. He made birds from mud mixed with raindrops. When the animals and birds asked for a companion, Black Hactcin created the first man from turquoise, coral, opal, jet, abalone, and other precious materials brought by the animals. Four times Black Hactcin commanded the man to speak, laugh, and shout, and each time he did. Man dreamed of a woman when lice were placed on his head, and he awoke to find Ancestral Woman beside him. They had children and the people multiplied, living in darkness until the sun and moon were created.
source: Morris Edward Opler, Myths and Tales of the Jicarilla Apache Indians (1938); World History Encyclopedia
full_text:
In the beginning there was nothing — no earth, no living beings, only darkness, water, and Cyclone the wind. Only the Hactcin existed, spirits of immense power who moved through the void like thoughts through a sleeping mind.

Black Hactcin, the most powerful among them, looked into the darkness and said, "There should be a world." He made the earth as a woman facing upward, her body the landscape itself — her breasts the mountains, her hair the forests, her veins the rivers. He made the sky as a man facing downward, his breath the wind, his voice the thunder.

Then Black Hactcin took clay and shaped the first four-legged animal. He breathed into it and it moved. From its body he made many animals — elk from its shoulders, deer from its haunches, rabbits from its ribs. He made birds from mud mixed with raindrops, giving each one a song appropriate to its size and nature.

The animals and birds gathered before Black Hactcin. "We are alone," they said. "We have no companion who thinks as we think, who speaks as we speak."

Black Hactcin listened. He sent the animals to gather sacred materials — turquoise, coral, opal, jet, abalone, white shell, red stone. From these precious substances he shaped the first man, placing in his chest a spark of his own power.

Four times Black Hactcin commanded: "Speak!" Each time the man spoke, his voice grew stronger. Four times: "Laugh!" Each laugh brought more warmth to his body. Four times: "Shout!" And with the fourth shout, the man was alive.

But the man was lonely. Black Hactcin placed lice in his hair, and the man scratched and slept, and in his sleep he dreamed of a woman. He awoke to find Ancestral Woman beside him, shaped from the same sacred materials but arranged differently — not lesser, not greater, but complementary.

Together they had children, and the people multiplied. They lived in darkness, for the sun and moon had not yet been created. But the Hactcin watched, and they knew the time would come when light would be needed.

The story is told to Hopi children to explain the origin of all living things and the sacred partnership between men and women, between humans and animals, between the visible world and the invisible spirits who shaped it.

title: The Emergence (Jicarilla Apache)
summary: In the Jicarilla Apache emergence story, White God of the East made a mountain that grew toward the sky and caused reeds to stand in the center. Four girls twisted the reeds, stopping their growth. Four ladders were made — black, blue, yellow, and variegated — and placed at the mountain. Whirlwind went to the upper world and found much water. Beaver built dams, Badger followed him, and they reported the land was exposed. The people climbed the ladders, starting with black, then blue, then yellow, and finally variegated. After the last ladder wore out, an old woman and old man remained behind. 'You will come back here to me,' one called after the departing people, establishing that the dead return to the underworld. The people moved east along four parallel trails under four chiefs, and leadership alternated between fortunate and unfortunate. They finally settled near Taos. The two who remained became the rulers of the dead.
source: Pliny Earle Goddard, Jicarilla Apache Texts (1911)
full_text:
In the Jicarilla Apache emergence story, White God of the East stood at the edge of the underworld and made a mountain that grew toward the sky like a prayer reaching toward the heavens. In the center of the mountain, reeds stood tall and straight, and four girls twisted them until they stopped growing, creating the means of ascent.

Four ladders were made — one black, one blue, one yellow, one variegated like the hide of a wild pony. They were placed at the mountain's four faces, and the people gathered at the base, looking up toward a world they had never seen.

Whirlwind went first, spiraling upward through the layers of rock and soil. When he reached the upper world, he found much water — a world covered in lakes and rivers, still and silent. He called down to the people: "Come! There is a world above, but it needs tending."

Beaver went next. He built dams in the rivers, diverting the water, and where the water receded, land appeared — brown and rich and waiting. Badger followed him, scratching at the soil, and where he dug, plants began to grow.

The people climbed. They started with the black ladder, moving carefully, children carried on their mothers' backs. Then the blue ladder, where they gained the ability to see — though the light of the upper world was painful after so long in darkness. Then the yellow ladder, where they gained speech, their first words clumsy and halting.

The last ladder was variegated, and it stretched the longest. As the people climbed, the ladder began to wear. An old woman and old man, slow with age, could not make the final rungs. They called up to the departing people: "We will stay here. We will become the rulers of the dead."

And so it was established that all who die must pass through the world of the old woman and old man before they can be reborn into the upper world.

The people moved east along four parallel trails, each led by a chief. They traveled for many days until they reached the place near Taos where the great mountain still stands — a reminder of the climb, of the ladders, of the world below that shaped them.

title: Holy Boy Makes the Sun and Moon
summary: In Apache tradition, Holy Boy was unhappy with the darkness in the underworld and decided to create a sun. He tried many materials without success. Cyclone, spying on the Hactcin, told Holy Boy that White Hactcin had the sun. Holy Boy went to White Hactcin who gave him the sun, and to Black Hactcin who gave him the moon. Black Hactcin taught Holy Boy how to make a sacred sandpainting on a buckskin to hold the sun and moon. Holy Boy, Red Boy, Black Hactcin, and White Hactcin held a ceremony with songs, and White Hactcin released the sun while Black Hactcin released the moon. Light grew stronger as the sun moved from north to south, becoming daylight. The medicine people immediately claimed credit for making the sun, arguing with each other. The Hactcin warned them about eclipses. When an eclipse came, the medicine people could not restore the sun — only the Hactcin could, teaching that humans should not claim divine powers.
source: Morris Edward Opler, Myths and Tales of the Jicarilla Apache Indians (1938); nativeamerican-art.com
full_text:
In the underworld, the Apache people lived in darkness. Holy Boy was unhappy. He was young and restless, and he wanted to see what light looked like, though no one in the underworld could describe it.

"I will make a sun," Holy Boy declared. He tried many materials — clay, which crumbled. Wood, which burned too quickly. Stone, which was too heavy to lift into the sky. Each attempt failed, and the people told him to stop trying.

But Cyclone, who had eyes that could see through walls and across dimensions, had been spying on the Hactcin. He returned to Holy Boy with news: "White Hactcin has the sun. Black Hactcin has the moon. They keep them hidden because they believe humans are not ready."

Holy Boy went to White Hactcin. "Lend me the sun," he said. "My people suffer in darkness."

White Hactcin studied him for a long time. Then he said, "You are not ready. But I will teach you how to hold it." He showed Holy Boy how to make a sacred sandpainting on a buckskin — a pattern of colored sand so precise and powerful it could contain the sun's energy without being consumed.

Holy Boy went to Black Hactcin and asked for the moon. Black Hactcin agreed, and taught him a second sandpainting, silver and gray, to hold the moon's cooler light.

Holy Boy, Red Boy, Black Hactcin, and White Hactcin held a ceremony. They sang four songs. On the fourth song, White Hactcin released the sun from his bundle, and Black Hactcin released the moon. Light blazed across the sky, so bright that the medicine people shielded their eyes.

But immediately the medicine people began to argue. "I made the sun!" cried one. "No, I did!" shouted another. Their argument grew so loud that it reached the ears of the Hactcin.

"Remember this," the Hactcin warned. "There will come a time when the sun disappears. You will think it has been stolen. Do not claim you can bring it back. Only the Hactcin can restore it."

When the first eclipse came, the medicine people panicked. They performed ceremonies, shouted spells, burned sacred herbs. The sun did not return. Only when the Hactcin sang their songs did the light reappear.

The story teaches Apache children that humans should never claim divine powers, and that some forces in the universe are beyond human control.

title: The Apache Origin of the Animals
summary: After the Apaches emerged from the underworld, they traveled south for four days with only seeds to eat. A Raven brought a quiver with meat to a teepee, and when children ate the meat they became instantly fat. The Raven's meat was stolen, and he flew to his eastern mountain home. An Apache boy was transformed into a puppy to spy on the Ravens. Hidden in a young raven's blanket, the puppy watched as an old raven removed a flat stone, revealing an opening to the underworld. Each evening, a buffalo emerged and was eaten. After four days, the boy resumed human shape, descended into the underworld with white and black feathers, and claimed the buffalo. All the animals followed him to the Apache camp. But an old grandmother struck a deer's nose with a fire stick, leaving a white mark and decreeing that animals would avoid humans. Thus the harmony between humans and animals ended, and deer now use their noses to detect humans from afar.
source: Morris Edward Opler, Myths and Tales of the Jicarilla Apache Indians (1938); Margot Edmonds and Ella Clark, Voices of the Winds (2021)
full_text:
After the Apaches emerged from the underworld, they traveled south for four days with nothing to eat but seeds. The children cried from hunger. The elders walked slowly, their steps weighted by emptiness.

Then a Raven appeared, carrying a quiver full of meat on its back. It flew to a teepee and dropped the quiver at the door. The children fell upon the meat, eating greedily, and within moments they were fat — their bellies round, their cheeks full, their laughter returning.

But the meat was stolen. Someone took the Raven's quiver while the bird was searching for more food. The Raven, discovering the theft, flew to his home on the eastern mountain, his cries of outrage echoing across the plains.

An Apache boy volunteered to follow. The spirits transformed him into a puppy — small, brown, unremarkable — so he could sneak into the Raven's camp without suspicion. Hidden among the young ravens, the puppy watched as an old raven removed a flat stone from the ground, revealing an opening to the underworld beneath.

Each evening, a buffalo emerged from the opening. The ravens surrounded it and ate. The puppy watched for four days, memorizing the pattern, the timing, the weakness in the ravens' guard.

On the fourth night, the boy resumed his human shape. He descended into the underworld carrying white and black feathers as talismans. There, in the vast cavern, he found the buffalo — a great herd, grazing in the eternal darkness.

"Come with me," the boy told the buffalo. "The people are hungry. They will honor you and remember you in their ceremonies."

The buffalo agreed, and they followed the boy to the Apache camp. All the animals came too — deer, elk, antelope — for the boy had spoken with authority and the animals trusted him.

But an old grandmother, sitting by the fire, saw a deer approaching too close. She struck its nose with a fire stick, leaving a white mark. "From now on," she decreed, "animals will avoid humans. They will use their noses to detect us from afar."

And so the harmony between humans and animals ended. The deer still carries the white mark on its nose, a reminder of the moment when the easy intimacy between species was broken by a single, irrevocable act.

title: The Gahe: Apache Mountain Spirit Dancers
summary: The Gahe (called Gaan by Western Apache) are the Mountain Spirits, powerful supernatural beings who live inside sacred mountains. The first Mountain Spirit ceremony originated when children of the Sun taught the Apache how to call and honor these spirits. The Mountain Spirits appear as masked dancers wearing distinctive tall, wooden-slat headdresses, with black-and-white body paint and black buckskin kilts. The Gahe ceremony is part of the Girls' Puberty Ceremony (Sunrise Ceremony), the longest and richest Apache ritual. Four Mountain Spirits typically dance together — one for each cardinal direction — along with a clown figure. The dancers move in a syncopated, swaying rhythm to singing and drumming, tracing sacred patterns in the dance ground with their feet. The Gahe are believed to possess healing powers and can cure illness, drive away evil influences, and bring blessings. Sierra Blanca (White Mountain) in New Mexico is considered the spiritual origin place of many Mountain Spirit dance groups.
source: Hoijer, Chiricahua Apache Texts (1938); openpublishing.psu.edu dissertation on Gahe/Gaan
full_text:
The Gahe — the Mountain Spirits — are among the most powerful supernatural beings in Apache tradition. They live inside the sacred mountains, hidden in caves of crystal and stone, and they emerge only when the people call them with the proper songs and offerings.

The first Mountain Spirit ceremony was taught to the Apache by the children of the Sun, who descended from the sky world carrying masks and rattles and the knowledge of how to summon the Gahe. The ceremony was part of the Girls' Puberty Ceremony — the Sunrise Ceremony — the longest and most sacred ritual in Apache life.

When the Gahe appear, they wear distinctive tall headdresses made of wooden slats painted black and white, arranged in patterns that represent the mountains themselves. Their bodies are painted with black and white designs — zigzags for lightning, circles for rain, lines for the paths the spirits travel between the mountain and the sky. They wear black buckskin kilts and carry spruce boughs.

Four Mountain Spirits dance together — one for each cardinal direction: East, South, West, North. Each carries the power of its direction. The eastern spirit brings the light of dawn and the promise of new beginnings. The southern spirit brings the warmth of midday and the power of growth. The western spirit brings the twilight and the wisdom of endings. The northern spirit brings the cold and the strength of endurance.

A clown figure dances with them, interrupting the solemn ceremony with comic gestures and absurd behavior. The clown serves a dual purpose — to remind the people not to take themselves too seriously, and to distract any malevolent spirits that might be lurking nearby.

The dancers move in a syncopated, swaying rhythm to the sound of singing and drumming. They trace sacred patterns on the dance ground with their feet, pressing designs into the dirt that mirror the patterns painted on their bodies.

The Gahe possess healing powers. They can cure illness, drive away evil influences, and bring blessings to the young woman undergoing her transformation into adulthood. When the ceremony is complete, the masks are returned to the mountain, for they are not costumes but faces — the Gahe's own faces, temporarily lent to human dancers.

Sierra Blanca — the White Mountain in New Mexico — is considered the spiritual origin place of many Mountain Spirit dance groups. It is from this mountain that the first Gahe emerged, and it is to this mountain that they return when the ceremony ends.

title: White Painted Woman and Child of the Water (Chiricahua Apache)
summary: In Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache tradition, the creation begins not with an emergence from the underworld but with a great flood that destroyed a malevolent world. After the flood, White Painted Woman (Changing Woman) appeared. She conceived Child of the Water (also known as Killer-of-Enemies in Lipan tradition) from the rays of the Sun. Child of the Water became the dominant culture hero who rids the world of monsters. He is sometimes described as the Sun himself in some versions, and his younger brother is the Wise One. White Painted Woman is identified with the Moon and Thunder. The Girls' Puberty Ceremony reenacts White Painted Woman's first menstruation, when she received her power from the Sun. The ceremony lasts four days and includes the Mountain Spirit dance, blessing the young woman with health, fertility, and a long life, just as White Painted Woman was blessed.
source: Morris Edward Opler, Myths and Tales of the Chiricahua Apache Indians (1994); nativeamerican-art.com
full_text:
In the beginning, there was a world before this one — a world of monsters and darkness, where beings of terrible power stalked the land and devoured anything that dared to live. Then came the great flood, sent by forces older than the monsters themselves, and the old world was washed clean.

After the flood, White Painted Woman appeared. She was Change itself — her body shifting with the seasons, her hair flowing between white and brown and black as the months turned. She was identified with the Moon and with Thunder, for she controlled the cycles that governed all life.

The Sun looked down upon White Painted Woman and was moved. Rays of light touched her, and she conceived. From this union was born Child of the Water — a boy who emerged from the waves already powerful, already knowing his purpose.

Child of the Water became the dominant culture hero of the Chiricahua and Mescalero Apache. He was sometimes described as the Sun himself in another form, and his younger brother, the Wise One, walked beside him.

Together they journeyed through the world, ridding it of the monsters that survived the flood. Child of the Water fought with weapons of lightning and stone, and where he walked, the land healed. Rivers ran clean. Plants grew. The people, who had been hiding in caves and canyons, emerged and followed in his footsteps.

White Painted Woman watched from above, her power flowing through the land like water through roots. Her first menstruation — the moment when her power became fully manifest — was reenacted in the Girls' Puberty Ceremony, the most sacred ritual of Apache life.

The ceremony lasts four days. On the first day, the young woman is painted with white clay, just as White Painted Woman was painted by the Sun. On the second day, she dances with the Mountain Spirits — the Gahe — who bless her with health and fertility. On the third day, she runs eastward toward the rising Sun, carrying a basket of sacred objects. On the fourth day, she is released into womanhood, her transformation complete.

The ceremony ensures that the young woman carries White Painted Woman's power into the future, just as she carried it from the old world into the new.

title: The Lipan Apache Killer-of-Enemies
summary: In Lipan Apache tradition, Killer-of-Enemies is the primary creator and culture hero, identified with the Sun. Killer-of-Enemies seems synonymous with Child-of-the-Water, and he is considered the child of Changing Woman (who is identified as the Moon and Thunder). The Lipan emergence story includes Killer-of-Enemies creating the world and fighting monsters. He has a younger brother called Wise One, who assists him. Killer-of-Enemies journeyed through the world, establishing the proper order of things, teaching the Apache how to hunt, conduct ceremonies, and live properly. He defeated powerful enemies including giant animals and spirits who threatened the people. His battles established the sacred geography of the Lipan Apache world. After completing his work, Killer-of-Enemies departed, promising to return if the people ever truly needed him. The Lipan version shares similarities with the Navajo Hero Twins tradition but emphasizes the role of the single Sun-figure more strongly.
source: Morris Edward Opler, Lipan Apache narratives; nativeamerican-art.com
full_text:
In Lipan Apache tradition, the story of creation begins not with a single act but with a journey — a movement from chaos to order that mirrors the journey every human life must make.

Killer-of-Enemies was the primary creator and culture hero, identified with the Sun. He was the child of Changing Woman, who was herself identified as the Moon and Thunder. From his first breath, Killer-of-Enemies understood his purpose: to make the world safe for the people who would come after him.

He journeyed through the world alone, establishing the proper order of things. Where the rivers ran backwards, he turned them. Where the mountains leaned dangerously, he straightened them. Where monsters lurked in the shadows, he destroyed them with weapons forged from lightning.

He had a younger brother called Wise One, who was smaller but cleverer. Wise One could see things that Killer-of-Enemies missed — the subtle trap, the hidden weakness, the path that looked wrong but was right. Together they were unstoppable.

Killer-of-Enemies defeated powerful enemies — giant animals and spirits who threatened the people. He fought the great serpent who lived in the river and caused floods. He fought the stone monster who blocked the sun. He fought the darkness itself, pushing it back until the sky was clear.

His battles established the sacred geography of the Lipan Apache world. Each mountain he climbed became a sacred site. Each river he crossed became a place of ceremony. The landscape was not merely physical but spiritual — a map of the hero's journey from chaos to order.

After completing his work, Killer-of-Enemies departed. He climbed into the sky and became the Sun, rising each morning to remind the people that darkness is temporary and light always returns.

Before he left, he made a promise: "If you ever truly need me, I will return."

The Lipan Apache remember this promise in their ceremonies. When the Sun Dance is performed, when the sacred fire is lit, when the prayers rise with the smoke, Killer-of-Enemies hears. And though he does not come back in body, his power flows through the light that warms the earth, the fire that cooks the food, the spark that ignites the heart.

title: The White Mountain Apache Creation
summary: In the White Mountain Apache creation myth from Noze (recorded in 1910), a maiden went to the top of a high mountain where the rays of the rising Sun first struck. She raised her skirt and the breath of the Sun entered her. She went up the mountain four mornings, and four times the Sun's breath entered her. This unmarried girl became pregnant, and the people gossiped about her. She gave birth to Naiyenezgani (Monster Slayer) and Tobatc'istcini (Child of the Water). The twins grew rapidly and were given weapons by their father the Sun. They killed the monsters threatening the people, including Naiye' who devoured humans. After proving their power by cutting a tree in half with a thrown weapon, they assured the people that no more monsters would trouble them. They established that a messenger would circle the earth in one day to keep them informed. The twins then resumed their roles as protectors of the people and warriors against evil.
source: Pliny Earle Goddard, Myths and Tales from the White Mountain Apache (1911/Project Gutenberg)
full_text:
In the White Mountain Apache creation myth recorded by Noze in 1910, a maiden climbed to the top of a high mountain where the rays of the rising Sun first struck the earth. She raised her skirt and the breath of the Sun entered her. She went up the mountain four mornings, and four times the Sun's breath entered her.

This unmarried girl became pregnant, and the people gossiped about her. Their whispers were sharp as thorns, and the maiden bore their judgment in silence, for she knew what she carried was not shame but purpose.

She gave birth to twins: Naiyenezgani — Monster Slayer — and Tobatc'istcini — Child of the Water. The boys grew with supernatural speed, their bodies strengthening with each sunrise, their weapons growing heavier in their hands.

Their father the Sun sent them gifts — weapons of power, shields that could turn aside any blow, arrows that flew straighter than any human could shoot. The twins received these gifts and understood their destiny: they were born to rid the world of monsters.

Naiyenezgani was the elder, and he was bold. He walked into the territory of Naiye', a monster that devoured humans, and challenged it to single combat. The earth shook as they fought. Naiye' was enormous, its teeth like daggers, its claws like scythes. But Naiyenezgani's weapon found its mark, and the monster fell.

Tobatc'istcini was quieter but no less powerful. He controlled water — he could call rain from clear skies and summon floods from dry riverbeds. Where his brother destroyed, he healed. Together they were complete.

After proving their power by cutting a great tree in half with a thrown weapon — a feat that left the people speechless with awe — the twins assured the village that no more monsters would trouble them.

They established that a messenger would circle the earth in one day to keep them informed of any new threats. The messenger was the wind itself, carrying news from every corner of the world to the twins' ears.

The twins then resumed their roles as protectors, watching from the sun and the moon, ready to descend if the people ever needed them again. The story explains the origin of the Apache Girls' Puberty Ceremony and the sacred relationship between the people and the Sun.

title: The Awonawilona Creation (Zuni)
summary: In the Zuni creation myth recorded by Frank Cushing, only Áwonawílona, the All-Father, Maker and Container of All, existed in the beginning. He made himself into the Sun Father (Yatoka). The mist clouds formed into the Great Waters, from which Earth Mother (Áwitelin Tsíta) and Sky Father (Ápoyan Ta'chu) emerged. Together they conceived all men and creatures in the four-fold womb of the world. The Sun Father and Earth Mother brought forth the Twin Children of the Sun — the brothers Ko'wituma and Wats'usi (the Ahayuta twins) — who were given sacred knowledge, caps, bows, arrows, and shields to have dominion over all beings. The twins descended into the first underworld (Ánosin Téhuli) and formed a ladder for people to ascend to the second cave-world (Moss World, K'ólin Téhuli), then to the third (World of Mud, Áwisho Téhuli), and finally the fourth cave-world (Wing World, Tépahaian Téhuli), where the twins taught men the ways of life before they entered the Daylight World (Ték'ohaian Úlahnane).
source: Frank Cushing, Outlines of Zuni Creation Myths (1896); The Mythic World of the Zuni (1988)
full_text:
Only Áwonawílona — the All-Father, Maker and Container of All — existed in the beginning. There was no earth, no sky, no beings of any kind. Only the All-Father, vast and formless, moving through himself like a thought moving through a mind.

Áwonawílona made himself into the Sun Father — Yatoka — and his light became the first thing that existed beyond himself. The mist clouds, stirred by his light, formed into the Great Waters, dark and deep and churning.

From the Great Waters emerged Earth Mother — Áwitelin Tsíta — and Sky Father — Ápoyan Ta'chu. They were separate but connected, like two hands belonging to the same body. Together they conceived all men and creatures in the four-fold womb of the world — a place of gestation where life formed in darkness before emerging into light.

The Sun Father and Earth Mother brought forth the Twin Children of the Sun — Ko'wituma and Wats'usi, the Ahayuta twins. The twins were given sacred knowledge, caps of power, bows and arrows, and shields forged from morning light. They were given dominion over all beings.

The twins descended into the first underworld — Ánosin Téhuli — and formed a ladder of reeds for the people to climb. The people ascended to the second cave-world, the Moss World — K'ólin Téhuli — where the walls were green and damp and the air smelled of rain. Then to the third, the World of Mud — Áwisho Téhuli — where the ground sucked at their feet and the sky was low and gray. Then to the fourth, the Wing World — Tépahaian Téhuli — where the twins taught men the ways of life: how to plant, how to hunt, how to pray.

Finally the people entered the Daylight World — Ték'ohaian Úlahnane — where the Sun Father's light was blinding after so long in darkness. They wept, and where their tears fell, sunflowers grew.

The Zuni say that the journey through the four worlds is not merely a story of the past but a map of the soul's journey through life — from the darkness of ignorance to the light of understanding, guided by the twins who remember the way.

title: The Zuni People Emerge into Daylight
summary: In Ruth Benedict's version of the Zuni emergence, people dwelt in total darkness deep in the fourth world. Awonawilona, the Sun, took pity on them. His two sons, the bow priests, located the opening to the fourth world in the southwest and led the people upward. They planted seeds that grew into pine, spruce, silver spruce, and aspen. Each tree became a prayer stick stretched to the next world. The people climbed through four worlds, each time finding themselves still incomplete. They had no mouths, anuses, or fingers; their hands and feet were webbed, and they had horns and tails. In the first world (the one below daylight), they could finally see — they were covered in filth and slime. The bow priests cut mouths into their faces with a knife sharpened on a red whetstone, then cut anuses with a soot-blackened knife. They cut fingers and toes, and finally removed the people's horns and tails. When the people emerged into sunlight at last, they cried from the brightness, and sunflowers grew where their tears fell.
full_text:
People dwelt in total darkness deep in the fourth world, a place of stone and shadow where the air was thick with the breath of those who had lived and died in the caves below. Awonawilona, the Sun, looked down and took pity on them.

His two sons — the bow priests — located the opening to the fourth world in the southwest corner of the sky. They planted seeds that grew into pine, spruce, silver spruce, and aspen, each tree stretching upward until its crown pierced the floor of the world above. These trees became prayer sticks, each one stretched to the next world like fingers reaching for a hand.

The people gathered at the base of the trees and began to climb. They were not yet fully formed — they had no mouths, no anuses, no fingers. Their hands and feet were webbed like frogs', and horns and tails protruded from their bodies. They were beings of potential, not yet complete.

In the first world below daylight, they could finally see. They looked at themselves and recoiled — they were covered in filth and slime, their bodies misshapen and strange. The bow priests took pity on them.

With a knife sharpened on a red whetstone, the bow priest cut mouths into their faces. The people screamed — their first sound, raw and terrified and beautiful. With a soot-blackened knife, he cut anuses. He cut fingers and toes, separating the webbed stumps into individual digits. Finally, he removed their horns and tails, which fell to the ground and became the first stones.

When the people emerged into the sunlight at last, they cried from the brightness. Their tears fell on the dry earth and sunflowers grew where they landed — golden faces turning toward the light that had nearly blinded them.

The Zuni tell this story to remind themselves that they were not always as they are now. The process of becoming human is ongoing — every generation must climb a little higher, see a little more clearly, shed a little more of what is no longer needed.

title: The Trial of Lovers: Maiden of Matsaki
summary: A Zuni folk tale about the beautiful Maiden of Matsaki, desired by many suitors. After the war god Áhaiyúta and his brother courted her, they discovered she was cruel — she had let the children of Field-mice die of cold while she gambled. The gods punished her but also showed compassion for the helpless mouse children, taking them to their grandmother who raised them. The story teaches that even gods can be cruel, but those who find helpless children must care for them. The Maiden of Matsaki's story illustrates Zuni values about compassion, the consequences of cruelty, and the duty to care for orphans and vulnerable children. It also demonstrates that even divine beings are subject to moral judgment and that mercy can follow justice.
full_text:
The Maiden of Matsaki was beautiful — so beautiful that the war god Áhaiyúta and his brother Mátsailéma traveled from Thunder Mountain to court her. They arrived expecting to find a woman worthy of divine attention.

But the Maiden of Matsaki was cruel. The brothers discovered that she had let the children of Field-mice die of cold while she gambled with turquoise and shell beads. The mouse babies — tiny, naked, helpless — had cried through the night, and the Maiden had turned up the heat of her fire and laughed.

The war gods were enraged. Áhaiyúta struck the Maiden with his lightning bolt, and Mátsailéma sealed her fate with his thunder stone. The earth opened and swallowed her, and she was never seen again.

But the war gods did not stop there. They went to the place where the mouse children had died and found them still warm, their tiny hearts still beating. Despite their terrible nature — the war gods were known for their cruelty as much as their courage — they gathered the mouse babies and carried them to their grandmother on Thunder Mountain.

The grandmother took the orphaned mice and raised them. She fed them cornmeal and warm milk, she wove tiny blankets for their bodies, she sang them songs that only grandmothers know. The mice grew strong and healthy, and they never forgot the kindness of the war gods' grandmother.

"Even gods can be cruel," the story teaches. "But those who find helpless children must care for them. This is the law that binds the powerful to the weak, the divine to the mortal, the sky to the earth."
