The Maiden of Matsaki's story is told to Zuni children as a warning against cruelty and gambling, and as a reassurance that the gods themselves — for all their power — are subject to moral judgment. Mercy can follow justice, and the cruelest beings can perform acts of tenderness.

title: The Youth and His Eagle
summary: A Zuni story about a young boy who raised an eagle and developed a deep spiritual bond with the bird. The eagle became his protector and provider, bringing him gifts from the sky world. However, jealous members of the village conspired against the boy and his eagle. The eagle, being a sacred creature connected to the Sun Father, possessed supernatural powers and could communicate with the spirit world. Through his relationship with the eagle, the boy learned important spiritual lessons about power, responsibility, and the consequences of greed. The eagle eventually returned to the sky world, but it left the boy with sacred knowledge that benefited his people. The story emphasizes the Zuni belief in the spiritual power of birds and the importance of maintaining proper relationships with animal spirits.
full_text:
In the days when the Zuni people were learning the ways of the world, a young boy found an eaglet blown from its nest by a storm. The chick was barely alive, its feathers matted, its eyes clouded with fever. The boy carried it home and nursed it with cornmeal and water, whispering prayers to the Sun Father as he worked.

The eagle grew. It became enormous — its wingspan wider than a man's outstretched arms, its feathers the color of midnight with streaks of gold. And it was no ordinary eagle, for the boy had raised it with prayers and offerings, and the Sun Father had blessed the bond between them.

The eagle brought the boy gifts from the sky world — feathers that glowed with inner light, stones that held the warmth of the sun, seeds that grew into plants no one had ever seen. The boy shared these gifts with his people, and they marveled.

But jealousy poisoned the village. Some men whispered that the boy had made a pact with dark spirits, that the eagle was a demon in disguise. They conspired against the boy and his eagle, setting traps and laying ambushes.

The eagle, being a sacred creature connected to the Sun Father, possessed supernatural powers. It could communicate with the spirit world, seeing things that human eyes could not perceive. When the conspirators attacked, the eagle rose into the sky and called down lightning to protect its foster parent.

Through his relationship with the eagle, the boy learned important spiritual lessons — that power comes with responsibility, that greed destroys what love creates, that the spirits watch over those who maintain proper relationships with the natural world.

The eagle eventually returned to the sky world, for it was a being of the air and could not remain forever on the ground. But before it left, it gave the boy sacred knowledge — the songs and ceremonies that the Zuni still perform to honor the spirits of the birds who carry prayers to the Sun Father.

The story emphasizes the Zuni belief in the spiritual power of birds and the importance of maintaining proper relationships with animal spirits — relationships built not on conquest but on care.

title: The Poor Turkey Girl
summary: A Zuni Cinderella-like story about a poor girl who was mistreated by her community and found companionship among the wild turkeys. The turkeys, taking pity on her, transformed her appearance with beautiful clothing and feathers so she could attend a sacred dance at the village. She danced beautifully and won the heart of a young man, but had to flee before dawn to return the turkeys' gifts. She lost one of her turkey-feather garments, which the young man used to find her. However, when the turkeys discovered she had not properly thanked them or kept her promises, they abandoned her and took back their gifts. The girl was left with nothing, learning that ingratitude and broken promises have consequences. The story teaches Zuni values of humility, gratitude, and keeping one's word.
full_text:
She was poor — so poor that her clothing was woven from bark and the ash of burned yucca leaves. The other girls of Matsaki mocked her ragged appearance and the scars on her hands from tending fires that were never hers to tend. But the turkeys of the high desert knew her. They watched her from the rocks and brush, and they saw what the people did not — that she was kind, that she was gentle, that she sang to them when she thought no one was listening.

One morning, the turkeys gathered around her as she gathered firewood. They draped their finest feathers across her shoulders, wove them into her hair, and wrapped her in plumage so beautiful it burned like sunset against her skin. The turkeys transformed her appearance entirely — she was radiant, unrecognizable, stunning.

She went to the sacred dance at the village. The people stared. A young man saw her and was captivated. They danced together through the evening, their movements fluid and synchronized as if they had practiced together for years.

But the turkeys had given her one condition: she must return before dawn and bring back every feather. The girl promised. But she was so happy, so alive with the young man's attention, that she lost track of the hours.

She fled at dawn, tearing herself away from the dance, but in her haste she lost one of her turkey-feather garments. The young man found it. He searched the village for the woman who had worn it, but no one recognized her without the turkeys' gift.

When the turkeys discovered she had not kept her promise — that she had lost their gift and had not returned the feathers — they abandoned her. They took back every strand and plume, and the girl was left standing in the dirt in her old rags, more ragged than before.

The story teaches Zuni values of humility, gratitude, and keeping one's word. The turkeys' generosity was a test, and the girl failed it. In Zuni tradition, gifts from the natural world are never free — they come with obligations, and those who break their word lose everything.

title: How the Summer Birds Came
summary: A Zuni myth explaining the origin of small summer birds. In the days of the ancients, there were no little birds — only large birds like eagles, crows, and hawks. A Zuni man discovered a magical bundle of feathers left by the spirits. When he walked into a field of flowers, the bundle began to flutter, and small wings flew out from it, becoming the Sacred Birds of Summerland. The feathers were made living by the lives of the birds that had once borne them, and they came to life again in the environment of flowers and summer that they had loved. This is why, according to Zuni tradition, there are jaybirds, sparrows, finches, willow-birds, and all the beautiful little birds that herald summer and hover over flowers. The story concludes with the storyteller noting that Zunis have books too — not with marks but with words in their hearts from the ancients.
full_text:
In the days of the ancients, before the world had settled into its final form, there were no small birds — only the great ones. Eagles soared above the mountains with wings that cast shadows across entire valleys. Crows blackened the sky in murder-flocks. Hawks patrolled the thermals with deadly precision. But the flowers in the meadows had no companions, no voices, no wings to carry their pollen.

A Zuni man named Kothluwalawa discovered a bundle of feathers left by the spirits in a place where the sunflowers grew tallest. The feathers were not ordinary — they shimmered with colors that had no names, and when the wind touched them, they hummed with a sound like distant singing.

Kothluwalawa carried the bundle into the field of flowers. The sunflowers turned toward him as if expecting something. He opened the bundle, and the feathers began to flutter. They shook and trembled and rose from his hands like living things.

Small wings unfolded. Tiny bodies formed from the energy of the feathers themselves. Beaks opened and sang. The Sacred Birds of Summerland were born — jaybirds with crests of blue, sparrows brown as earth, finches yellow as corn silk, willow-birds green as spring leaves.

They had been made living by the lives of the great birds that had once borne them. Each feather contained the memory of flight, the instinct of the nest, the knowledge of migration. And they came to life again in the environment of flowers and summer that they had loved.

The little birds took their places among the flowers, hovering over the blossoms, singing songs that made the petals open wider. They carried pollen from flower to flower, and the meadows grew more beautiful with each passing season.

The Zuni say that this is why there are so many kinds of small birds — each one born from a different great bird's feather, each one carrying a different memory of the sky. And they say that Zunis have books too — not with marks on paper but with words in their hearts, passed down from the ancients who first told this story.

title: The Serpent of the Sea (Kolowisi)
summary: A Zuni legend about Kolowisi, the great horned water serpent that lives in the sacred lake. A maiden from Zuni went to the lake and was seen by Kolowisi, who took her as his bride beneath the waters. She lived with the serpent in his underwater home, where there was no light but she was treated well and given abundance. The people mourned her loss and held ceremonies to bring her back. Eventually, Kolowisi allowed her to return to the surface, but she was transformed and carried spiritual power from her time in the serpent's realm. She brought knowledge of healing ceremonies and water-songs back to the Zuni people. Kolowisi is generally a benevolent figure, associated with water, fertility, and the life-giving forces of the natural world. The serpent's horn symbolizes power, and offerings are made to Kolowisi during ceremonies asking for rain.
source: Frank Cushing, Zuñi Folk Tales (1901); various Zuni oral traditions
full_text:
The sacred lake lay at the heart of Zuni country, its waters so clear that you could see the stones at the bottom thirty feet below the surface. The people came there to pray, to draw water for their ceremonies, and to listen to the silence that hung over the water like a held breath.

A maiden from the village went to the lake one evening to gather water in her olla. She knelt at the edge, her reflection merging with the sky in the still water, and she did not notice the shadow moving beneath her — the great horned water serpent Kolowisi, whose body was as long as a cottonwood tree and whose scales shimmered like polished turquoise.

Kolowisi saw the maiden and desired her — not with the desire of a predator but with the longing of a being who had lived alone for centuries beneath the water. He rose from the lake, his horn catching the last light of the sun, and he spoke to her in a voice like water rushing over stones.

The maiden was terrified at first. But Kolowisi treated her with gentleness. He gave her gifts from the underwater world — pearls that glowed in darkness, shells that sang when held to the ear, stones that held the memory of every rain that had ever fallen into the lake.

She descended with him beneath the water, where there was no light but everything was illuminated by the serpent's own radiance. She lived in his underwater home for a time, learning the water-songs and the healing ceremonies that the serpent spirits know.

The people mourned her loss. They performed ceremonies for many days, calling her back to the surface. Kolowisi, moved by their grief, allowed her to return. She emerged transformed — her hair flowing like water, her eyes holding the depth of the lake.

She brought knowledge back to the Zuni — songs for calling rain, ceremonies for healing the sick, and the understanding that the water spirits are allies, not enemies. Kolowisi is generally a benevolent figure, associated with water, fertility, and the life-giving forces of the natural world. His horn symbolizes power, and offerings are made to him during ceremonies asking for rain.

title: The Maiden of the Yellow Rocks
summary: A Zuni story about the beautiful daughter of the high priest of the Village of the Yellow Rocks. Despite her beauty, her pride and coldness drove away suitors. The twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, living with their grandmother on Thunder Mountain, decided to court her. They appeared as ugly pygmies — boys who never grew to manhood. Meanwhile, the Field-mice, who were prolific and needed wool for their families, gambled with the gods. The mice lost everything, including the wool for their nests, and their babies died of cold. The war gods, despite their terrible nature, took the orphaned mouse babies to their grandmother, who raised them. The story teaches the Zuni value of caring for helpless children — if even the cruelest gods showed mercy, surely humans must care for abandoned infants and orphans.
full_text:
The beautiful daughter of the high priest of the Village of the Yellow Rocks was so stunning that men traveled from distant pueblos just to catch a glimpse of her. But her beauty was matched by her pride — she dismissed every suitor who came, mocking their gifts and their ambitions.

The twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, living on Thunder Mountain with their grandmother, heard of her cruelty. They decided to visit, not to court her but to test her character.

They appeared as ugly pygmies — small, misshapen boys who never grew to manhood, their faces marked with the scars of a hundred battles. The people of Yellow Rocks stared. The beautiful daughter laughed at them.

Meanwhile, the Field-mice who lived in the walls of the pueblo were in desperate need of wool for their nests. They gambled with the pygmy strangers — a game of chance played with marked sticks. The mice lost everything, including the wool they had gathered for winter. Without wool, their babies would freeze.

The beautiful daughter knew this. She saw the mouse babies shivering in their nests, their tiny bodies barely covered by thin bark and dry grass. She did nothing. She returned to her chamber and admired her reflection in a polished stone.

But the war gods — for all their terrible reputation — took action. They gathered the orphaned mouse babies in their arms and carried them to their grandmother on Thunder Mountain. The grandmother, old and wise and fierce in her tenderness, took the mice and raised them as her own.

She wove wool from her own hair for their blankets. She ground cornmeal into their tiny bowls. She sang them the songs that grandmothers sing when the fire is low and the night is long.

The mice grew strong and grateful, and they never forgot who had saved them. But the beautiful daughter of Yellow Rocks — she who had laughed at the suffering of the small — lost everything. Her beauty faded. Her pride turned to dust.

The story teaches the Zuni value of caring for helpless children. If even the cruelest war gods showed mercy to the weakest of beings, surely humans must care for abandoned infants and orphans. Beauty without compassion is a hollow shell.

title: The Foster-Child of the Deer
summary: A Zuni story about a child abandoned in the wilderness who was adopted and raised by deer. The deer taught the child to live in harmony with nature, to understand the language of animals, and to know the sacred plants of the forest. When the child grew up and encountered human hunters, a conflict arose between the human and deer worlds. The deer-mother bid farewell to her foster-child, who was torn between two worlds — the human world of their birth and the deer world of their raising. The story teaches respect for deer and the proper relationship between hunters and prey. It is connected to Zuni hunting rituals and the belief that deer willingly give themselves to respectful hunters who perform the correct ceremonies and prayers. The foster-child became a mediator between humans and deer, teaching people the rituals that honor the spirits of slain animals.
full_text:
A child was abandoned in the wilderness — left at the edge of the forest where the piñon trees grew thick and the shadows deepened. Whether the child was abandoned by cruel parents or lost by desperate ones, the story does not say. What matters is what happened next.

A doe, heavy with young and recently bereaved of her own fawn, heard the baby crying. She came through the underbrush, her hooves silent on the pine needles, and she nuzzled the child with her warm nose. The baby stopped crying. The doe lay down beside it and gave it her warmth through the cold desert night.

When morning came, the doe led the child to a hidden valley where water ran clear and the grass grew green even in summer. She nursed the child as she would have nursed her own fawn. The child grew fat and strong on deer's milk, learning to walk on all fours before learning to walk upright.

Years passed. The child — now a young man — learned the language of animals from the deer. He understood the warning in a hawk's cry, the invitation in a rabbit's drumming, the sorrow in a wolf's howl. He knew the sacred plants of the forest — which ones healed, which ones harmed, which ones opened the mind to visions.

Then the human hunters came. They walked into the hidden valley with bows drawn, seeking game. The young man stood between them and his foster mother. "She is not prey," he told them. "She is my mother."

The hunters were confused. They saw a human boy standing among deer, and they did not understand.

The doe-mother bid farewell to her foster-child. She touched her nose to his forehead one last time, then turned and led her herd into the trees. The young man was torn — the human world of his birth pulling him one way, the deer world of his raising pulling him another.

He became a mediator between humans and deer, teaching people the rituals that honor the spirits of slain animals. He showed them how to offer cornmeal and prayer sticks before a hunt, how to thank the deer's spirit, how to waste nothing of what the deer gives.

This is the origin of Zuni hunting ceremonies — the teaching that all life is sacred and must be taken with gratitude. The deer willingly give themselves to respectful hunters who perform the correct ceremonies, for the deer remember the boy who was raised among them and who taught humans to deserve their sacrifice.

title: The Boy Hunter Who Never Sacrificed to the Deer
summary: A Zuni story about a boy who was an excellent hunter but never performed the proper sacrifices or prayers to the spirits of the deer he killed. As a result, the deer spirits became angry. The boy's disrespectful hunting caused supernatural consequences — his kills became tainted, and he began to have bad luck. The spirits of the deer he had killed without proper ceremony confronted him. To make amends, the boy had to learn the proper rituals of the hunt, including making prayer sticks, offering cornmeal, and speaking words of gratitude to the deer's spirit. This story explains the origin of the Society of Rattlesnakes, which has the power to heal snakebites and conduct ceremonies that maintain balance between humans and animals. The story reinforces the Zuni teaching that all life is sacred and must be taken with gratitude and proper ceremony.
full_text:
He was an excellent hunter — the best in his village, perhaps the best in all Zuni country. His arrow never missed. His tracking was uncanny. He could read the signs of deer the way a priest reads the stars.

But he never performed the proper sacrifices. He never offered cornmeal to the spirits of the deer he killed. He never spoke words of gratitude over the body of the animal. He took without asking, killed without ceremony, and he wasted what he did not eat.

At first, nothing seemed wrong. The deer came easily, as they always had. But the spirits of the deer noticed. They gathered in the shadow world beneath the earth and spoke of the hunter's disrespect.

The consequences came slowly, then all at once. The hunter's luck soured. His arrows flew wide. His legs grew heavy on the chase. The deer he wounded escaped into the brush and died where he could not find them. His kills became tainted — the meat rotted overnight, the hides cracked and split.

Then the spirits of the deer he had killed without proper ceremony came to him in dreams. They stood around his sleeping body, their antlers crowned with starlight, their eyes holding the sorrow of beings who had given their lives without being honored.

"You took us without thanks," they said. "You ate us without prayer. You wore our skins without acknowledging our sacrifice. The balance is broken."

The hunter woke in terror. He went to the medicine people and told them what he had seen. They taught him the proper rituals — how to make prayer sticks from willow and feathers, how to scatter cornmeal at the four directions, how to speak words of gratitude to the deer's spirit before drawing the bow.

He performed every ceremony with sincerity. Gradually, his luck returned. The deer came again. The meat was sweet, the hides supple.

This story explains the origin of the Society of Rattlesnakes, which has the power to heal snakebites and conduct ceremonies that maintain balance between humans and animals. The story reinforces the Zuni teaching that all life is sacred and must be taken with gratitude and proper ceremony — for even the spirits of the dead demand justice.

title: Átahsaia the Cannibal Demon
summary: A Zuni legend about Átahsaia, a giant cannibal demon who terrorized the people. Átahsaia is described as a huge, monstrous being with burning eyes and an insatiable hunger for human flesh, especially children. The demon would descend from the mountains to raid villages, carrying off victims in a large basket on its back. The twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma confronted Átahsaia to save their people. They used their divine weapons and cunning to defeat the demon. In some versions, they tricked Átahsaia into falling into a pit of fire or into a canyon. The battle between the divine twins and the cannibal demon represents the eternal struggle between good and evil, order and chaos. After Átahsaia's defeat, the people were safe, but the story reminds Zuni children to be cautious and to respect the boundary between the civilized pueblo and the wild lands where dangerous spirits dwell.
source: Frank Cushing, Zuñi Folk Tales (1901); Wikipedia: Zuni mythology
full_text:
Átahsaia was a giant — so tall his head scraped the clouds, so wide his shadow covered entire villages. His eyes burned like coals, and his breath smelled of blood and old death. He lived in the mountains above Zuni country, and when hunger drove him down from his cave, the people hid.

He carried a basket on his back — a great woven thing as large as a house, lined with the bones of those he had already taken. Children were his favorite. He could smell them from miles away, could hear their heartbeats through the stone walls of their homes.

The people prayed to the twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma. "Save us," they cried. "Átahsaia grows bolder. He comes closer each night. Soon there will be no one left."

The twins climbed Thunder Mountain and looked down at the monster. They saw the trail of destruction — flattened houses, trampled fields, the scattered belongings of those Átahsaia had carried away.

Áhaiyúta spoke first. "We cannot fight him with weapons. He is too large. We must use cunning."

Mátsailéma agreed. They devised a plan. They built a great pit in the path Átahsaia always traveled, covering it with branches and earth so it looked like solid ground. At the bottom of the pit, they placed burning coals.

Then they sent a child — a brave girl with quick legs — to the edge of Átahsaia's cave. She danced and shouted until the monster rose from his sleep and charged. Átahsaia ran with terrifying speed, the ground shaking with each step.

The girl led him toward the pit. At the last moment, she leaped aside. Átahsaia, unable to stop, plunged into the pit. The coals erupted around him. He burned and thrashed, his roar shaking the mountains.

The twins stood at the edge and struck him with their lightning weapons until he lay still. His body fell into the canyon, and where he lay, the earth became scorched and red — a reminder of the monster who once terrorized the people.

After Átahsaia's defeat, the people were safe. But they remembered the lesson: the boundary between the civilized pueblo and the wild lands is not merely physical but spiritual. The wilderness holds dangerous spirits, and respect for that danger is the first protection against it.

title: How the Coyote Joined the Dance of the Burrowing-Owls
summary: A Zuni trickster tale about Coyote who stumbled upon a sacred dance of the Burrowing-owls. The owls were performing a ceremonial dance in the moonlight, and Coyote, ever the opportunist, wanted to join. At first the owls were suspicious, but Coyote insisted he could dance as well as they. He joined their circle, but his clumsy, undisciplined dancing disrupted the sacred ceremony. The owls, annoyed by his foolish behavior, played a trick on him. When Coyote tired and wanted to leave, he found that the owls' dance had placed him under a spell — he could not stop dancing. He was forced to dance until dawn, exhausted and humiliated. The story explains why coyotes are often seen running in circles or acting strangely at night. It teaches the Zuni lesson that not all dances are for everyone and that sacred ceremonies require proper preparation and respect.
full_text:
Coyote was walking through the desert at dusk when he heard music — a strange, rhythmic chanting that rose and fell with the wind. He followed the sound to a flat clearing where the Burrowing-owls had gathered in a circle beneath the full moon.

They were performing a ceremonial dance — their small bodies swaying in perfect unison, their round eyes half-closed in trance. The moonlight painted their feathers silver, and the air around them shimmered with spiritual power.

Coyote watched from behind a rock, his ears forward, his tail swishing. He wanted to join. He always wanted to join.

"Let me dance with you," he called out.

The owls stopped. They looked at Coyote with their great amber eyes. "This is a sacred ceremony," the eldest owl said. "It requires preparation, prayer, and purity of heart."

"I have all of those things," Coyote lied, stepping into the clearing. He began to dance — but his steps were clumsy, his rhythm erratic. Where the owls moved like water, Coyote lurched like a drunk. Where the owls chanted in harmony, Coyote howled off-key.

The ceremony began to unravel. The shimmer in the air dimmed. The moonlight flickered. The other owls grew agitated.

The eldest owl whispered to the others, and they devised a trick. They told Coyote he must dance faster, harder, with more passion. Coyote, puffed up with pride, danced wildly, spinning and jumping and kicking up dust.

But the owls' chant had placed him under a spell. The harder he danced, the more he couldn't stop. His legs moved of their own accord. His arms flailed. His tongue hung from his mouth.

He danced through the night. He danced until the stars faded and the dawn crept across the horizon. He danced until his legs turned to wood and his breath came in ragged gasps. Only when the sun fully rose did the spell break, and Coyote collapsed in the dust, exhausted and humiliated.

The owls had already returned to their burrows. Coyote lay alone in the clearing, his fur matted with sweat, his dignity in tatters. This is why coyotes are often seen running in circles or acting strangely at night — they are still dancing the owls' dance, still trapped in the spell of their own vanity.

title: The Coyote and the Locust
summary: A Zuni trickster story about Coyote who heard Locust singing and playing his flute on a piñon branch. Coveting the song, Coyote demanded Locust teach it to him. Locust, wary of Coyote's intentions, tricked him by shedding his skin and placing a stone inside the empty shell on the branch. When Coyote returned and Locust refused to sing again, Coyote angrily bit the locust shell — but it was actually a stone wrapped in skin. Coyote broke his teeth, which is why coyotes have broken-looking teeth to this day. The story explains both the physical characteristic of coyotes and warns against anger, impatience, and not minding one's own business. Locusts, for their part, still sometimes shed their skins and leave their likenesses on trees to fool predators.
full_text:
Coyote was sitting on a rock, feeling sorry for himself, when he heard a beautiful melody — a song so pure and sweet that it made the desert flowers open their petals even though it was nearly dark.

He followed the sound to a piñon tree where a Locust sat on a branch, playing a tiny flute made from a reed. The music flowed from the Locust like water from a spring, filling the evening with gold.

Coyote listened until the song ended. Then he said, "Teach me that song."

The Locust, who was wise in the ways of Coyote, said carefully, "This song is not for everyone. It was given to me by the spirits, and it carries power."

"I am not everyone," Coyote said, drawing himself up to his full height. "I am Coyote. Teach me."

The Locust sighed. "Very well. But you must promise to treat the song with respect."

Coyote promised. But his promise was as hollow as a dried gourd, and the Locust knew it.

The Locust said, "First, you must shed your skin and leave it on this branch while you learn. It is the way of the ceremony."

Coyote, impatient and greedy, shed his skin without hesitation. He left it draped over the branch, where the Locust placed a small stone inside the empty skin, giving it the shape and weight of a sleeping Coyote.

Then the Locust flew away, his tiny wings carrying him into the gathering dark.

Coyote waited. And waited. When the Locust did not return, Coyote grew angry. He bit the skin on the branch, expecting to feel the Locust's flesh.

He hit the stone instead. His teeth shattered against it — not all of them, but enough. Enough to leave him with the broken, crooked teeth that coyotes carry to this day.

The Locust, watching from a safe distance, shed his own skin and left it hanging on a tree. To this day, locusts sometimes leave their empty shells on branches, a reminder of the night they tricked Coyote and kept their song for themselves.

title: The Prairie-Dogs and Their Priest the Burrowing-Owl
summary: A Zuni story about a village of Prairie-dogs who were suffering from a drought. They held a council and decided to ask their grandfather, the Burrowing-owl who lived on top of their mountain, for help. The Burrowing-owl, a powerful priest, agreed to intercede with the rain gods. He collected a foul-smelling beetle and instructed his wife to cook beans. He placed the beetle and beans in a bag and climbed to the top of his mountain. As the storm clouds gathered, the Owl struck the bag with a stick, releasing such a terrible odor that even the Rain-gods themselves fled in retreat. The clouds scattered and the sky cleared. The Prairie-dogs emerged from their holes and cheered their grandfather, the Burrowing-owl. The story explains why burrowing-owls make their nests in prairie-dog holes — they have been friends ever since. The Burrowing-owl's control over the weather demonstrates the Zuni belief that spiritual power can reside in unexpected beings.
full_text:
The Prairie-dogs were suffering. The rain had not fallen for many weeks, and their burrows were dry as bone. The streams that once ran through their territory had shrunk to trickles, then to dust. The young were thin, their ribs showing through their fur.

The elder Prairie-dogs called a council. They gathered in the largest burrow, their round eyes reflecting the dim light of a fire made from dried sage. "We must ask our grandfather for help," the eldest said.

Their grandfather was the Burrowing-owl, a powerful priest who lived on top of the mountain above the prairie-dog town. He was old and wise, and he had friends among the Rain-gods.

The Prairie-dogs sent a delegation — their fastest runner and their most eloquent speaker — to climb the mountain and deliver their petition. The Burrowing-owl listened patiently, his great amber eyes unblinking.

"I will help you," he said. "But the Rain-gods are difficult to move. They require persuasion."

The owl gathered his supplies. He found a beetle — large, dark, and foul-smelling — and placed it carefully in a bag. Then he instructed his wife to cook beans, the stronger the better. He added the bean broth to the bag with the beetle.

He climbed to the top of his mountain with the bag over his shoulder. The sky was clear, the sun blazing. Not a cloud in sight.

The Burrowing-owl sat at the summit and began his ceremony. He sang the songs that move the Rain-gods. He played his rattle. And when the storm clouds finally gathered — dark and heavy and promising — he struck the bag with a stick.

The smell that erupted from the bag was beyond foul. It was a smell so terrible that the Rain-gods themselves recoiled. They scattered in every direction, fleeing the stench, and as they fled, they dropped the rain they had been carrying.

The downpour was sudden and violent. It hammered the prairie, filling the streams, flooding the burrows, turning the dust to mud. The Prairie-dogs emerged from their holes and cheered, dancing in the rain, their voices carried up the mountain to their grandfather.

The Burrowing-owl smiled. He climbed down from the summit, his bag empty, his mission accomplished.

This is why burrowing-owls make their nests in prairie-dog holes — they have been friends ever since that day. And the Burrowing-owl's control over the weather demonstrates the Zuni belief that spiritual power can reside in unexpected beings, even in a small bird with great amber eyes.

title: How Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma Stole the Thunder-Stone and Lightning-Shaft
summary: In this Zuni myth, the twin war gods Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma acquired the powerful weapons of thunder and lightning. The thunder-stone and lightning-shaft were kept by powerful beings who did not want to share their power. The twins, known for their cunning and bravery, devised a plan to steal these sacred weapons. Using their shapeshifting abilities and the help of their grandmother (Spider Woman often fills this role), they infiltrated the home of the thunder beings. They stole the thunder-stone (which creates thunder when struck) and the lightning-shaft (which shoots bolts of lightning). These weapons made them invincible in battle and allowed them to defeat enemies too powerful for ordinary weapons. The acquisition of thunder and lightning represents the transfer of cosmic power to the heroes who protect the Zuni people and maintain order in the world.
full_text:
The thunder-stone and the lightning-shaft were the most powerful weapons in the world. The thunder-stone, when struck against the earth, produced a sound so violent it could shatter mountains. The lightning-shaft, when hurled, burned with a fire that consumed anything it touched.

These weapons were kept by the Thunder-beings, powerful spirits who lived in the highest reaches of the sky, where the clouds were so thick you could walk on them. The Thunder-beings did not want to share their power. They had held these weapons since the beginning of the world, and they believed no one else was worthy.

But Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma — the twin war gods — wanted them. Not for conquest but for protection. The monsters that plagued the Zuni people were too powerful for ordinary weapons, and the twins knew that only thunder and lightning could destroy them.

The twins devised a plan. With the help of their grandmother — Spider Woman, who wove the threads of fate itself — they infiltrated the home of the Thunder-beings. Spider Woman wove a web so fine that it was invisible, and she stretched it across the door of the Thunder-beings' lodge. When the spirits stepped through, they were caught and delayed.

The twins slipped inside. They found the thunder-stone wrapped in clouds, pulsing with power. They found the lightning-shaft sheathed in rain, crackling with energy. They took both weapons and fled.

The Thunder-beings pursued them across the sky. The chase was terrible — clouds parted, winds howled, the earth shook with the Thunder-beings' rage. But the twins were swift, and Spider Woman's web held their pursuers long enough for the twins to reach safety.

With the thunder-stone and lightning-shaft in their possession, the twins became invincible. They defeated enemies too powerful for any mortal weapon — stone giants, water serpents, cannibal demons. The weapons made them the protectors of the Zuni people, guardians of the order that the Sun Father had established.

The acquisition of thunder and lightning represents the transfer of cosmic power to the heroes who protect the Zuni people and maintain order in the world. It is a story told whenever storms rage across the mesas — a reminder that the weapons of the gods still flash and crash above the pueblos, still guarding the people from the darkness below.

title: The Giant Cloud-Swallower
summary: A Zuni story about a giant being who swallowed clouds, causing drought and suffering among the people. With the clouds gone, no rain fell, and the crops withered. The people performed ceremonies and made prayer offerings, but nothing worked. The twin war gods took action, pursuing the Giant Cloud-swallower across the sky. They shot their lightning arrows at the giant, who was so large he could be seen against the horizon. The battle raged across the heavens. Finally, the twins struck the giant in the throat, causing him to release all the clouds he had swallowed. Rain poured down upon the parched earth, and the people rejoiced. The dying giant's body became the first rainbows and his scattered bones became the clouds that still drift across the sky. The story reinforces the Zuni understanding of weather phenomena as the actions of spiritual beings and the ongoing role of the war gods as protectors.
full_text:
A giant walked across the sky, and where he walked, the clouds disappeared into his belly. He was enormous — his body the size of a mountain, his mouth a cave that could swallow a river. He was the Cloud-swallower, and he had decided that the world below was too green, too alive, too hopeful.

With the clouds gone, the sun blazed without mercy. Rivers dried. Crops withered. The people of the pueblo looked at the sky and saw only emptiness — a blue so deep and clear it hurt to look at.

The people performed ceremonies. They danced. They prayed. They offered cornmeal and turquoise to the sun. But the clouds did not return, for they were inside the giant, and the giant was walking west.

The twin war gods took action. They climbed to the highest mesa and launched themselves into the sky. Áhaiyúta carried the thunder-stone. Mátsailéma carried the lightning-shaft.

The battle raged across the heavens. The giant turned to face them, his eyes burning like furnaces, his breath hot enough to melt stone. He swallowed their first arrows without effect. He swallowed their second volley. But the twins did not tire — they drew power from the prayers of the people below.

They shot their lightning arrows at the giant's throat. The bolts struck with the force of a thousand storms. The giant gagged, his body convulsing. He opened his mouth and released everything he had swallowed — clouds and rain and mist and fog, pouring forth in a torrent that blackened the sky.

Rain fell upon the parched earth. The rivers ran again. The crops lifted their heads. The people emerged from their homes and danced in the downpour, their faces turned upward, their mouths open to drink.

The dying giant's body became the first rainbows — arched across the sky in colors that had never existed before. His scattered bones became the clouds that still drift across the Zuni world, carrying the memory of the storm that saved the people.

The story reinforces the Zuni understanding of weather phenomena as the actions of spiritual beings and the ongoing role of the war gods as protectors of the world.

title: The Maiden the Sun Made Love To
summary: A Zuni story about a maiden whom the Sun desired. The Sun came to her in human form and courted her, and she gave birth to twin boys — the ancestors of the Zuni war gods. The Sun's attention to the maiden brought both blessing and burden. The boys grew rapidly and displayed extraordinary abilities. They became the first culture heroes, teaching their people how to hunt, farm, and perform ceremonies. The story explains the origin of anger in the world — the maiden's anger at the Sun's departure (or at the gossip of the villagers) introduced this emotion to humanity. This origin myth establishes that both positive and negative emotions are part of the human condition and that even divine parentage does not exempt one from human struggles. The twins' journey to find their father the Sun and receive his blessing mirrors the Navajo Hero Twins tradition.
full_text:
The Sun desired a maiden of the Zuni — a woman whose beauty was matched only by her stubbornness. He came to her in human form, his skin warm as a summer afternoon, his eyes bright as the morning star. He courted her with gifts of light and warmth, and she consented.

But the Sun's attention brought both blessing and burden. The people whispered about the maiden. They judged her. They said she had been foolish to accept the Sun's courtship, for the Sun was a spirit, not a man, and spirits do not stay.

She gave birth to twin boys. They were not ordinary children — from the moment they opened their eyes, they saw the world differently. They could see the spirits that moved through the air, could hear the songs that the plants sang to each other, could feel the pulse of the earth beneath their feet.

The boys grew rapidly, their bodies strengthening with each sunrise. They became the first culture heroes, teaching their people how to hunt, how to farm, how to perform the ceremonies that keep the world in balance.

But the story also tells of anger — for when the Sun departed, returning to the sky where he belonged, the maiden was consumed with rage. She shook her fist at the horizon and cursed the day she had met him. Her anger was so intense that it changed the world — storms gathered, the earth trembled, the sky darkened.

This is the origin of anger in the world, the Zuni say. It came from the maiden's fury at the Sun's departure, and from the gossip of the villagers who had judged her without understanding. Anger, like joy and sorrow, is part of the human condition. Even divine parentage does not exempt one from human struggles.

The twins' journey to find their father the Sun and receive his blessing mirrors the Navajo Hero Twins tradition. They climbed through the four worlds, faced monsters and challenges, and finally reached the sky where the Sun sat in his house of light.

"We are your sons," they told him. "We have come to learn what you know."

The Sun tested them — with heat, with drought, with the blinding brightness of his own power. But the twins endured, and the Sun taught them the songs and ceremonies that would protect the people for generations to come.

The story establishes that both positive and negative emotions are part of the human experience, and that the relationship between the divine and the human is not simple but complex — filled with love and abandonment, power and vulnerability, light and shadow.

title: The Hermit Mitsina
summary: A Zuni story about Mitsina, a hermit who lived in seclusion with spiritual power. Mitsina had withdrawn from human society to live in a remote cave, where he communed with the spirits and gained deep knowledge of the sacred world. When the people faced a crisis, they sought him out for his wisdom and power. Mitsina, despite his isolation, felt compassion for his people and agreed to help. He used his spiritual knowledge to perform ceremonies and prayers that resolved the village's problems. Afterward, he withdrew again to his cave, teaching that spiritual power requires solitude and discipline to maintain. The story presents the Zuni concept of the shaman or medicine person who lives between worlds — part of the human community yet separate, possessing power that comes from sacrifice and isolation.
full_text:
Mitsina was a hermit who lived alone in a cave high in the mountains, far from the noise and complication of human society. He had withdrawn from the world years ago, driven by a need to understand the spiritual forces that governed existence. In his isolation, he communed with the spirits and gained deep knowledge of the sacred world.

The people of the pueblo below knew of Mitsina. They spoke of him in whispers, half in awe and half in suspicion. A man who chose solitude over community was unusual, and unusual men were either holy or dangerous.

When a crisis came — a drought so severe that the crops had failed three seasons in a row, and the people were beginning to weaken — they sought Mitsina out. A delegation climbed the mountain, carrying offerings of cornmeal and turquoise.

Mitsina received them at the mouth of his cave. He was old but vital, his eyes sharp as obsidian. He listened to their petition in silence, then said, "I will help you. But you must understand — the power I carry comes from sacrifice. From being alone. From giving up the comforts you take for granted."

The people nodded. They did not fully understand, but they were desperate.

Mitsina performed ceremonies that lasted four days and four nights. He sang songs that had not been heard in the pueblo for generations. He made prayer sticks and placed them at the four sacred mountains. He fasted and prayed until his body was thin as a reed.

On the fourth night, the rain came. It fell softly at first, then harder, then in great sheets that turned the dry earth to mud and filled the rivers and streams. The crops revived. The people survived.

Afterward, Mitsina returned to his cave. "Do not come back unless the need is truly great," he told them. "My power requires solitude. If I live among you, I will lose what makes me useful."

The people honored his request. They left offerings at the base of the mountain but did not climb. The story presents the Zuni concept of the shaman or medicine person who lives between worlds — part of the human community yet separate, possessing power that comes from sacrifice and isolation.

title: The Kachina Tradition (Zuni)
summary: In Zuni tradition, the Kachinas (Kâkâ) originated from the search for itiwana, the Middle Place. The priest Ka'wimosa sent his sons in different directions to find the center of the world. Kiaklo went north, the Ánahoho áchi went south, and Síweluhsiwa and Síwiluhsitsa went east, where they had ten children from an incestuous union — the first Koyemshi (Mudheads), sacred clowns who speak idocies yet utter prophecies. Meanwhile, the Zuni divided into groups led by the Beloved Twins. Children who fell into the river during a crossing became lizards, frogs, turtles, and newts — the lost Little Ones who learned the Dance of Good (Kókokshi) from the god priests of Kóthluwalawan. Duck brought Kiaklo to the council hall where he learned the story of creation and the sacred dances. He returned to teach the Zuni the Kachina ceremonies, the masks, costumes, and rituals that connect the living with the spirits and the ancestors. The masks are considered so sacred that they guarantee the owner's admission to the dance house of the gods after death.
source: Frank Cushing, Outlines of Zuni Creation Myths (1896); Ruth Bunzel, Introduction to Zuni Ceremonialism
full_text:
In Zuni tradition, the Kachinas — the Kâkâ — originated from the search for itiwana, the Middle Place, the center of the world where all things are in balance.

The priest Ka'wimosa sent his sons in different directions to find this center. Kiaklo went north, seeking the middle through cold and snow. The Ánahoho áchi went south, seeking it through heat and dust. But Síweluhsiwa and Síwiluhsitsa went east, toward the rising sun.

In the east, the brothers had ten children from a union that was forbidden — an incestuous coupling that produced the first Koyemshi, the Mudheads. The Koyemshi were sacred clowns who spoke idocies yet uttered prophecies, who acted foolish yet revealed truths that the wise could not see. Their faces were masked with mud, their bodies painted with the colors of earth and sky.

Meanwhile, the Zuni people divided into groups led by the Beloved Twins, each group searching for the Middle Place. Some groups were lost along the way. Children who fell into a great river during a crossing were not drowned but transformed — they became lizards, frogs, turtles, and newts, the lost Little Ones who learned the Dance of Good from the god priests of Kóthluwalawan.

Duck — a water bird of great wisdom — carried Kiaklo to the council hall where the story of creation was told and the sacred dances were recorded. Kiaklo listened as the priests spoke of the emergence through four worlds, of the Twins who guided the people, of the Kachinas who had always been with them.

Kiaklo returned to the Zuni people carrying the knowledge of the Kachina ceremonies — the masks, the costumes, the rituals that connect the living with the spirits and the ancestors. He taught them the dances, the songs, the prayers. He showed them how to carve the tihu — the Kachina dolls — and how to give them to children so the young would recognize the spirits.

The masks are considered so sacred that they guarantee the owner's admission to the dance house of the gods after death. To wear the mask is not to pretend but to become — the dancer's identity is subsumed, and the Kachina speaks through human lips.

The search for the Middle Place is not merely geographical. It is the search for balance in all things — between joy and sorrow, between the sacred and the ordinary, between the living and the dead.

title: Yanauluha Brings Medicine and Agriculture
summary: In Zuni mythology, Yanauluha is the benevolent culture hero who brought the arts of medicine and agriculture to the people. Unlike trickster figures in some traditions, Yanauluha is a dignified, wise teacher. After the emergence into the daylight world, the people were struggling to survive. Yanauluha appeared among them carrying seeds, digging sticks, and sacred objects. He taught them which plants were edible and medicinal, how to plant corn, beans, and squash together in hills, when to plant by observing the stars and the position of the sun, and how to prepare and store food. He also taught them how to use plants for healing — which roots, leaves, and barks cured various illnesses. Yanauluha established the pattern of the agricultural year and the ceremonies that accompany planting and harvest. He is associated with the directions and with the sacred mountains that surround the Zuni world. After teaching the people, Yanauluha departed, but his knowledge continues through Zuni farmers and medicine people.
source: Frank Cushing, Outlines of Zuni Creation Myths (1896); various Zuni oral traditions
full_text:
Yanauluha was not a trickster. He was not a warrior. He was a teacher — dignified, wise, and patient, carrying seeds and digging sticks in hands that trembled with age but not with weakness.

After the emergence into the daylight world, the people struggled. They did not know which plants were safe to eat. They did not know when to plant or when to harvest. They survived on whatever the earth offered without being asked — roots, berries, the occasional rabbit that wandered too close.

Yanauluha appeared among them carrying a bag of seeds and a set of sacred objects. He was accompanied by no one, and the people did not know where he had come from. But his knowledge was unmistakable.

He taught them which plants were edible and which were poisonous. He showed them how to plant corn, beans, and squash together in hills — the Three Sisters, each one supporting the others. Corn provided the stalk for beans to climb. Beans fixed nitrogen in the soil for corn. Squash spread its leaves to shade the ground and keep the water from evaporating.

He taught them to plant by observing the stars. When the Pleiades appeared on the horizon in spring, it was time to prepare the fields. When the sun reached its highest point at midsummer, it was time to pray for rain. When the days began to shorten, it was time to harvest.

Yanauluha also taught them how to use plants for healing. He showed them which roots cured fever, which leaves stopped bleeding, which bark soothed a child's cough. He carried the knowledge of a thousand plants in his memory, and he gave it freely.

He established the pattern of the agricultural year and the ceremonies that accompany planting and harvest. He is associated with the directions and with the sacred mountains that surround the Zuni world — each mountain a landmark, each landmark a reminder of the gifts Yanauluha brought.

After teaching the people, Yanauluha departed. He walked toward the western mountain and disappeared into the sunset. But his knowledge continues through Zuni farmers and medicine people, passed down in the way the ancients intended — not through marks on paper but through words in the heart.

title: Coyote and Eagle Steal the Sun and Moon
summary: A Zuni story explaining the origin of day and night and the changing seasons. In the beginning, the Sun and Moon were kept locked in boxes by a powerful being who would not release them. The world was in perpetual twilight. Coyote and Eagle, two of the most clever animals, devised a plan. Eagle flew to the being's home with Coyote hidden in his feathers. While the being slept, Coyote crept out, opened the boxes, and Eagle seized the Sun and Moon with his talons. They fled, pursued by the angry being. Eagle rose higher and higher into the sky, placing the Sun and Moon in their proper positions. But in the chaos, Coyote dropped the box containing half the daylight, which shattered. This is why days are shorter in winter than in summer, and why daylight decreases after the summer solstice. The story reflects the Zuni understanding of astronomical cycles and the partnership between sky and earth creatures.
full_text:
In the beginning, the world was in perpetual twilight. The Sun and Moon existed, but they were locked in boxes by a powerful being who believed the world was not ready for their light. The boxes were made of obsidian, dark as the space between stars, and they sat in the being's lodge, wrapped in bundles of eagle feathers.

Coyote and Eagle devised a plan. They were different in every way — Eagle was noble and patient, Coyote was reckless and clever — but they shared a conviction that the world needed light.

Eagle flew to the being's home with Coyote hidden in his feathers. They waited until the being fell asleep, his snores shaking the walls of the lodge. Then Coyote crept out, his paws silent on the earthen floor.

He found the boxes. The first contained the Sun — golden and warm, pulsing with life. The second held the Moon — silver and cool, glowing with gentle light. Coyote opened the Sun box first, and Eagle seized the Sun with his talons. Then Coyote opened the Moon box, and Eagle grabbed that too.

They fled. The being woke with a roar. The chase was furious — across the sky, through canyons, over mountains. Eagle rose higher and higher, placing the Sun in its proper position in the east, the Moon in its proper place in the west.

But in the chaos, Coyote dropped the box containing half the daylight. It shattered on the ground, and the light spilled out and was lost.

This is why days are shorter in winter than in summer. The Sun travels its full path during the summer solstice, giving the longest day. But after that, the lost daylight — the portion Coyote dropped — is missing, and the days grow shorter until the winter solstice, when the cycle begins again.

The story reflects the Zuni understanding of astronomical cycles and the partnership between sky and earth creatures. Eagle represents the noble qualities needed to carry the light, and Coyote represents the clever but flawed nature that sometimes causes loss.

title: The Corn Maidens (Zuni)
summary: In Zuni tradition, the Corn Maidens are sacred beings who embody the spirit of corn. They are associated with Paiyatuma, the god of the dawn and of music, and with the Kachina society. According to the myth, Paiyatuma courted the Corn Maidens, who were beautiful but shy. He played his flute for them, and they danced. Through this union, the sacred connection between corn and the people was established. The Corn Maidens taught the Zuni women how to grind corn, make piki bread, and prepare corn ceremonially. Each color of corn has its own maiden — Blue Corn Maiden, Yellow Corn Maiden, White Corn Maiden, Red Corn Maiden, Black Corn Maiden, and Speckled Corn Maiden. During ceremonies, the Corn Maidens are represented by Kachina dancers who carry ears of corn and bless the fields. The story of the Corn Maidens is central to Zuni agricultural ceremonies and reinforces the sacredness of corn as a gift from the spirit world.
source: Frank Cushing, Zuñi Folk Tales (1901); Ruth Bunzel, Zuni Ceremonialism
full_text:
The Corn Maidens were sacred beings who embodied the spirit of corn — each one a different color, each one carrying a different power. Blue Corn Maiden held the strength of the earth. Yellow Corn Maiden held the warmth of the sun. White Corn Maiden held the purity of snow. Red Corn Maiden held the fire of transformation. Black Corn Maiden held the depth of night. And Speckled Corn Maiden held the mystery of variation — the promise that no two things in creation are exactly alike.

They were associated with Paiyatuma, the god of the dawn and of music, who courted them with his flute. Paiyatuma was a gentle god — his music was not the loud, percussive sound of war but the soft, melodic whisper of morning. He played for the Corn Maidens at dawn, when the light was pink and gold and the world felt new.

The Corn Maidens were beautiful but shy. They hid in the fields, their bodies swaying with the cornstalks, their faces peering out from behind the leaves. When Paiyatuma played, they emerged. They danced in the rows of corn, their movements mirroring the rustling of the stalks in the wind.

Through this union, the sacred connection between corn and the people was established. The Corn Maidens taught the Zuni women how to grind corn on the metate, how to make piki bread thin as paper and sweet as honeydew, how to prepare corn ceremonially with songs and prayers.

Each color of corn has its own maiden and its own ceremony. During the planting season, the Corn Maidens are represented by Kachina dancers who carry ears of corn and bless the fields. They walk through the rows, touching each hill with a feather wand, and where they touch, the corn grows taller.

The story of the Corn Maidens is central to Zuni agricultural ceremonies. It reinforces the sacredness of corn as a gift from the spirit world — not merely food but a living being with which humans have a reciprocal relationship. To plant corn is to honor the Corn Maidens. To harvest corn is to accept their gift. To waste corn is to insult them.

The Zuni say that when the Corn Maidens are honored, the harvest is abundant. When they are neglected, the fields wither. This is not a threat but a truth — the relationship between humans and corn is as real and as fragile as any human relationship.

title: The Cock and the Mouse (Zuni)
summary: A Zuni folktale of the hybrid type, combining Native and European story elements. The Cock (rooster) and the Mouse were friends living together. Mouse was industrious, gathering food and maintaining their home, while Cock was boastful and lazy. When danger came in the form of a cat or predator, Cock's crowing alerted everyone, but his bravado failed when actual confrontation occurred. Mouse, though small, used cleverness to escape danger. The story humorously contrasts the small, practical Mouse with the showy but ineffective Cock. It teaches that real value lies not in appearance or loudness but in practical skills and quiet diligence. Like many Zuni animal tales, it contains elements of social commentary, humor, and moral instruction wrapped in an engaging narrative.
full_text:
The Cock and the Mouse were friends — an unlikely pair, for the Cock was vain and boastful while the Mouse was small and quiet. But they shared a burrow beneath the old trading post, and they shared their food, and they shared their stories.

The Mouse was industrious. Each morning he rose before dawn and gathered seeds from the fields, carrying them one by one to the burrow. He wove grass into blankets, packed earth into walls, and kept their home clean and warm.

The Cock, by contrast, spent his mornings preening. He admired his red comb in the reflection of the water jar. He practiced his crow, making it louder and more impressive with each attempt. "Listen to me!" he would shout. "I am the most magnificent creature in the village!"

The Mouse said nothing. He simply continued his work.

One day, a cat appeared. It sat at the entrance to the burrow, its yellow eyes fixed on the darkness within, its tail twitching with anticipation.

The Cock puffed up his chest and crowed at the cat — a tremendous, ear-splitting crow that echoed through the compound. The cat was unmoved. It simply sat there, patient and hungry.

"Do something!" the Mouse whispered from behind the Cock.

"I am doing something!" the Cock replied. "I am terrifying it with my voice!"

The cat was not terrified. It stepped closer.

The Mouse, who had no voice to boast of, crept along a side tunnel and emerged behind the cat. He nipped its tail. The cat yowled and spun around, and in that moment of confusion, the Mouse darted back into the tunnel and the Cock flew to the roof.

The cat left, annoyed but unhurt. The Cock descended, preening as if the entire rescue had been his idea.

"That was close," the Mouse said.

"Yes," said the Cock. "My crow was just beginning to work."

The Mouse smiled and returned to his gathering. Real value, he knew, lay not in appearance or loudness but in practical skills and quiet diligence. The Cock would never understand this, but the Mouse loved him anyway.

title: The How the Twins of War and Chance Fared with the Unborn-Made Men
summary: In this complex Zuni myth, Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma, the Twins of War and Chance (or Morning Star and Evening Star), journeyed to the underworld to confront the Unborn-made Men. These were unfinished beings who had not yet been given their final form — they existed in a state of potential. The twins had to navigate the dark underworld, using their wits and divine weapons. They encountered various spirits and obstacles, including the guardians of the underworld. The story explores themes of destiny, free will, and the nature of creation — why some beings are completed and others are not. The twins' journey through the underworld mirrors the soul's journey after death and the process by which spirits become ancestors. The Unborn-made Men represent the untold potential that exists in every being before it takes its final form in the daylight world.
full_text:
Áhaiyúta and Mátsailéma — the Twins of War and Chance, the Morning Star and the Evening Star — descended into the underworld to confront the Unborn-made Men.

These were beings who had not yet been given their final form. They existed in a state of potential — half-formed, half-conscious, waiting for the moment when the Creator would complete them. Some had the beginnings of faces but no eyes. Some had the beginnings of limbs but no purpose. They were the untold potential of the universe, gathering dust in the dark.

The twins navigated the underworld using their wits and divine weapons. The darkness was absolute — no stars, no moon, no fire. Only the faint glow of the twins' own spiritual power, casting long shadows that moved of their own accord.

They encountered the guardians of the underworld — spirits made of shadow and stone, whose purpose was to keep the Unborn-made Men from escaping into the light. The guardians did not speak. They simply stood in the twins' path, their bodies blocking the narrow passages.

Áhaiyúta struck the first guardian with his thunder-stone. The sound was so violent that the guardian crumbled into dust. Mátsailéma hurled his lightning-shaft at the second, and it split the guardian in two.

But for every guardian they destroyed, two more appeared. The underworld was vast, and its defenders were endless.

The twins realized that they could not fight their way through. They had to understand. They stopped fighting and listened. In the silence of the underworld, they heard the Unborn-made Men whispering — not words but the sound of potential itself, the hum of creation waiting to happen.

The twins understood. The Unborn-made Men were not evil. They were incomplete. And the underworld was not a prison but a womb — a place of gestation where beings formed before emerging into the light.

The twins left the underworld without completing their mission, for they realized the mission was never to destroy but to understand. The Unborn-made Men would emerge when the time was right, taking their final forms in the daylight world.

The story explores themes of destiny, free will, and the nature of creation. It teaches that not all battles are won with weapons, and that some things must be allowed to take their natural course.

title: The Warrior Suitor of Moki (Hopi)
summary: A Zuni story about a warrior from Zuni who traveled to the land of the Hopi (called Moki in Zuni) to win a bride. The warrior had to prove his worth through feats of strength, courage, and skill. He faced challenges set by the Hopi elders, including hunting dangerous game, competing in races and games, and demonstrating his knowledge of proper ceremonial conduct. Through his bravery and skill — and with the help of the war gods — he succeeded in all the trials and won the maiden. The marriage between the Zuni warrior and the Hopi woman established ties between the two nations. The story reflects historical relationships between the Zuni and Hopi peoples, who share similar cultural roots and maintain trade and marriage connections. It also illustrates the Zuni values of courage, perseverance, and cross-cultural respect.
full_text:
A warrior from Zuni heard of the beauty of a maiden in the land of the Hopi — called Moki by the Zuni. He decided to travel there and win her hand, for he was proud and skilled and believed no challenge could defeat him.

The journey was long — across mesas and canyons, through lands where the Zuni were not always welcome. But the warrior traveled swiftly, carrying his weapons and his prayers.

When he arrived at the Hopi pueblo, the elders were suspicious. They did not know this man. They did not trust his intentions. So they set him trials.

First, he had to hunt dangerous game — a mountain lion that had been raiding the pueblo's sheep pens. The warrior tracked the lion for three days, following its paws prints through the sandstone. On the third day, he found it sleeping in a cave. He drew his bow and loosed a single arrow. The lion fell.

The elders nodded but were not yet satisfied. They sent him to compete in races and games against the Hopi's finest athletes. The warrior ran faster, threw farther, and wrestled longer than any of them. But he did not gloat. He honored his opponents and thanked the spirits for his strength.

Finally, the elders tested his knowledge of proper ceremonial conduct. They asked him about the rituals of planting, the songs of the seasons, the prayers for rain. The warrior answered correctly, for he had been well taught by the Zuni priests.

The elders were satisfied. They presented the maiden to the warrior, and she looked upon him and was pleased. They were married in a ceremony that combined Zuni and Hopi traditions — the best of both peoples, woven together like the threads of a blanket.

The marriage established ties between the two nations, who share similar cultural roots and maintain trade and marriage connections to this day. The story illustrates the Zuni values of courage, perseverance, and cross-cultural respect — the understanding that excellence transcends tribal boundaries.

title: How the Rattlesnakes Came to Be What They Are
summary: A Zuni story explaining the origin of rattlesnakes and their relationship with humans. In the days of the ancients, rattlesnakes did not have their distinctive rattle or their dangerous venom. A man who had been saved by a rattlesnake or had made a pact with one became the founder of the Rattlesnake Society. The snake was given its rattle as a warning device so that humans could hear it and avoid being bitten. The venom was given as a defense but also carries healing power in the hands of those who know the proper ceremonies. The story teaches that rattlesnakes are not merely dangerous creatures but sacred beings with a role in the spiritual ecology of the world. Members of the Rattlesnake Society can handle rattlesnakes without harm and use them in healing ceremonies. The rattle is understood as a gift — a way for the snake to say 'I am here, please step carefully.'
full_text:
In the days of the ancients, rattlesnakes did not have their distinctive rattle or their dangerous venom. They were ordinary snakes — small, harmless, easily stepped on.

A man who lived in the pueblo had made a pact with a rattlesnake. The snake had saved his life during a flood, wrapping itself around the man's body and holding him above the water until the currents receded. In gratitude, the man promised the snake that he would honor it and teach others to do the same.

The man became the founder of the Rattlesnake Society — a sacred order of men and women who understood the snake's power and knew how to communicate with it. They were healers, for the snake's venom, in the right hands, could cure as well as kill.

The snake was given its rattle as a warning device. Each time it shed its skin and added a new segment, a new rattle was formed. The sound was designed to alert humans — to say, "I am here, please step carefully." The rattle was not a threat but a gift — a way for the snake to protect itself and the humans who might otherwise harm it.

The venom was given as a defense, but it also carries healing power in the hands of those who know the proper ceremonies. Members of the Rattlesnake Society can handle rattlesnakes without harm, for they know the songs that calm the snake and the prayers that protect the handler.

During ceremonies, the rattlesnakes are brought into the dance ground and allowed to move among the people. The dancers step carefully, respecting the snake's space, acknowledging its power. The snake does not strike, for it recognizes the members of the society and knows they mean no harm.

The story teaches that rattlesnakes are not merely dangerous creatures but sacred beings with a role in the spiritual ecology of the world. The rattle is understood as a gift — a way for the snake to say, "I am here, please step carefully." And the venom is understood as a tool — dangerous in the wrong hands but healing in the right ones.

title: The Two Little Ones and Their Turkeys
summary: A Zuni story about two orphaned children who were cared for by a flock of wild turkeys. The turkeys provided them with feathers for warmth, eggs for food, and protection from danger. The children lived in harmony with the turkeys, learning the ways of the forest and the language of birds. When the children grew older, they faced pressure to return to human society, but the turkeys warned them about the dangers of human greed. Eventually, the children had to choose between the freedom of the wild and the community of humans. The story explores themes of adoption — being raised by non-human caretakers — and the tension between wild and civilized life. The turkeys, like the deer in other Zuni stories, represent the generosity of the natural world and the reciprocal obligations between humans and animals.
full_text:
Two orphaned children wandered the wilderness, hungry and alone. Their parents had died in a fever that swept through the pueblo, and the relatives who should have cared for them were too consumed by their own grief to notice two small figures slipping away into the desert.

The children found shelter in a grove of piñon trees where a flock of wild turkeys lived. The turkeys watched the children with their round, bright eyes and felt something that turkeys do not often feel — pity.

The lead turkey, an old hen with feathers like bronze, approached the children. She offered them her warmth through the cold nights. She led them to nests where they could find eggs. She showed them which berries were safe and which were poison.

The children lived with the turkeys for many seasons. They learned the ways of the forest — the language of birds, the warnings of the wind, the signs that predicted rain. They grew strong on turkey eggs and piñon nuts, and they were happy.

But the turkeys warned them about the dangers of human greed. "People take without asking," the old hen said. "They hunt for sport, not for need. They wear feathers as decoration, not as honor."

The children knew this was true. They had seen it in the pueblo before their parents died.

When the children grew older, they faced pressure to return to human society. Hunters from the pueblo found them and tried to bring them back. The children were torn — the human world of their birth calling them one way, the turkey world of their raising calling them another.

They chose to return to the pueblo, but they carried the turkeys' teachings with them. They taught the people to honor the turkeys, to ask permission before hunting, to waste nothing of what the bird gives.

The turkeys, for their part, continued to live in the grove, generous and watchful. They represent the generosity of the natural world and the reciprocal obligations between humans and animals — obligations that exist whether we acknowledge them or not.

title: White Buffalo Calf Woman and the Sacred Pipe
summary: During a time of great famine, two Lakota scouts encountered a mysterious woman in white buckskin. One scout approached her with lustful intent and was reduced to bones. The woman instructed the remaining scout to prepare the tribe. She gave the people the chanupa (sacred pipe) made of red stone carved with a buffalo calf, taught them the Seven Sacred Rites including the Sun Dance and vision quest, and showed them how to pray to Wakan Tanka. Before departing she transformed through four colors—black, red, brown, and white—becoming a white buffalo calf who promised to return when the people needed her most.
source: Wikipedia / Lakota Times / World History Encyclopedia
full_text:
During a time of great famine, when the buffalo had vanished and the people were thin as reeds, two Lakota scouts — young men with sharp eyes and hollow bellies — ventured far from camp in search of game. They found nothing. The plains were empty, the rivers still, the sky a sheet of gray.

As they rested beneath a cottonwood tree, a figure appeared on the horizon. She was beautiful beyond description — a woman dressed in white buckskin that shimmered like fresh snow. She carried a sacred pipe and walked with a grace that made the grass bend beneath her feet.

One scout was overcome with desire. He approached her with lustful intent, thinking only of her beauty. Where he touched her, his flesh turned to bone. His companion, witnessing this horror, knelt in respect.

The woman smiled at the second scout. "I am Ptesáŋ Wiŋ — White Buffalo Calf Woman. I have come to bring your people the sacred pipe, the chanupa, so that they may pray and survive this hard time."

She instructed the scout to prepare the tribe for her arrival. He ran back to camp, his legs carrying him faster than they ever had. The people gathered in a circle, and the White Buffalo Calf Woman walked among them, teaching them the Seven Sacred Rites — the Sun Dance, the vision quest, the sweat lodge, the pipe ceremony, and the rites of passage that would guide their spiritual life.

She gave them the chanupa — a pipe made of red stone carved with the image of a buffalo calf. She showed them how to fill it with the sacred mixture of bark and tobacco, how to offer the smoke to the four directions, how to pray to Wakan Tanka, the Great Mystery.

Before departing, she transformed through four colors — black, then red, then brown, then white — becoming a white buffalo calf who spoke one final promise: "I will return when the people need me most."

The pipe remains the most sacred object in Lakota spirituality. When it is raised, Wakan Tanka listens. When it is smoked, the prayers rise with the smoke to the sky world. And the White Buffalo Calf Woman's promise endures — a light in the darkness, a hope in the famine.

title: Iktomi the Spider Trickster
summary: Iktomi is the spider trickster of Lakota mythology, born fully grown with the body of a spider and the cunning of a man. He is known for his clever schemes and predictions, but his selfishness and mischievous nature often backfire. In one tale, Iktomi tried to keep a pot of fish soup for himself rather than share with a visitor, devising a race trick that ultimately failed. In another, Iktomi angered a boulder and was crushed, only to be freed by bats who were turned into stones. Despite his flaws, Iktomi is considered wise and his stories teach moral lessons about generosity and respect.
full_text:
Iktomi was born fully grown — no childhood, no learning, no gradual awakening. One moment he was nothing, and the next he was a spider with the body of a spider and the cunning of a man. He emerged into the world already knowing its tricks, already planning his schemes.

He was known as the trickster, the weaver of false webs, the maker of predictions that came true in ways no one expected. His stories were told around the fire, each one a warning wrapped in laughter.

In one tale, Iktomi found a pot of fish soup simmering over a fire. It was not his soup. He knew this. He sat down beside it anyway and began to eat. When a visitor arrived — a traveler with hollow cheeks and hopeful eyes — Iktomi devised a trick to keep the soup for himself.

"Let us race," Iktomi said. "The winner takes the soup."

The traveler agreed. Iktomi drew a line in the dirt and told the traveler to run to the cottonwood tree and back. But while the traveler ran, Iktomi ate the soup. When the traveler returned, breathless and victorious, the pot was empty.

The traveler looked at the empty pot. Then he looked at Iktomi. Then he smiled. "You have won the soup," he said. "But you have lost something more valuable — the trust of anyone who hears this story."

Iktomi laughed, but the laughter was hollow, for he knew the traveler was right.

In another tale, Iktomi angered a boulder by insulting its weight and stubbornness. The boulder chased him and crushed him flat. Bats came to help, pecking at the boulder until it cracked open.
