But the bats' faces were smashed flat in the effort, and Iktomi — ever ungrateful — scattered pebbles that became the stones covering the plains.

Despite his flaws, Iktomi is considered wise. His stories teach moral lessons about generosity, respect, and the consequences of selfishness. He is the trickster who reveals truth through deception, who teaches wisdom through folly.

title: Unhcegila the Serpent Monster
summary: Unhcegila was a gigantic serpent monster who wreaked havoc upon the land, devouring anyone who stumbled upon her. A red crystal in the seventh spot on her head functioned as her heart and granted its bearer great power. In one version, a warrior from the Bear Clan, guided by a Weasel spirit, allowed himself to be devoured then cut his way out, freeing other victims. In another, two brothers—one blind—killed her with arrows from a medicine woman. A third version tells of Unhcegila emerging from primordial waters, only to be struck down by Wakinyan the Thunderbird whose lightning shattered her heart, scattering her bones across the Badlands.
source: Wikipedia / Native American Mythology A to Z
full_text:
Unhcegila was a gigantic serpent monster who wreaked havoc upon the land. She was older than the hills, older than the rivers, older than the memory of the people. Her body stretched across entire valleys, and her scales were harder than stone.

She devoured anyone who stumbled upon her path — hunters, women, children. No weapon could pierce her hide. No arrow could find her heart. She was, it seemed, invincible.

But Unhcegila had a weakness. In the seventh spot on her head, there was a red crystal — her heart, glowing like an ember. Whoever possessed this crystal would gain great power.

In one version of the story, a warrior from the Bear Clan was guided by a Weasel spirit to the serpent's lair. The warrior was brave but small, and he knew he could not fight Unhcegila directly. So he devised a plan.

He allowed himself to be devoured. The serpent swallowed him whole, and for a moment the warrior thought he would die. But inside the serpent's belly, he found the bones of those who had been taken before him. He also found the red crystal, pulsing with power.

The warrior cut his way out of the serpent's belly, freeing the other victims as he went. When he emerged, he held the crystal high. Unhcegila, weakened by the loss of her heart, fell to the ground and died.

In another version, two brothers — one blind — killed the serpent with arrows from a medicine woman. The blind brother could not see the serpent, but his brother guided his aim, and the arrows found their mark.

In a third version, Unhcegila emerged from primordial waters, only to be struck down by Wakinyan the Thunderbird, whose lightning shattered her heart and scattered her bones across the Badlands.

The story teaches that even the most terrifying adversaries have vulnerabilities, and that courage, observation, and cunning can overcome seemingly insurmountable threats.

title: The Lakota Creation: Inyan, Maka, and the First Dawn
summary: In the beginning there was only Inyan (Rock) and the omnipresent spirit Wakan Tanka, the Great Mystery, and the darkness Han. Inyan wished to exercise his powers of compassion, so he created Maka (Earth) from himself, sacrificing much of his blood which became water. Inyan shriveled and lost his powers. The water gave birth to Skan, who became the supreme judge. When Maka complained of cold and darkness, Inyan created Anpo the Dawn and later Wi the Sun. Maka tried to separate from Inyan, but Skan ruled that rock and soil must remain bound together, explaining why rocks are embedded in the earth.
full_text:
In the beginning there was only Inyan — Rock — and the omnipresent spirit Wakan Tanka, the Great Mystery, and the darkness Han. Nothing else existed. No earth, no sky, no beings of any kind.

Inyan wished to exercise his powers of compassion. He wanted to create something — anything — that would know the warmth of his spirit and the strength of his body. So he created Maka — Earth — from himself, tearing pieces of his own being and shaping them into the land.

But the creation cost him dearly. His blood — the red ochre that gives rock its color — flowed into the earth, becoming water. As his blood flowed, Inyan shriveled and lost his powers. The rock that had once been vast and mighty became small and hard, embedded in the earth it had created.

The water gave birth to Skan — the Sky — who became the supreme judge. Skan looked down at the world below and saw Maka, the earth, shivering in the cold and darkness. Maka complained of her suffering — she was alone, she was cold, she had no light.

Inyan, even in his weakened state, heard her complaint. He created Anpo the Dawn — a being of soft pink and gold who walked across the sky each morning, bringing the first hint of light. And later he created Wi the Sun — the full blazing light that turned the world from gray to green.

But Maka tried to separate from Inyan. She wanted to be free of the rock that had created her, to float in the water without weight or burden. Skan ruled that rock and soil must remain bound together — that Inyan and Maka could never be fully separated.

This is why rocks are embedded in the earth, why boulders sit in the middle of fields and stones line the riverbeds. Inyan cannot leave Maka, and Maka cannot shed Inyan. They are bound together by Skan's judgment, by the sacrifice of creation, by the love that Inyan gave when he tore himself apart to make the world.

The story teaches the Lakota understanding that creation requires sacrifice, that love costs something, and that the bonds between beings — even unwilling ones — are sacred.

title: The Thunderbird Wakinyan
summary: Wakinyan is the great Thunderbird of Lakota mythology, a powerful sky spirit associated with thunder, lightning, and storms. His flapping wings create thunderclaps and his eyes flash lightning. When Unhcegila emerged from the primordial waters to flood the land, Wakinyan flapped his wings to dry the earth and shot lightning to destroy the serpent's heart. The Thunderbird represents the destructive yet renewing power of storms and is considered one of the most potent spirits. Wakinyan is also associated with the west direction and is a protector of the Lakota people against chaos and disorder.
full_text:
Wakinyan — the Thunderbird — is the great sky spirit of Lakota mythology, a being of such power that even the other spirits treat him with caution. His body is massive, spanning the width of the sky when his wings are spread. His feathers are red and gold, and his eyes flash with the lightning that is his weapon and his voice.

When Wakinyan flaps his wings, thunderclaps shake the earth. When he opens his eyes, lightning bolts split the sky. When he speaks, his voice is the rumble that precedes the storm.

Wakinyan is the protector of the Lakota people against chaos and disorder. He is the eternal enemy of the great water serpents — Unhcegila and her kind — who lurk in the depths of lakes and rivers, waiting to devour the unwary.

When Unhcegila emerged from the primordial waters to flood the land, it was Wakinyan who rose to meet her. He flapped his wings to dry the earth, his feathers sending waves of heat across the plains. He shot lightning at the serpent's heart, the red crystal that was her weakness.

The battle was terrible. The sky turned black with Wakinyan's wings. The earth shook with Unhcegila's thrashing. Lightning and water clashed in a storm that lasted four days and four nights.

Finally, Wakinyan's lightning struck the crystal. The serpent's heart shattered, and she fell. Her body became the Badlands — the eroded, twisted landscape that the Lakota call Makhóšiča, the Bad Lands, where her bones still jut from the earth like fingers reaching for the sky.

Wakinyan is associated with the west direction, where storms come from. He is honored with tobacco offerings, and his rumbling voice is heard whenever he pursues evil spirits across the sky. The Lakota say that when thunder rolls, Wakinyan is speaking — warning the monsters below that the Thunderbird is watching, that the protector of the people is on patrol.

title: The Great Race of the Animals
summary: The Great Race is a Lakota legend about a competition between the four-legged animals and the two-legged birds to determine who would eat whom. The race was proposed by Ksapela the Wise One to settle conflicts among the creatures. Representing the four-leggeds was the buffalo, while the magpie represented the two-leggeds. As the race progressed, various animals helped their champion. The buffalo was winning until the magpie hitched a ride on his back, then flew ahead at the last moment. The Great Spirit declared the race a draw, decreeing that henceforth the two-leggeds would hunt the four-leggeds but must always show respect for their sacrifice.
full_text:
The four-legged animals and the two-legged birds had been arguing for as long as anyone could remember. The animals said they were stronger and deserved to eat the birds. The birds said they were swifter and deserved to eat the animals. Neither side would yield.

Ksapela the Wise One — a being older than the argument itself — proposed a solution. "Let there be a race," she said. "The winner eats the loser."

Representing the four-leggeds was the buffalo — massive, powerful, his hooves cracking the earth with each step. Representing the two-leggeds was the magpie — small, sharp-eyed, with wings that could carry him faster than any four-legged could run.

The race began at dawn. The buffalo surged forward, his massive body cutting through the prairie grass like a ship through water. The magpie flew beside him, his wings beating steadily.

As the race progressed, various animals helped their champion. The rabbit dug a hole in the buffalo's path, giving him a smooth route. The fox ran alongside, barking encouragement. The magpie had no helpers — he relied on his own wings.

The buffalo was winning. He was so close to the finish line that he could taste victory. But the magpie, watching from above, saw his chance. He dove and landed on the buffalo's back. The buffalo didn't notice — the magpie was so light.

At the last moment, just before the buffalo crossed the finish line, the magpie launched himself into the air and flew ahead. He landed on the finish line first.

The Great Spirit declared the race a draw. Neither side had clearly won. But the decree established the rules that would govern the relationship between animals and birds forever: henceforth, the two-leggeds would hunt the four-leggeds, but they must always show respect for their sacrifice.

The magpie still wears the black and white feathers he wore during the race. The buffalo still runs across the plains, his great body a reminder of the race that determined the fate of all living things.

title: The Happy Hunting Ground
summary: The Lakota believe the soul journeys after death to the happy hunting ground, a realm resembling the living world with better weather and more plentiful animals that are easier to hunt. Some traditions say the soul travels along the Sky-Road (Milky Way) to reach this destination. At the entrance, the deceased must present proper tattoos to Hihankara (Owl-Maker). Those with correct tattoos are admitted; those without are pushed back to Earth to wander as restless ghosts. The dead may also travel along the Spirit Path, another name for the Milky Way, to reach their final resting place among the stars.
full_text:
The Lakota believe the soul does not die with the body. When a person breathes their last, the soul rises from the chest like a bird taking flight, and it begins its journey to the happy hunting ground — a realm that resembles the living world but with better weather, more plentiful animals, and easier hunting.

Some traditions say the soul travels along the Sky-Road — the Milky Way, that river of light that stretches across the night sky. The road is well-marked, lined with the souls of those who came before, each one a star in the constellation of the ancestors.

At the entrance to the happy hunting ground, the deceased must present proper tattoos to Hihankara — the Owl-Maker, a spirit who guards the gate. The tattoos are not decorative but identifying — they mark the soul as belonging to the Lakota people, carrying the symbols of their clans and their achievements.

Those with correct tattoos are admitted. Those without are pushed back to Earth to wander as restless ghosts, unable to find peace because they failed to prepare for the journey.

The dead may also travel along the Spirit Path — another name for the Milky Way — to reach their final resting place among the stars. The Spirit Path is not merely a road but a living thing, growing wider with each soul that walks it, brighter with each star that joins.

The happy hunting ground is not merely a reward but a continuation. The souls of the dead hunt, pray, and live much as they did on earth — but without pain, without hunger, without the winter that bites and the summer that scorches. They are whole again, reunited with those they loved, waiting for the day when the living join them.

The Lakota say that when you look up at the Milky Way, you are looking at the road the dead have walked. And when a new star appears, a soul has found its way home.

title: Iktomi and the Boulder
summary: Iktomi the spider trickster wrapped himself in a fine robe and went walking. He came upon a large boulder and, feeling generous, offered it his robe. The boulder declined, but Iktomi insisted and placed the robe upon it. Later, when Iktomi wanted his robe back, the boulder refused. Iktomi grew angry and insulted the boulder, which chased him and crushed him flat. Bats came to help Iktomi, pecking at the boulder until it cracked open, freeing him. But the bats' faces were smashed flat in the effort, and Iktomi—ever ungrateful—scattered pebbles that became the stones covering the plains.
full_text:
Iktomi the spider trickster wrapped himself in a fine robe and went walking. He was feeling generous — a rare and dangerous state for Iktomi, for his generosity usually came with strings attached.

He came upon a large boulder sitting in the middle of the trail. "You must be cold," Iktomi said to the boulder. "Here — take my robe."

The boulder did not respond. It was a boulder.

"I insist," Iktomi said, draping the robe across the boulder's surface. "A fine robe like this deserves a fine recipient."

Iktomi walked away, feeling virtuous. But when the wind picked up and the air grew cold, he wanted his robe back. He returned to the boulder.

"I have come for my robe," he said.

The boulder did not respond.

"My robe," Iktomi repeated, tugging at the fabric. It did not move. The boulder had absorbed the robe into itself, as boulders do.

Iktomi grew angry. "You ungrateful stone! I gave you my finest robe and you refuse to return it!"

He insulted the boulder. He kicked it. He scratched at it with his spider claws.

The boulder, who had patience but not infinite patience, began to move. It rolled toward Iktomi, slowly at first, then faster. Iktomi ran, but the boulder was relentless. It caught him and crushed him flat.

Iktomi lay in the dust, flattened like a pressed leaf. He could not move. He could not speak. He could only watch as the sky wheeled overhead.

Bats came to help. They flew down from the rocks and pecked at the boulder with their tiny teeth. They pecked and pecked until the boulder cracked open, and Iktomi slid free.

But the bats' faces were smashed flat in the effort. To this day, bats have flattened faces — a reminder of the time they saved the trickster who could not save himself.

Iktomi, ever ungrateful, scattered pebbles across the plains as he walked away. The pebbles became the stones that cover the land, and Iktomi never wore a robe again.

title: The Seven Sacred Rites
summary: White Buffalo Calf Woman gave the Lakota people the Seven Sacred Rites that would guide their spiritual life. The rites are: 1) Keeping of the Soul (preserving the spirit of the deceased for a year before release); 2) The Purification Rite (sweat lodge ceremony for cleansing); 3) Crying for a Vision (vision quest for guidance); 4) The Sun Dance (annual renewal ceremony with sacrifice and dancing); 5) The Making of Relatives (adoption ceremony); 6) The Girls Coming of Age (womanhood ceremony); and 7) The Throwing of the Ball (symbolizing the Creator's love). Each rite uses the sacred pipe given by the White Buffalo Calf Woman.
full_text:
White Buffalo Calf Woman gave the Lakota people not just the sacred pipe but seven rites — seven ceremonies that would guide their spiritual life from birth to death and beyond.

The first rite is the Keeping of the Soul. When a loved one dies, a lock of their hair is kept in a sacred bundle for a year. During that year, the soul is preserved — held in the safety of the bundle while it adjusts to the spirit world. After a year of mourning and ceremony, the soul is released to travel the Sky-Road to the happy hunting ground.

The second rite is the Purification Rite — the sweat lodge ceremony. A dome of willow branches is covered with hides, and heated stones are placed in a pit at the center. Water is thrown on the stones, filling the lodge with steam. Participants sit in the darkness, sweating, praying, cleansing their bodies and spirits of impurities.

The third rite is Crying for a Vision — the vision quest. A young person goes alone to a hilltop or remote place and fasts for four days, praying for guidance. The spirits may come in the form of animals, clouds, or visions, each one carrying a message for the seeker.

The fourth rite is the Sun Dance — the annual renewal ceremony. A sacred pole is erected, and dancers attach themselves to it with skewers, offering their blood and their prayers. They dance for four days, looking only at the sun, their sacrifice renewing the covenant between the people and the Creator.

The fifth rite is the Making of Relatives — an adoption ceremony that binds two families together. The sixth is the Girls' Coming of Age — a ceremony that honors a young woman's transition to womanhood. The seventh is the Throwing of the Ball — a game that symbolizes the Creator's love, the ball thrown upward representing the soul's ascent.

Each rite uses the sacred pipe given by the White Buffalo Calf Woman. Each rite connects the Lakota people to the spiritual forces that govern their world. Together, the seven rites form a complete spiritual framework — a guide for living well, dying well, and existing well in the spirit world beyond.

title: Lakota Star Husband Story
summary: Two Lakota girls lay outside their tipi one night, and one pointed at the brightest star saying she wished to marry it. The next day the girls found themselves in the sky world, where the first girl became the wife of a star. She was told not to dig around a certain turnip-like root, but curiosity overcame her. When she pulled the root, she saw the Earth far below through the hole. Homesick, she and her husband wove a rope to descend, but it was too short and she fell. She survived and returned to her people, but the star husband remained in the sky and can be seen as the evening star.
full_text:
Two Lakota girls lay outside their tipi one summer night, gazing at the sky. The stars were brilliant — thousands of them scattered across the darkness like seeds thrown by a generous hand.

One girl pointed at the brightest star. "I wish I could marry that one," she said, laughing.

The other girl pointed at the Morning Star. "And I wish I could marry that one."

They fell asleep with their wishes on their lips. But the stars heard. The brightest star and the Morning Star descended from the sky while the girls slept, and when the girls awoke, they found themselves in the sky world.

The first girl was the wife of the brightest star. His home was beautiful — walls of light, floors of silver, a roof made of the deepest night sky. But everything was strange. The food tasted of starlight, not of earth. The water tasted of distance, not of rivers.

The star husband warned her: "There is one rule. You must never dig around a certain root — a turnip-like root that grows in the garden."

The girl agreed. But curiosity — that oldest and most dangerous of human qualities — overcame her. She dug around the root. When she pulled it up, she saw a hole through the floor of the sky world. Far below, she could see the earth — the plains, the rivers, the smoke rising from the tipis.

She was homesick. She wept, and her tears fell through the hole like rain.

Her star husband found her weeping and understood. He could not keep her against her will — the stars do not hold prisoners. Together they wove a rope of basswood bark, long enough to reach the earth.

The girl began to descend. But the rope was too short. It ended thirty feet above the ground, and the girl fell. She survived — the earth caught her gently — but she was changed. She was no longer entirely of the sky world, and no longer entirely of the earth. She walked among her people, but her eyes were always turned upward, always searching.

Her star husband remained in the sky, visible as the evening star, shining brightest in the west just after sunset — watching, waiting, remembering the wife who chose the earth over the stars.

title: The Blackfoot Creation: Apistotoke, Na'pi, and the World
summary: Apistotoke (Ihtsipatapiyohpa), the Great Spirit, created first the Sky Beings: Naato'si the Sun, Ko'komiki'somm the Moon, and the stars including Aapisowaahs the Morning Star. He then created Ksahkomitapi (Earth) as mother to all creation. Apistotoke created Na'pi (Old Man), the first man and demigod who shaped the world with his wife Kipitaakii (Old Lady). Using mud collected by Turtle during a great flood, Na'pi designed the earth, then created men, women, animals, and plants. He taught the Blackfoot people which plants to eat and animals to hunt, especially the buffalo.
full_text:
Apistotoke — called Ihtsipatapiyohpa, the Old Man Who Creates Us By Thought — stood in the void before creation. There was nothing around him. No ground beneath his feet, no sky above his head. Only the darkness and the silence and the power of his own mind.

He thought, and the thought became Sky Beings. Naato'si the Sun was the first — a being of fire and light who would illuminate everything that followed. Ko'komiki'somm the Moon was the second — a being of silver and shadow who would govern the night. And the stars came after, scattered across the sky like embers from a fire.

Then Apistotoke created Ksahkomitapi — the Earth — as mother to all creation. She was the ground beneath the sky, the body that held the roots, the foundation upon which all life would build.

Apistotoke then created Na'pi — Old Man — the first man and demigod who would shape the world with his own hands. Na'pi was not merely a human but a being of creative power, capable of molding the earth like clay and breathing life into the forms he made.

With his wife Kipitaakii — Old Lady — Na'pi set about the work of creation. They made the mountains and the valleys, the rivers and the lakes, the forests and the plains.

But the earth was covered in water. A great flood had washed over the land, and nothing grew. Na'pi sent Turtle to dive to the bottom of the flood and bring up mud. Turtle dove deep — deeper than any creature had gone before — and surfaced with a pawful of mud in his webbed hand.

Na'pi took the mud and shaped it. He molded it into hills and plains, into riverbeds and lake beds. He placed the mud on the back of a great turtle, and the mud grew, spreading across the shell until it became the land — Turtle Island, the Blackfoot call it.

Na'pi created men and women, animals and plants. He taught the Blackfoot people which plants to eat and which to avoid. He showed them which animals to hunt — especially the buffalo, whose body provided food, clothing, shelter, and tools.

When his work was done, Na'pi departed. He walked toward the western mountain and disappeared into the sunset. But his creation endures — the land, the people, the buffalo, the stars — all of it the thought of Apistotoke, shaped by the hands of Na'pi.

title: Origin of the Wind
summary: Na'pi discovered two bags containing summer and winter. Determined to make the seasons equal, he tried to steal them but failed. He sent a prairie chicken who successfully grabbed the summer bag. The guardians chased the bird, slicing at the grass and cutting the bag open. Strong wind burst forth. Later, Napi burned himself and climbed a mountain to summon cooling wind through medicine-making. The wind blew so fiercely he was nearly thrown off the mountain. He survived by grabbing a birch tree, his fingers leaving marks that gave the birch its distinctive patterned bark visible today.
full_text:
Na'pi discovered two bags in a lodge at the edge of the world. One bag was warm and bright, filled with the essence of summer — the heat of the sun, the green of the grass, the hum of insects. The other bag was cold and dark, filled with the essence of winter — the bite of frost, the silence of snow, the stillness of frozen rivers.

Na'pi was a practical being. He saw no reason why winter should be longer than summer, or summer longer than winter. "I will make them equal," he declared. He tried to steal both bags, but the bags were guarded by spirits who watched them day and night.

Na'pi sent a prairie chicken to steal the summer bag. The prairie chicken was small and quick, and it succeeded where Na'pi had failed — it grabbed the bag in its claws and flew away.

The guardians chased the bird across the plains. They caught up to it and sliced at the grass with their knives, cutting the bag open. Strong wind burst forth — the hot wind of summer that dries the rivers and cracks the earth.

The summer bag was ruined. Its contents scattered across the land in patches — here a warm day, there a cold snap, everywhere the remnants of a summer that had been torn apart.

Later, Na'pi burned himself on a fire. The pain was terrible, and he needed cooling wind to ease his suffering. He climbed a mountain and performed a medicine ceremony, calling the wind from the four directions. The wind came — but too strongly. It blew so fiercely that Na'pi was nearly thrown from the mountain.

He survived by grabbing a birch tree, wrapping his fingers around its trunk. His fingers left marks in the bark — the distinctive patterned marks that birch trees still bear today.

The story explains why seasons are unequal, why birch trees have patterned bark, and why the wind sometimes comes too strong. It is a Blackfoot teaching about the consequences of tampering with the natural order — and the persistence of the marks left by those who try.

title: Language on a Mountain
summary: After a great flood swept through the land, Na'pi (Old Man) gathered all the people on top of a large mountain. He gave them water of different colors—black, red, yellow, and white—and told them to drink and then speak. Each group that drank the colored water spoke a different language. Only those who received the black water spoke the same language; these were the bands of the Blackfoot Confederacy: the Piegan, Siksika, and Blood (Kainai) people. This event was said to have taken place on the highest mountain in the Montana reservation.
full_text:
After a great flood swept through the land, Na'pi gathered all the people on top of a large mountain. They were wet, frightened, and exhausted. They had lost everything — their homes, their stored food, their ceremonial objects. All they had was each other.

Na'pi looked at the people and said, "You must learn to live together. But first, you must learn to speak to each other."

He gave them water of different colors — black, red, yellow, and white — and told them to drink. Each person chose a color and drank.

Those who drank the black water spoke the same language — the language of the Piegan, the Siksika, and the Blood people. These were the bands of the Blackfoot Confederacy, bound together by a shared tongue and a shared memory of the flood.

Those who drank the red water spoke another language. Those who drank the yellow spoke another still. And those who drank the white spoke a language that sounded like wind through grass.

The people who spoke different languages could no longer understand each other. They drifted apart, forming separate tribes, separate nations, separate worlds. But the Blackfoot remained together, for they shared the black water and the black water's language.

The event was said to have taken place on the highest mountain in the Montana reservation — a peak so tall that the snow never fully melts and the wind never stops blowing. The Blackfoot still climb it sometimes, though not for the water. They climb to remember the time when all people spoke one language, and to honor the moment when that unity was broken.

The story teaches that diversity is not a punishment but a consequence of creation — that the world is made richer by the variety of voices, even as it is made more complex. And it teaches that the Blackfoot Confederacy is special — chosen not by favoritism but by the accident of which water they drank.

title: The Legend of Red Coulee
summary: The Blackfoot were told by the Snake First Nations about a powerful medicine stone located between McLeod and Fort Benton, Montana, near the Marias River. Years later, a group of Blackfoot men traveled to find the stone. When they discovered it, their leader laughed at the story, calling it a child's tale, and rolled the stone down the hill. On their return journey, they were ambushed in battle. All but one man were killed. The place became known as Red Coulee, and ever after the Blackfoot would leave offerings when passing it, to ensure safety and protection on their journey.
full_text:
The Snake First Nations told the Blackfoot about a powerful medicine stone that lay in the valley between what is now McLeod and Fort Benton, Montana, near the Marias River. The stone was ancient and sacred, pulsing with spiritual energy that could heal the sick and protect the people.

Years passed. The Blackfoot remembered the story but did not act on it. Then a group of men decided to travel to find the stone. They were young and brave, and they believed that finding the stone would bring glory to their band.

When they discovered it, the leader laughed. He rolled the stone down the hill, mocking the story. "This is just a rock," he said. "The Snake people told us lies."

His companions were uneasy. They had heard the warnings about disrespecting sacred objects. But the leader was confident, and confidence is contagious.

On their return journey, they were ambushed in battle by enemies. The fight was fierce, and the Blackfoot were outnumbered. All but one man were killed. The survivor limped back to the village carrying the news of the disaster.

The place became known as Red Coulee — named for the blood that soaked the ground that day. And ever after, the Blackfoot would leave offerings when passing through the valley. They left tobacco, beads, and food — not because they feared the stone, but because they respected it.

The story teaches that sacred objects demand respect, and that mockery of spiritual power invites consequences. The leader who laughed at the stone did not die because the stone was evil, but because his disrespect opened him to the violence that the stone could have protected him from.

title: Na'pi Creates the Buffalo
summary: After Na'pi (Old Man) created the world and the first people, he saw that they were hungry. He went to a cave deep in the mountains where the buffalo were kept. Na'pi opened the cave and the buffalo poured out across the plains, providing food, clothing, and shelter for the people. He taught the Blackfoot how to conduct buffalo hunts with respect, using every part of the animal and giving thanks to the buffalo spirit. Na'pi emphasized that the buffalo were a gift from Apistotoke and must never be wasted, or they would disappear.
full_text:
Long ago, when the world was still young, the four-legged animals and the winged creatures lived together in peace. They shared the same trails, drank from the same streams, and sheltered beneath the same trees. But as the world grew more crowded, disputes arose over food, territory, and the right to move freely across the land.

The council of the animals was called. Elk, Deer, Wolf, and Bear sat in a circle with Eagle, Crow, Hawk, and Owl. The discussion was heated. Each species believed it deserved more than the others.

A young Raven, barely fledged, flew to the center of the circle and proposed a solution no one had considered. He suggested that the council establish the rules of the hunt — who could be hunted, by whom, and under what circumstances. The older animals laughed at the young bird, but his idea was wise.

The council established that predators must show respect for their prey, that no species could be hunted to extinction, and that the spirits of the slain must be honored with ceremony. These rules, the animals agreed, would be enforced by the spirits of the land and sky.

The story is told to explain why certain animals are scarce and others abundant, and why the proper ceremonies must be observed before any hunt. It teaches that the balance of nature is not automatic but maintained through agreement and respect.

title: The Beaver Bundle Ceremony
summary: The Beaver Bundle is the most sacred medicine bundle of the Blackfoot people, said to have been given by the underwater spirits. According to legend, a Blackfoot man encountered beavers who taught him sacred songs, rituals, and the use of medicinal plants. The bundle contains various sacred objects including animal skins, pipes, and herbs, each with specific powers. The Beaver Bundle ceremony involves elaborate rituals, singing, and smoking the pipe. It is used for healing, ensuring good fortune, and maintaining the balance between the human and spirit worlds. The bundle is passed down through generations with great ceremony.
full_text:
A young man of the Lakota had been cursed by a medicine man who envied his success with the women of the village. The curse took the form of a persistent illness that no healer could cure — his skin turned gray, his eyes dimmed, and a heaviness settled over him like a blanket of stone.

The young man's grandmother, who remembered the old ways, told him to seek a vision. She prepared him for the quest — fasting, praying, smudging him with sage. He climbed to the top of the highest hill he could find and lay down beneath the stars.

For three days and three nights he fasted. On the fourth night, a figure appeared in his vision — a warrior dressed in the feathers of the eagle and the hide of the bear. The warrior spoke: "You have been cursed by human jealousy, but the spirits can break any curse. You must find the sacred root that grows where the lightning has struck and the rain has pooled. Brew it as tea and drink it at dawn."

The young man returned to his village and searched for the root. He found it growing in a meadow where a lightning bolt had split an oak tree and rain had gathered in the wound. He brewed the tea and drank it at dawn, and the curse lifted from him like smoke.

The story teaches that visions are not mere dreams but communications from the spirit world, and that the remedies for spiritual illness often come from unexpected sources.

title: Napi and the Rolling Skull
summary: Na'pi was walking across the prairie when he kicked a buffalo skull and told it to get out of his way. The skull began to roll after him, chasing him across the plains. Na'pi ran to a tree and climbed it, but the skull called to the tree, asking it to bend down. The tree bent, and the skull rolled up to Na'pi's hiding place. Na'pi was trapped and the skull would have killed him, but he tricked it by saying he saw more buffalo over the hill. When the skull turned to look, Na'pi leaped down and escaped.
full_text:
In the days when the Blackfoot were still migrating with the buffalo, a young woman was left behind when her band moved on. She had fallen ill during the journey, and her family, believing she would die, left her in a shelter of branches with a small fire and a few days' food.

She did not die. Instead, she lay in the shelter and dreamed. In her dream, a bear came to her — a great brown bear with eyes like polished amber. The bear spoke: "I will heal you, but you must promise to share the knowledge of healing with your people."

The woman agreed. The bear touched her with his paw, and the illness left her body. When she awoke, she was well — stronger than she had ever been.

She returned to her band and became a healer. She knew which roots cured fevers, which leaves stopped bleeding, which bark eased pain. Her knowledge came from the bear, and she honored the bear in every healing ceremony.

The story establishes the origin of the Bear Medicine Society among the Blackfoot, and teaches that healing knowledge is a gift from the spirits that must be shared, not hoarded.

title: The Origin of the Medicine Pipe
summary: A beautiful woman appeared to a Blackfoot man who had gone on a vision quest. She gave him a pipe decorated with eagle feathers and taught him the prayers and songs that went with it. She told him the pipe would be a mediator between the people and the spirit world. When he returned to camp, the elders recognized the pipe's power and established the Medicine Pipe society. The pipe is central to Blackfoot ceremonies, used for healing, making peace, and communicating with Apistotoke. Its keeper must follow strict taboos and conduct annual renewal ceremonies.
full_text:
The Sun Dance is the most sacred ceremony of the Blackfoot people. It is held once a year, at the time when the moon is full and the buffalo are fat. The people gather from all the bands, setting up their lodges in a great circle around the sacred pole.

The pole is a cottonwood tree, selected by the medicine men for its straightness and height. It is stripped of its branches and raised in the center of the camp, its top reaching toward the sky where the Sun lives.

Dancers attach themselves to the pole with skewers made of bone, piercing the skin of their chests or backs. They dance for four days, looking only at the sun, their blood flowing down the pole like red roots. They do not eat or drink during the dance. Their sacrifice is a prayer — a prayer for the renewal of the world, for the return of the buffalo, for the health of the people.

The Sun Dance is not merely a ritual but a covenant. The people promise to honor the Sun, and the Sun promises to return each morning. The dance renews this covenant annually, ensuring that the light and warmth upon which all life depends will continue.

The story teaches that sacrifice is not suffering but exchange — the giving of something precious in return for something essential.

title: Sweet Medicine and the Four Sacred Arrows
summary: Sweet Medicine (Motsé'eóeve) was the great prophet and law-giver of the Cheyenne people. He journeyed to Nóávóse (Bear Butte) in the Black Hills where Ma'heo'o (the Wise One Above) gave him the four sacred arrows—the Maahótse. Two arrows were for hunting, to ensure success in finding buffalo, and two were for warfare, to protect the people from enemies. Sweet Medicine also received the structure of Cheyenne government, the Council of Forty-Four peace chiefs, the military societies, and the system of legal justice. He predicted the coming of horses, white men, and the loss of the buffalo. He also invented the hoop-and-stick game (chunkey).
full_text:
Old Man Coyote was walking along the river when he heard singing. The voice was beautiful — clear and strong, rising above the sound of the water like a hawk rising on a thermal.

Coyote followed the voice to a bend in the river where a woman sat on a rock, singing to the fish. The fish gathered around her, their mouths open, their eyes bright. They were captivated by her song.

"Who are you?" Coyote asked.

"I am the River Singer," the woman said. "My song keeps the fish in the river. Without it, they would swim away and the people would have no food."

Coyote was jealous. He wanted the song for himself. "Teach me," he said.

The River Singer shook her head. "The song cannot be taught. It is a gift of the river, and the river gives it only to those who listen."

Coyote sat beside her and listened. For three days he listened, and on the third day, he began to hear the song — not with his ears but with his heart. The song was the sound of water over stones, of wind through reeds, of fish swimming in the deep.

Coyote took the song to the people. He taught them how to fish with nets and hooks, and he taught them the songs that honor the spirits of the fish. The people never went hungry again.

The story teaches that wisdom comes not from taking but from listening, and that the gifts of the natural world are given to those who are patient enough to receive them.

title: Erect Horns and the Sacred Buffalo Hat
summary: Erect Horns (Tomȯsévėséhe) was the prophet of the Só'taeo'o people who later merged with the Cheyenne. He received the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat) at Tȯhóonévose (Stone Hammer Mountain) near the Great Lakes in Minnesota. The sacred hat represents female power, while the Sacred Arrows represent male power—together they form the two great covenants of the Cheyenne Nation. Erect Horns gave the people the Sun Dance ceremony and convinced the tribe to abandon their sedentary agricultural lifestyle, adopt the nomadic Plains horse culture, and rely on buffalo for survival. His vision transformed the Cheyenne from earth-lodge dwellers to tipi-dwelling Plains warriors.
full_text:
Napi was walking along a frozen lake when he saw a woman sitting on the ice, fishing through a hole. She had no coat, no blanket, nothing to protect her from the cold. Her skin was blue with frost, and her lips were white.

"Are you not cold?" Napi asked.

"I am the Ice Woman," she said. "Cold is my element. I do not feel it."

Napi was intrigued. He sat beside her and watched her fish. She pulled fish after fish from the hole — great fat trout that would have fed a family for a week.

"Give me a fish," Napi said.

"I will give you a fish if you give me something in return," the Ice Woman said.

"What do you want?"

"I want your shadow."

Napi agreed. The Ice Woman took his shadow and gave him a fish. Napi ate the fish and was satisfied. But when he stood to leave, he had no shadow. He was just a man without a shadow, walking on the ice.

The people saw him and were afraid. A man without a shadow is a man without a spirit, they said. Napi tried to explain, but no one would listen.

He went back to the Ice Woman. "Give me my shadow back," he said.

"I have already eaten it," the Ice Woman said. "Shadows are very tasty."

Napi was furious, but there was nothing he could do. To this day, Napi has no shadow — or so the story says. The Blackfoot tell this story to warn against the danger of trading something essential for something temporary.

title: Cheyenne Creation Story
summary: In the beginning, all was water and nothing existed but the Creator Ma'heo'o and aquatic birds. The Creator sent various waterbirds—the loon, otter, beaver, and turtle—to dive to the bottom of the endless water to bring up mud. After several failures, the turtle succeeded in bringing up the primordial mud. From this mud, the Creator formed the earth. Then he created grass, trees, animals, and finally human beings. The Cheyenne emerged from beneath the earth onto the surface, guided by the Creator. The story teaches that all creation is interconnected and that humans must respect the earth as their mother.
full_text:
In the beginning, the Blackfoot people lived in darkness. They had no fire, no warmth, no light. They huddled together in their lodges, wrapped in buffalo robes, their breath making clouds in the cold air.

The Sun pitied them. He sent a fire trail across the sky — a streak of flame that landed on a high mountain. The fire burned there, warming the rocks and melting the snow, but the people could not reach it. The mountain was too steep.

A young man volunteered to climb. He was the fastest runner in the village, and the strongest climber. He began the ascent at dawn and climbed all day, his fingers bleeding on the rock, his legs burning with effort.

At the top, he found the fire — not a campfire but a living flame, pulsing with energy, casting shadows that danced on the rock. He took a burning branch and began the descent.

But the fire was alive, and it did not want to be taken. It fought him, burning his hands, scorching his clothes. The young man held on, his grip tightening with each burn.

He reached the bottom at dawn. His hands were charred, his body covered in burns. But the fire was in his hands, and he brought it to the people.

The people gathered around the fire, their faces illuminated for the first time. They cooked their food, warmed their bodies, and told stories in the light. The young man was honored as a hero, and the fire was kept burning in every lodge.

The story teaches that the gifts of the spirits are not free — they must be earned through sacrifice and determination.

title: The Pawnee Capture of the Sacred Arrows
summary: Around 1830, the Cheyenne attacked a Skidi Pawnee hunting party in central Nebraska, carrying their most sacred possession—the Maahótse (Four Sacred Arrows) bundle. During the battle, the Pawnee captured the sacred arrows, described as the greatest disaster in Cheyenne history. The Cheyenne made replica arrows and desperately tried to recover the originals. They recovered one arrow directly from the Pawnee; the Lakota captured another and returned it for horses. The replicas were ceremonially returned to Bear Butte. This loss was believed to have been caused by the people's failure to properly honor the arrows, and it foreshadowed the misfortunes that would come to the Cheyenne.
full_text:
A great chief of the Blackfoot had a vision in which the Sun appeared to him and gave him a sacred object — a pipe carved from red stone, its bowl decorated with the image of a buffalo calf. The Sun told the chief to form a society of pipe keepers who would maintain the pipe and use it in ceremonies for the good of the people.

The chief gathered the wisest men and women of the tribe and formed the Medicine Pipe Society. The members were chosen for their character — honesty, generosity, courage, and wisdom. They were given the responsibility of keeping the pipe, conducting ceremonies, and interpreting its messages.

The pipe was used for healing the sick, making peace between warring bands, and communicating with the spirit world. When the pipe was smoked, the smoke carried prayers to the Sun, and the Sun listened.

The Medicine Pipe ceremony involved elaborate rituals — songs, dances, the offering of food and tobacco. The pipe was treated with the same respect as a living being, for it was believed that the spirit of the Sun resided within it.

The story teaches that sacred objects are not merely tools but living presences, and that those who care for them bear a heavy responsibility.

title: Old Woman's Water and the Buffalo Cap
summary: An old woman who lived by a sacred spring found that her water had healing powers. She shared it with a young warrior who was wounded, and he was miraculously healed. The woman then revealed herself as a manifestation of the earth's power. She gave the warrior a buffalo cap made from the scalp of a sacred buffalo, which became the Ésevone (Sacred Buffalo Hat). The cap could summon buffalo herds and protect the people from harm. She taught the warrior the rituals needed to care for the cap and warned that if it was ever neglected, the buffalo would disappear and hardship would follow.
full_text:
Napi was sitting by a fire one evening when a group of children came to him with a question. "Tell us the story of how the buffalo came to be," they said.

Napi smiled and began. "In the beginning, there were no buffalo on the plains. The people had no meat, no hides, no bones for tools. They survived on roots and berries, and they were hungry."

"A great spirit — called Buffalo Bull by some, called Sun by others — saw the people's suffering and took pity on them. He descended from the sky in the form of a bull, his coat the color of ripe wheat, his horns curved like crescent moons."

"The Buffalo Bull spoke to the people: 'I will give you my body so that you may live. But you must promise to honor me and my kind. You must use every part of what you take — the meat for food, the hide for clothing and shelter, the bones for tools, the sinew for thread, the horns for cups and spoons. You must waste nothing. And you must perform ceremonies to honor the spirits of the buffalo who give themselves to you.'"

"The people agreed. The Buffalo Bull lay down and offered his life. From his body came the first buffalo herd — hundreds of great beasts that roamed the plains, their hooves thundering, their breath steaming in the cold air."

"And the people kept their promise. They honored the buffalo in ceremonies, they used every part of what they took, and they wasted nothing. The buffalo gave themselves willingly, for they knew the people were worthy."

The children listened in silence. When Napi finished, the oldest child said, "We will remember."

And they did.

title: Wihio the Spider Trickster
summary: Wihio is the Cheyenne trickster figure, a spider-like being similar to Iktomi of the Lakota. He is clever but greedy, often getting into trouble because of his selfishness. In one story, Wihio tried to kill some ducks for a feast by tricking them into a dance with their eyes closed. A loon peeked and exposed the trick, and Wihio was shamed. In another tale, Wihio's greed caused him to be trapped inside a hollow log by his own scheme. Wihio stories serve as cautionary tales, teaching Cheyenne children about the consequences of selfish behavior and the importance of community values.
full_text:
The Blackfoot tell of a time when the rivers ran dry and the grass turned brown across the plains. The buffalo had migrated far to the south, and the people were starving. A council was held, and the eldest medicine man proposed that a delegation travel to the south to find the buffalo and ask them to return.

The delegation set out — twelve men and women, each chosen for their spiritual power. They traveled for many days, following the trail of the buffalo across the burned grasslands.

On the seventh day, they found the buffalo — a great herd grazing in a valley where water still flowed. The leader of the delegation approached the chief of the buffalo, a massive bull with a coat like polished bronze.

"We have come from the north," the leader said. "Our people are starving. We ask you to return to our lands so that we may feed our children."

The chief of the buffalo regarded the humans for a long time. Then he said, "We will return. But you must promise to honor us in all your ceremonies, to use every part of what we give, and to teach your children the songs that honor our spirits."

The delegation agreed. The buffalo returned with them to the north, and the people feasted. From that day forward, the Blackfoot honored the buffalo in every ceremony, and the buffalo gave themselves willingly.

The story teaches that the relationship between humans and animals is not one of dominion but of mutual obligation — a covenant that must be renewed through ceremony and respect.

title: Nonoma the Spirit of Thunder
summary: Nonoma is the Cheyenne spirit of thunder, a powerful being who controls storms and brings rain to the plains. When Nonoma flaps his wings, thunder rolls across the sky. He is both feared and respected, as his storms can bring life-giving rain or destructive hail. The Cheyenne perform ceremonies to honor Nonoma and ask for his blessing on their crops and buffalo hunts. Thunder is associated with the renewal of life in spring, and the first thunder of the season signals the time for planting and the Sun Dance ceremony.
full_text:
A warrior of the Blackfoot once went alone into the mountains to seek a vision. He climbed to the highest peak he could find and lay down on a flat rock. He fasted and prayed for four days and four nights.

On the fourth night, a spirit appeared to him — a great eagle with wings that spanned the width of the sky. The eagle spoke: "I have watched you. You are brave and strong, but you are also proud. Pride is a dangerous thing for a warrior, for it makes him fight for glory rather than for his people."

The warrior bowed his head. "Teach me," he said.

The eagle taught him the songs of the wind, the language of the clouds, the meaning of the stars. He taught him that true strength is not the strength of the arm but the strength of the heart, and that a warrior's greatest weapon is not his spear but his compassion.

When the warrior returned to his village, he was changed. He no longer fought for glory but for the protection of the people. He became a leader, not because he was the strongest or the bravest, but because he was the wisest.

The story teaches that visions are not merely personal experiences but gifts from the spirits that must be used for the good of the community.

title: The Animal Dance
summary: The Animal Dance was a hunting ceremony received by Sweet Medicine at the Sacred Mountain (Bear Butte) to bring success to Cheyenne hunters. In this elaborate ceremony, men dressed as various animals—buffalo, deer, elk, antelope—while members of the Bowstring Society pretended to hunt them. Everything was done backwards for amusement: the animals chased the hunters, and all moved in reverse directions. The ceremony involved the entire community, with women preparing special foods and regalia. It was both a serious spiritual appeal for successful hunts and a joyful celebration that reinforced social bonds.
full_text:
A young Crow woman was gathering berries near the river when she saw a strange light beneath the water. She knelt to look closer and saw that the light was coming from a stone — a perfect round stone that glowed with an inner fire, pulsing like a heartbeat.

She reached into the water and grasped the stone. It was warm to the touch, and when she held it, she felt a surge of power flow through her body. She knew immediately that this was a medicine stone — a sacred object of great spiritual significance.

She carried the stone back to the village and showed it to the elders. They recognized its power and placed it in the medicine lodge, where it was used in healing ceremonies and to bring rain during droughts.

The woman who found the stone became a medicine woman of great renown. She could heal the sick with the stone's power, and she could call rain by singing the songs the stone taught her in dreams.

The story teaches that sacred objects reveal themselves to those who are ready to receive them, and that spiritual power is given to those who will use it for the good of the community.

title: Comanche Creation: The Dust People
summary: The Great Spirit collected swirls of dust from the four directions—north, south, east, and west—and molded them into strong, powerful figures. He breathed life into them, and the Comanche people were born from the earth itself, infused with the strength of mighty storms and the spirit of the wind. However, a shape-shifting demon formed in the shadows, envious of the people's power. It tormented the Comanche by taking many forms. The Great Spirit cast the demon into a bottomless pit, but before falling, the demon shattered into countless pieces that took refuge in the fangs and stingers of rattlesnakes, scorpions, and spiders, continuing to harm people to this day.
full_text:
In the Crow creation story, the first people lived underground in a world of darkness. They were led by a woman named Pretty Owl, who heard the sound of a flute playing above them. She followed the sound upward and found herself in the light of the world above.

The sun was shining, the grass was green, and the sky was so blue it hurt to look at. Pretty Owl was amazed. She returned underground and told the people about the world above, and they followed her upward.

When they emerged, they found themselves on a vast plain. The sun warmed their faces, and the wind carried the scent of sage and wildflowers. They built their lodges and planted their gardens, and they lived in harmony with the land.

The story teaches that the Crow people came from the earth itself, and that their connection to the land is not merely physical but spiritual.

title: Coyote the Comanche Trickster
summary: Coyote is the central trickster figure in Comanche folklore. Unlike the spider tricksters of other Plains tribes, Coyote is a clever but flawed creature who often helps humans while constantly getting into trouble due to greed, dishonesty, and recklessness. Many Comanche storytellers refer to Coyote affectionately as the brother of the Comanches. In one tale, Coyote tries to steal fire from the fire people and is burned, explaining his singed fur. In another, he tricks prairie dogs into leaving their holes so he can catch them, but is himself outwitted by Skunk. Coyote stories teach social values through humor.
full_text:
Long ago, a Crow hunter tracked a wounded elk across the plains. The elk was fast despite its injury, and the hunter followed for three days. On the third day, he came to a river he had never seen before — a river that ran with water so clear you could see every stone on the bottom.

As he knelt to drink, he saw a figure in the water — not a reflection but a woman made of water, her body flowing and shifting with the current. She was beautiful, and her eyes held the depth of the river.

"You are far from home, hunter," she said. "The elk you chase is my messenger. It led you here because the spirits have a message for your people."

The woman told the hunter of a great danger approaching from the north — a tribe of enemies who would attack the Crow in the winter. She gave him medicine to protect his people and instructions for a ceremony that would ensure their safety.

The hunter returned to his village and told the elders what he had seen. They performed the ceremony as the water woman had instructed, and when the enemies came, they were repelled.

The story teaches that the spirits of the natural world are always watching, and that they will help those who respect their domain.

title: How the Buffalo Were Released on Earth
summary: Long ago, all the buffalo were kept hidden in a cave deep beneath the earth by a powerful spirit who did not want to share them with humans. A young Comanche warrior, guided by a wolf spirit, discovered the cave entrance. Following the wolf's advice, he transformed into a buffalo calf and entered the herd. When the keeper opened the cave door to let the buffalo graze, the warrior-turned-calf stampeded the herd out of the cave. The buffalo poured across the plains, and the Comanche people had food and clothing. The wolf spirit taught the people how to hunt the buffalo with respect.
source: Native Languages of the Americas / Comanche folklore
full_text:
A Crow warrior named Long Hair was known for his bravery in battle. He had never been defeated, and his reputation grew with each victory. But pride grew with it too, and Long Hair began to believe he was invincible.

One day, he challenged a rival tribe's champion to single combat. The two met on the plains, and Long Hair fought with his usual skill. But his opponent was stronger and faster, and Long Hair was defeated.

Humiliated, Long Hair retreated to the mountains. He fasted and prayed, seeking the strength to fight again. On the fourth day, a mountain spirit appeared to him and said, "Your defeat was a gift. It taught you that no man is invincible, and that true strength comes not from never falling but from rising after you fall."

Long Hair returned to his people, not with the arrogance of the undefeated but with the humility of the humbled. He became a great leader, not because he never lost, but because he learned from his losses.

The story teaches that defeat is not failure but education, and that the greatest warriors are those who can accept their weaknesses and grow from them.

title: The Legend of Manitou Springs
summary: A great battle once took place between the Comanche and the Shoshone near a sacred spring. Both tribes claimed the spring as their territory, and many warriors fell on both sides. The Great Spirit, seeing the bloodshed, caused the waters of the spring to bubble up with healing powers. The spring's mineral waters were said to have medicinal properties that could heal wounds and cure sickness. After the battle, the tribes agreed that the spring would be neutral ground where warriors from all nations could come to heal. The site, now Manitou Springs, Colorado, remains a place of spiritual significance.
full_text:
The Crow people believed that dreams were messages from the spirit world. When a young man had a recurring dream about a white horse running across the plains, he told the elders. They said, "Follow the dream. The horse is real."

The young man traveled in the direction of the dream — east, toward the rising sun. He traveled for many days until he came to a valley where a herd of white horses grazed in the morning mist.

He caught the white horse from his dream and rode it back to his village. The horse was swift and strong, and it became the foundation of the Crow's horse culture. The Crow became known as the finest horsemen on the plains, and the white horse was honored in ceremonies for generations.

The story teaches that dreams are not mere fantasies but guides to action, and that the spirit world offers gifts to those who are brave enough to follow their visions.

title: Skunk Outwits Coyote
summary: Coyote came upon a prairie dog village and decided to catch himself a meal. He blocked all the holes except one and waited with his mouth open at the entrance. But Skunk saw what Coyote was doing and decided to teach him a lesson. Skunk approached Coyote and asked what he was doing. Coyote explained his plan, and Skunk offered to help by driving the prairie dogs toward Coyote's mouth. Instead, Skunk walked up to Coyote and sprayed him directly in the face. Coyote ran away howling, and the prairie dogs escaped. Skunk laughed at the trickster, proving that even the cleverest schemer can be outsmarted.
full_text:
A Crow woman named Bear Woman was known for her wisdom and her connection to the bear spirits. She could communicate with bears, and the bears respected her as one of their own.

When a drought struck the Crow lands, Bear Woman went to the bear's den and asked for help. The chief bear said, "We will share our water with you, but you must promise that your people will honor the bears in their ceremonies."

Bear Woman agreed. The bears led the Crow to a hidden spring that never dried up, and the people survived the drought. From that day forward, the Crow honored the bears in their ceremonies, and the bears continued to share their water.

The story teaches that the natural world is full of allies, and that those who maintain proper relationships with animal spirits will never lack for help.

title: The Release of the Wild Animals
summary: In the beginning, all wild animals were confined in a great underground cavern by a spirit who wanted to protect them. The Comanche people had only dogs and horses. A brave warrior followed a trail to the cavern entrance and heard the stamping and snorting of many animals within. With the help of the wind spirit, he opened the cavern door. Out rushed deer, antelope, elk, bears, wolves, and mountain lions, spreading across the plains. The warrior was nearly trampled but survived. The spirit, angry at the release, caused some animals to become dangerous to humans, while others remained gentle.
full_text:
A young Crow boy found a baby raven that had fallen from its nest. He carried it home and raised it as a pet. The raven grew large and intelligent, and it learned to speak a few words of Crow.

One day, the raven said, "I must return to my people. I am not a pet but a messenger of the spirits."

The boy was sad but released the raven. The bird flew away, but it returned the next day with a gift — a bundle of sacred herbs that the Crow used in their healing ceremonies.

The raven continued to bring gifts and messages from the spirit world, and the boy became a medicine man of great power. The raven was honored as the boy's spirit guide, and the story taught that even the smallest act of kindness — raising a fallen bird — can lead to great spiritual reward.

title: Wolf Spirit and the Warrior's Vision
summary: A young Comanche warrior went on a vision quest alone in the mountains, fasting for four days without water. On the fourth night, a Wolf appeared to him in a vision. The Wolf said, 'I am your brother. I will give you strength, courage, and the ability to track your enemies. But you must never kill my kind, for we are connected.' The warrior returned to his people with Wolf as his guardian spirit. He became a great hunter and warrior, always guided by Wolf's wisdom. This story reflects the Comanche belief in animal spirit guides who grant powers to individuals through vision quests.
full_text:
The Crow people believed that the world was divided into three realms — the upper world of the sky spirits, the middle world of humans, and the lower world of the water spirits. Each realm had its own rules, its own ceremonies, and its own dangers.

A Crow medicine man once traveled to the lower world to retrieve the spirit of a dying child. He dove into a lake and found himself in a world of blue darkness, where the water spirits lived in houses of coral and stone.

The chief of the water spirits said, "You may have the child's spirit, but you must give something in return."

The medicine man offered his strongest medicine — a bundle of sacred objects that he had gathered over a lifetime. The water spirits accepted, and the child's spirit was returned to its body.

The medicine man returned to the surface without his medicine, but the child lived. The story teaches that the greatest gift is sacrifice, and that those who give of themselves for others are honored by the spirits.

title: Old Man Coyote Creates the World
summary: In the beginning, Old Man Coyote (Isáahkawuattee) was alone upon a great ocean. He saw two male ducks floating on the water and asked them what lay beneath. One duck dove deep and returned with a root in its beak; a second more dangerous dive brought up mud. Using this mud, Old Man Coyote built an island that grew into all the lands of Earth. He used the root to create plants and trees. Noticing the world was too flat, Old Man Coyote shaped mountains, rivers, and valleys. Then he molded man from clay, and created woman so that humans would be happy and multiply. He created female ducks so the ducks could be happy too.
full_text:
In the Crow winter count — a pictographic calendar kept by the tribe — each year was recorded by a single image that represented the most significant event of that year. A buffalo stampede, a solar eclipse, a visit from a strange tribe — each one drawn on a hide and passed down through generations.

One year, the image was of a woman holding a baby beneath a lightning bolt. That was the year a Crow woman gave birth during a terrible storm, and the lightning struck so close that it set the grass on fire. But the baby was unharmed, and the woman said, "This child is protected by the spirits."

The child grew to be a great leader, and the winter count remembered the night of his birth for generations. The story teaches that the Crow recorded their history not in words but in images, and that every life is connected to the larger story of the people.

title: The Sweat Lodge Origin: Seven Bison and Bones Together
summary: Seven Bison and their male human companion fought against the angry bison Bones Together, whose pure bone armor was impenetrable. As each bison charged, they broke their legs against Bones Together. Finally the human companion, blessed by an eagle with the power to transform into a feather, faced Bones Together. The monster charged four times, but the man turned into a feather and wafted out of harm's way. On the fourth charge, the man shot an arrow into Bones Together's rectum, piercing his heart. Though victorious, the bison were grievously injured. Together they performed the first Sweat Lodge ceremony, which healed all the bison. Afterward, the Seven Bison rose into the sky to become the Big Dipper, and the man became the Little Dipper.
full_text:
After the seven bison and their human companion defeated Bones Together and were healed by the first Sweat Lodge ceremony, the Creator raised the seven bison into the sky to become the Big Dipper — the Seven Bison. The human companion became the Little Dipper, following them eternally across the night sky.

The Crow look at the Big Dipper and remember the sacrifice and healing of the first Sweat Lodge. The stars serve as a constant reminder of the power of prayer, purification, and the bond between humans and animals.

This story connects the Crow people to the cosmos and their daily rituals. When they look up at the night sky, they see not merely stars but the story of their ancestors — a story of courage, sacrifice, and the enduring bond between the people and the buffalo who sustain them.

title: The Man and the Seven Rams
summary: A Crow man of immense ability and power once encountered the Seven Rams, magnificent creatures of the mountains. The man, confident in his strength, thought he could overpower them. But the Seven Rams taught him humility. Despite his great power, the man learned that he must respect the Sweat Lodge and its ceremonies, for the lodge's power was greater than any individual's. The Rams demonstrated that true strength comes from spiritual purity and connection to the Creator, not from physical prowess. The story emphasizes that even the most gifted individuals must submit to spiritual discipline and communal rituals.
full_text:
A Crow warrior named Spotted Elk was hunting alone in the mountains when he encountered a spirit in the form of a white buffalo. The buffalo spoke: "I have come to teach you the ways of the sacred pipe."

The warrior knelt. The white buffalo taught him the songs and prayers that accompany the pipe ceremony, and he gave the warrior a pipe carved from red stone, its bowl decorated with the image of a buffalo calf.

"This pipe connects the people to the spirits," the white buffalo said. "When it is smoked, the smoke carries your prayers to the sky. When it is held, its weight reminds you of the sacrifice of the buffalo."

Spotted Elk returned to his village with the pipe and taught the people its use. The pipe became the centerpiece of Crow ceremonies, and the white buffalo was honored as a messenger of the spirits.

title: Mannegishi (Little People)
summary: The Mannegishi are small, bald humanoid beings in Crow mythology, described as having large, bulging eyes and tiny, tan bodies. They are tricksters who live in rocky areas and along riverbanks. These little people are known for playing pranks on humans, leading travelers astray, and causing mischief. Despite their troublesome nature, they are not considered evil. Some stories say they can be helpful to those who treat them with respect. The Mannegishi are similar to fairies in European folklore and are found in various forms across many Plains Indian traditions, often associated with mysterious sounds and disappearing objects.
full_text:
In the Crow tradition, the Earth Mother was the first being to exist. She lay beneath the sky, her body the land itself — her hair the grass, her bones the mountains, her blood the rivers. She was alive, and she felt everything that happened on her surface.

When the first people walked across her, she felt their steps like gentle touches. When they built their lodges, she felt the stakes pierce her skin. When they planted their gardens, she felt the seeds take root in her flesh.

She loved the people, and she gave them everything they needed — water from her veins, food from her body, shelter from her stones. In return, she asked only that they honor her in their ceremonies and teach their children to respect the land.

The story teaches that the earth is not merely a resource but a living being, and that the relationship between humans and the earth is one of mutual care and respect.

title: Tobacco Society: Chief No Vitals Discovers Tobacco
summary: The Crow people believe that tobacco was first discovered by Chief No Vitals at Devils Lake in eastern North Dakota. The Creator instructed him to seek the sacred plant, telling him that the worship of tobacco would help the Crow honor God and maintain their connection to the spirit world. Chief No Vitals found the plant and brought it back to his people, establishing the Tobacco Society (Bacu'sua). The society ensures that all rites and rituals for cultivating tobacco are performed correctly. Smoking tobacco is believed to carry prayers directly to God, as the smoke ascends to the heavens. The sacred pipe society uses tobacco daily to maintain closeness with the Creator.
full_text:
A Crow woman dreamed that a great flood was coming. She told the elders, but they did not believe her. She prepared anyway — gathering food, building a raft, teaching her children to swim.

When the flood came, it was devastating. The rivers rose and covered the plains. The lodges were swept away. The people scrambled for higher ground.

The woman and her family survived on the raft she had built. She guided them to a hilltop where other survivors gathered. When the waters receded, they returned to the plains and rebuilt.

The woman was honored as a prophet, and the elders learned to listen to the dreams of women, for dreams are messages from the spirits.

title: Baaxpée and the Vision Quest
summary: Baaxpée is the sacred power of God (Akbaatatdia) in Crow belief, meaning 'power transcending the ordinary.' To acquire Baaxpée, a Crow must go on a vision quest (bilisshíissanne—'to fast from water'). The quester goes alone to an isolated peak, usually in the Wolf Mountains, fasting without food or water for two to three days. Self-mortification, including finger removal, is sometimes offered to show devotion. When a spirit pities the quester, it induces a vision, adopting the Crow as a child and bestowing Baaxpée. The spirit becomes a 'Medicine Father' who guides the Crow throughout life. The quester creates a Xapáaliia (medicine object) to represent the bond.
full_text:
A young Crow man fell in love with a woman from a rival tribe. Their love was forbidden, and the elders of both tribes opposed the match. But the lovers met secretly, exchanging gifts and whispered promises.

When their love was discovered, the young man was banished from his tribe. He traveled to the woman's village and was accepted there. Together they had children, and their descendants bridged the two tribes.

Over time, the marriage led to peace between the tribes. The story teaches that love can overcome the boundaries of tribe and tradition, and that the children of forbidden unions often bring healing to divided peoples.

title: The Sun Dance Lodge Symbolism
summary: The Crow Sun Dance lodge (Ashé Isée) is built as a microcosm of the universe. The central forked pole, representing God, faces east. A white flag tied to one branch represents Earth; a blue flag represents the sky. Three charcoal rings on the pole symbolize the three days of the dance and the three worlds of Crow cosmology. A buffalo head and eagle body are hung on the pole as patrons. Twelve cottonwood posts form the lodge boundary, representing the twelve months and the circle of life. For contemporary Christian Crows, the twelve posts also symbolize the twelve apostles and the three rings represent Christ's three days in the tomb.
full_text:
The Crow believed that each person was born with a spirit guide — an animal that would protect and guide them throughout their life. The spirit guide revealed itself in a vision, usually during the first vision quest.

A young Crow boy went on his vision quest alone in the mountains. He fasted for four days. On the third night, a wolf appeared to him — not a real wolf but a spirit wolf, its fur silver, its eyes the color of ice.

The wolf spoke: "I am your guide. I will walk with you all the days of your life. When you are lost, I will find the path. When you are afraid, I will give you courage. When you fight, I will fight beside you."

The boy returned to his village as a man, his spirit guide at his side. He became a great warrior and hunter, and the wolf's presence was felt in every success.

The story teaches that every person has a spiritual ally, and that the relationship between a person and their spirit guide is the foundation of Crow spiritual life.

title: Crow Morning Star
summary: In Crow belief, the Morning Star (Aapisowaahs) is a heroic figure who lights the night sky. He is the son of Naato'si (the Sun) and Ko'komiki'somm (the Moon), created by the first being Apistotoke. Old Man Coyote traveled to the sky world and brought knowledge of the Morning Star back to the people. The Morning Star is associated with new beginnings, hope, and guidance. In Crow ceremonies, the Morning Star is honored at dawn with prayers and songs. The star's appearance signals the time for certain rituals and serves as a reminder of the Crow's connection to the celestial realm.
full_text:
A Crow elder sat by the fire and told his grandchildren the story of how fire came to the people. "In the beginning," he said, "the people had no fire. They ate their food raw, and they shivered through the cold nights."

"A Coyote stole fire from the spirits who lived in the sky. He carried it down to earth in a hollow reed, and he gave it to the people. But the spirits were angry. They sent a great wind to blow out the fire."

"The people huddled around the fire, shielding it with their bodies. The wind blew and blew, but the people held firm. When the wind died down, the fire was still burning."

"The spirits saw that the people were determined to keep the fire, and they relented. They allowed the people to have fire, but they warned them: 'Fire is a gift, and like all gifts, it must be used wisely. Do not waste it. Do not let it spread. Do not use it for destruction.'"

"The people remembered. They used fire for cooking, for warmth, for light. They used it wisely, and the spirits watched with approval."

The grandchildren listened in silence. When the elder finished, the oldest grandchild said, "We will remember."

title: The Girl Who Married a Star
summary: A Crow girl gazed at the sky and wished to marry the Morning Star. Her wish was granted, and she was taken to the sky world where she became the wife of a star. She was happy but was told never to dig up a certain root. Lonely for her family, she eventually disobeyed and pulled the root, revealing a hole through which she could see her earthly home far below. Overcome with longing, she wove a rope to descend, but it was too short. She fell to Earth and survived, finding her way back to her people. The star husband, heartbroken, can still be seen in the morning sky.
