Raven's voraciousness is both a humorous trait — he is constantly scheming to get food, his plans becoming more elaborate and more ridiculous with each attempt — and a serious warning about what happens when consumption becomes uncontrolled.

The story is part of the larger Tsimshian Raven cycle that portrays Txamsem as both a world-creating culture hero and a deeply flawed, comic figure. Raven brings gifts to the people — light, fish, fire — but he also brings trouble, and his hunger is the source of both his generosity and his destruction.

title: Wolf Clan and the Salmon (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian legend tells of a volcanic eruption caused by disrespect for the salmon. The Wolf Clan, one of the four major Tsimshian clans, had specific protocols for harvesting and honoring the first salmon of the season. One year, a member of the Wolf Clan failed to follow the proper rituals — he did not welcome the salmon chief properly, did not prepare the first salmon with the required ceremony, and showed disrespect to the salmon people. In response, the supernatural forces beneath the mountains grew angry. A great volcanic eruption occurred, devastating the land and reminding all Tsimshian people of the sacred obligation to honor the salmon. The story reinforces the fundamental Northwest Coast principle that humans and salmon are in a reciprocal relationship: humans must treat salmon with respect or face catastrophic consequences. It also explains volcanic activity in the Nass and Skeena River regions through the lens of spiritual cause and effect.
full_text:
This Tsimshian legend tells of a volcanic eruption caused by disrespect for the salmon. The Wolf Clan, one of the four major Tsimshian clans, had specific protocols for harvesting and honoring the first salmon of the season. The first salmon was a gift from the salmon people, and it demanded proper treatment — a welcome ceremony, a respectful preparation, a careful distribution of the flesh.

One year, a member of the Wolf Clan failed to follow the proper rituals. He did not welcome the salmon chief properly, did not prepare the first salmon with the required ceremony, and showed disrespect to the salmon people. He cut the fish carelessly, discarded the head and bones, and cooked it without the proper prayers.

In response, the supernatural forces beneath the mountains grew angry. The earth trembled. Smoke rose from the peaks. A great volcanic eruption occurred, devastating the land — the lava flow destroyed the village, the ash cloud darkened the sky, and the rivers ran hot with melted rock.

The eruption reminded all Tsimshian people of the sacred obligation to honor the salmon. The story reinforces the fundamental Northwest Coast principle that humans and salmon are in a reciprocal relationship: humans must treat salmon with respect or face catastrophic consequences.

The salmon are not simply food; they are people — the salmon people, who return to the rivers each year to give themselves to the humans. To disrespect the salmon is to disrespect the gift, and to disrespect the gift is to invite the wrath of the spirits who control the natural world.

It also explains volcanic activity in the Nass and Skeena River regions through the lens of spiritual cause and effect. The volcanoes are not simply geological features; they are the anger of the salmon people, expressed through the fire and stone of the earth.

title: The Porcupine and the Beaver (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth from the William Beynon collection tells of a time when animals spoke like human beings and possessed great powers to change the weather. Porcupine and Beaver, two animal-people, had a contest of abilities that determined their roles in the world. Porcupine demonstrated his cleverness and defensive capabilities, while Beaver showed his industrious nature and engineering skills. The story carries important teachings about using one's natural gifts wisely and respecting the different abilities of others. It is also an etiological tale explaining the physical characteristics and behaviors of both porcupines and beavers. Porcupine's quills and Beaver's tail receive supernatural explanations in the narrative. Recorded by William Beynon, a Tsimshian ethnographer who worked with Franz Boas, this story represents one of the many animal-person tales that convey moral teachings while explaining the natural world.
source: William Beynon, Tsimshian Stories; Columbia University Library
full_text:
This Tsimshian myth from the William Beynon collection tells of a time when animals spoke like human beings and possessed great powers to change the weather. Porcupine and Beaver, two animal-people, had a contest of abilities that determined their roles in the world.

Porcupine demonstrated his cleverness and defensive capabilities. He showed how his quills could be used as weapons — sharp, barbed, painful — and how they could be used as tools — needles, pins, fishhooks. He showed how his ability to curl into a ball protected him from predators, how his quiet movement through the forest allowed him to observe without being observed.

Beaver showed his industrious nature and engineering skills. He demonstrated how he could fell a tree with his teeth, how he could build a dam that held back a river, how he could create a pond that provided food and shelter for many animals. He showed how his flat tail could be used as a tool — a hammer for pounding stakes, a rudder for swimming, a signal for warning others of danger.

The story carries important teachings about using one's natural gifts wisely and respecting the different abilities of others. Neither Porcupine nor Beaver is superior; each has a unique set of skills, and each contributes to the world in a way that the other cannot.

It is also an etiological tale explaining the physical characteristics and behaviors of both porcupines and beavers. Porcupine's quills and Beaver's tail receive supernatural explanations in the narrative — gifts from the Creator, earned through the contest of abilities.

Recorded by William Beynon, a Tsimshian ethnographer who worked with Franz Boas, this story represents one of the many animal-person tales that convey moral teachings while explaining the natural world.

title: The Four Carpenters and the Creation of the World (Nuxalk)
summary: When the world was first created, the Creator Alhkw'ntam had help from Four Carpenters called the Masmasalanicw, who were like human beings with wings — angels. They carved the first ancestors from the cosmic tree Tcncniyaaq (the Milky Way). There were 45 original families, each with their own room in the House of Smayusta (the Creator's house in the upper world). The ancestors were given cwmnwas (spirit) placed in the bone of the back of their neck, and slhup'tsta (breath). They were given names, food, tools, a code of ethics, and protocols, all placed within a nuslhiixwta (treasure box). Hanging on the walls were animal, bird, and sea creature cloaks. Each ancestor chose a cloak — grizzly bear, raven, eagle, killer whale, wolf, mountain goat, heron — and danced with it. The Creator threw his sun blanket over himself and transformed into the sun. The ancestors did the same, transforming into their chosen animals. Guided by the eyelashes of the sun, they floated down to earth and removed their cloaks, which returned to heaven. This is the Nuxalk creation story, explaining the origin of all Nuxalk clans and their crests.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Nuxalk Nation official website
full_text:
When the world was first created, the Creator Alhkw'ntam had help from Four Carpenters called the Masmasalanicw, who were like human beings with wings — angels, beings of light and purpose who moved through the air with the ease of birds.

They carved the first ancestors from the cosmic tree Tcncniyaaq — the Milky Way, the great spiral of stars that stretches across the sky. The tree was vast beyond imagining, its branches reaching from one end of the sky to the other, its roots plunging into the depths of the ocean. From its wood, the Four Carpenters carved the first humans — forty-five original families, each with their own room in the House of Smayusta, the Creator's house in the upper world.

The ancestors were given cwmnwas — spirit — placed in the bone of the back of their neck, and slhup'tsta — breath. They were given names, food, tools, a code of ethics, and protocols, all placed within a nuslhiixwta — a treasure box, a container of cultural knowledge that each family carried with them.

Hanging on the walls of the House of Smayusta were animal, bird, and sea creature cloaks — garments of power, each one representing a different aspect of the natural world. Each ancestor chose a cloak — grizzly bear, raven, eagle, killer whale, wolf, mountain goat, heron — and danced with it, absorbing its power, learning its ways.

The Creator threw his sun blanket over himself and transformed into the sun. The ancestors did the same, transforming into their chosen animals. Guided by the eyelashes of the sun, they floated down to earth and removed their cloaks, which returned to heaven. The ancestors remained in their animal forms, and from them came the clans of the Nuxalk — each clan bearing the name and the crest of the animal it had chosen.

This is the Nuxalk creation story, explaining the origin of all Nuxalk clans and their crests.

title: Raven Brings Light (Nuxalk - Qwaxw)
summary: In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata (the land above) and let no one see it. The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the eldest, Yulm, grabbed a piece of charcoal and shook it in his hands. When he opened his hands, it was a bird. The second Carpenter made its wings, the third made its eyes, and the youngest gave it life. They asked the bird to say its name and it flew into the sky crying 'Qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw!' — they named it Qwaxw, Raven. The people begged Raven to get the light. He flew to Nusmata and observed Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina. He transformed into eagle down, then a hemlock needle, but she blew him away. Finally he muddied her drinking water, and she drank him in. She became pregnant and Raven was born as her child. Raven cried for the box holding the light until Alhkw'ntam gave in. Raven broke the globe against the wall, and light leaked through the smoke vent to become the sun, stars, and moon. The people were no longer sad.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Nuxalk Nation official website; Franz Boas, The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians
full_text:
In the beginning, when the world was covered in darkness, the people were in constant sadness and prayed to the Creator Alhkw'ntam for light. Alhkw'ntam held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata, the land above, and let no one see it. The box was locked, and the key was hidden, and the people's prayers went unanswered.

The Four Carpenters who made the world were sitting around a fire when the eldest, Yulm, grabbed a piece of charcoal and shook it in his hands. When he opened his hands, it was a bird — small, black, and ordinary. The second Carpenter made its wings, the third made its eyes, and the youngest gave it life.

They asked the bird to say its name and it flew into the sky crying 'Qwaxw, qwaxw, qwaxw!' — they named it Qwaxw, Raven.

The people begged Raven to get the light. He flew to Nusmata and observed Alhkw'ntam's granddaughter Skimina. He transformed into eagle down — soft, white, drifting — but she blew him away. Then he transformed into a hemlock needle — small, sharp, ordinary — but she blew him away again. Finally he muddied her drinking water, and she drank him in.

She became pregnant and Raven was born as her child. The child cried incessantly, his voice high and piercing, until Alhkw'ntam gave in and offered him the box holding the light. Raven broke the globe against the wall, and light leaked through the smoke vent to become the sun, stars, and moon.

The people were no longer sad. They looked up and saw the light — warm, bright, beautiful — and they celebrated the gift that Raven had brought them.

This myth emphasizes the cooperative work of the carpenters, Raven's role as mediator between heaven and earth, and the Nuxalk belief that the sun is a living being with whom they maintain a spiritual relationship.

title: The Story of Ista (Nuxalk)
summary: Ista is the name of the First Woman who descended to Nuxalknalus (King Island) in Nuxalk tradition. She came down to earth and decorated her crest on a blanket with abalone shell and danced up the coast. Ista was greatly admired for how she chose to show her connection to the Creator. Her story is part of the Nuxalk understanding of how the first ancestors established territories and rights to the land. Traditional family names are handed down and validated at potlatches. The Ista story also includes the tale of Patsallht (First Born), who thought he was the only one on earth. He was given a medicine box containing a 'mukw' of shame, stubbornness, and jealousy. He met the Sisawk people (Society of Chiefs) but was ashamed he was not a member. Later, he met a beautiful woman wearing a red blanket who proposed marriage. She was a grizzly bear woman who built him a home from hemlock. When she left him, First Born refused to leave the house. People followed his puppy to find him and convinced him to feast with them by offering to paint their faces black. The Ista people were ultimately wiped out by a cannibal raiding party from far away.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Skwucwlikwana (Lucy Mack); Nuxalk Nation
full_text:
Ista is the name of the First Woman who descended to Nuxalknalus — King Island — in Nuxalk tradition. She came down to earth and decorated her crest on a blanket with abalone shell and danced up the coast, her movements graceful and purposeful, her blanket shimmering with the iridescent light of the shell.

Ista was greatly admired for how she chose to show her connection to the Creator. Her dance was not entertainment; it was a declaration, a statement of identity, a way of marking the land with her presence. Everywhere she danced, she left behind a trace of her spirit — in the rocks, in the trees, in the water itself.

Her story is part of the Nuxalk understanding of how the first ancestors established territories and rights to the land. Traditional family names are handed down and validated at potlatches — the great ceremonies where wealth is distributed, histories are recited, and rights are affirmed. To hold a name is to hold a connection to the land, and to validate that name at a potlatch is to renew the connection.

The Ista story also includes the tale of Patsallht — First Born — who thought he was the only one on earth. He was given a medicine box containing a 'mukw' of shame, stubbornness, and jealousy — three human failings that would shape his character and his interactions with others.

He met the Sisawk people — the Society of Chiefs — but was ashamed he was not a member. Later, he met a beautiful woman wearing a red blanket who proposed marriage. She was a grizzly bear woman who built him a home from hemlock, her paws shaping the wood with a precision that rivaled any human carpenter.

When she left him, First Born refused to leave the house. People followed his puppy to find him and convinced him to feast with them by offering to paint their faces black — a gesture of mourning that was also a gesture of welcome.

The Ista people were ultimately wiped out by a cannibal raiding party from far away. Their story is a reminder that even the most powerful lineages can be destroyed, and that the land remembers those who once walked upon it.

title: The Sun Tests His Son-in-Law (Nuxalk)
summary: In this Nuxalk myth, the daughter of the Sun married a human man known as Salmon Boy. The Sun was not pleased with his daughter's choice and subjected his new son-in-law to a series of deadly tests. The Sun took Salmon Boy to a mountain of unparalleled steepness where mountain goats climbed, commanding him to kill one. Salmon Boy succeeded with the help of his wife. Next, the Sun required him to draw water from a spring whose walls closed in on anyone who approached. Again his wife helped him. The Sun tried to bake him in a supernaturally hot sweat lodge, burn him on hot stones, and crush him with a falling tree. Each time Salmon Boy survived through his wife's guidance and his own growing supernatural power. Finally recognizing his son-in-law's worth, the Sun accepted him and bestowed upon him the gift of bringing salmon to the people. Salmon Boy returned to earth as a powerful being who taught the Nuxalk people how to properly catch, prepare, and honor the salmon, establishing the sacred relationship between the people and the salmon runs.
source: Franz Boas, The Mythology of the Bella Coola Indians; Nuxalk oral tradition
full_text:
In this Nuxalk myth, the daughter of the Sun married a human man known as Salmon Boy. The Sun was not pleased with his daughter's choice — Salmon Boy was mortal, poor, and unremarkable — and he subjected his new son-in-law to a series of deadly tests.

The Sun took Salmon Boy to a mountain of unparalleled steepness where mountain goats climbed, commanding him to kill one. The mountain was so steep that the goats climbed on their hind legs, their hooves finding purchase in cracks no wider than a finger. Salmon Boy succeeded with the help of his wife, who told him where to stand and when to throw.

Next, the Sun required him to draw water from a spring whose walls closed in on anyone who approached. The walls were made of stone, and they moved — slowly, inexorably — like the jaws of a great beast. Again his wife helped him, telling him when to reach in and when to pull back.

The Sun tried to bake him in a supernaturally hot sweat lodge, burn him on hot stones, and crush him with a falling tree. Each time Salmon Boy survived through his wife's guidance and his own growing supernatural power. He was learning, with each trial, to harness the forces that the Sun controlled.

Finally recognizing his son-in-law's worth, the Sun accepted him and bestowed upon him the gift of bringing salmon to the people. Salmon Boy returned to earth as a powerful being who taught the Nuxalk people how to properly catch, prepare, and honor the salmon, establishing the sacred relationship between the people and the salmon runs.

The tests of the Sun are not simply trials of strength; they are initiations. Each test stripped away a layer of Salmon Boy's humanity and replaced it with something greater — knowledge, power, connection to the natural world. By the end, he was no longer simply a man; he was Salmon Boy, the one who brought the salmon, the bridge between the sun and the sea.

title: The Child and the Cannibal (Nuxalk)
summary: This Nuxalk legend tells of a magical boy who defeats a man-eating monster that terrorized the people. A cannibal giant (Boqs) had been stealing children from a Nuxalk village, carrying them off to his remote mountain lair to devour. The people were helpless against the monster's supernatural strength and ferocity. A young boy, born with extraordinary powers and protected by supernatural helpers, volunteered to confront the cannibal. Using cleverness, courage, and his spirit-given abilities, he tracked the monster to its den. He outwitted the slow-witted giant, leading it into traps and finally killing it with the help of the forest spirits. He freed all the captured children and returned them safely to the village. The boy became a great chief and his descendants established one of the Nuxalk clans. This is part of a broader Nuxalk tradition of hero-child stories where young protagonists overcome powerful supernatural adversaries, demonstrating that age and size are less important than courage and spiritual power.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; native-languages.org; Franz Boas
full_text:
This Nuxalk legend tells of a magical boy who defeats a man-eating monster that terrorized the people. A cannibal giant — Boqs — had been stealing children from a Nuxalk village, carrying them off to his remote mountain lair to devour. The people were helpless against the monster's supernatural strength and ferocity.

A young boy, born with extraordinary powers and protected by supernatural helpers, volunteered to confront the cannibal. The boy was small for his age, with quick eyes and quicker feet, and he carried with him the blessings of the spirits — a shirt that turned aside arrows, a hat that made him invisible, a club that never missed its mark.

Using cleverness, courage, and his spirit-given abilities, he tracked the monster to its den. The den was a cave high in the mountains, its entrance stained with blood, its floor littered with bones. The air smelled of death.

He outwitted the slow-witted giant, leading it into traps and finally killing it with the help of the forest spirits. The spirits appeared as animals — a bear with claws of stone, a bird with wings of wind, a fish with scales of iron — and they fought alongside the boy, their supernatural power combining with his to destroy the monster.

He freed all the captured children and returned them safely to the village. The children were thin and frightened, but they were alive, and their parents wept with joy.

The boy became a great chief and his descendants established one of the Nuxalk clans. This is part of a broader Nuxalk tradition of hero-child stories where young protagonists overcome powerful supernatural adversaries, demonstrating that age and size are less important than courage and spiritual power.

title: Origin of the Chinook People (Chinook)
summary: When Old Man South Wind was traveling north, he met an Old Woman who was a giant. Hungry and tired, he asked for food. She gave him a net and told him to catch fish. South Wind caught a little whale and was about to cut it crossways when the old giantress warned him to slit it down the back instead. He ignored her and cut crossways. The whale transformed into a huge bird so big that when it flew into the air it hid the sun and the noise of its wings shook the earth — it was Thunderbird. Thunderbird flew north and landed on Saddleback Mountain near the Columbia River, where it laid a nest full of eggs. The old giantress followed and found the nest. She broke an egg, found it not good, and threw it down the mountainside. Before it reached the valley, it became an Indian. She broke more eggs and each one became an Indian. This is how the Chinook people were created. The story also explains why Indians never cut the first salmon crossways — they always slit it down the back, following the lesson of South Wind's mistake.
source: James Swan (1857); Chinook oral tradition; native-languages.org
full_text:
When Old Man South Wind was traveling north, as he often did in the early days when the world was still being arranged, he came upon an Old Woman who was a giant. She sat by a river, enormous and calm, her back against a mountain, her legs stretched across the valley. She was so large that the trees grew only to her knees, and the river ran between her fingers like a thread.

South Wind was hungry and tired. He had been traveling for many days, and his stomach was empty, and his legs ached with the effort of constant movement. He approached the giantress and asked for food.

She gave him a net. "Catch fish," she said.

South Wind waded into the river and cast the net. He was not a skilled fisherman, but the river was generous, and in a short time he had caught a little whale — a small, fat creature with smooth skin and a round eye that looked at him with an expression that might have been pleading.

He was about to cut the whale crossways — through the middle, the way a careless person cuts anything — when the old giantress spoke.

"Do not cut it that way. Slit it down the back."

South Wind paused. He looked at the whale. He looked at the giantress. He was tired, and he was hungry, and he did not see why it mattered which way he cut a fish.

He cut it crossways.

The moment the blade passed through the whale's body, something extraordinary happened. The whale transformed. Its body expanded, its fins spread, its tail split, and it rose from the water like a great bird — no, not a bird, but something larger than any bird, something that blotted out the sky as it rose.

It was Thunderbird.

The creature was so enormous that when it flew into the air it hid the sun. The beat of its wings shook the earth — not a gentle tremor but a violent convulsion that rattled the mountains and sent rocks tumbling down the slopes. The noise of its wings was thunder, and the flash of its eyes was lightning.

Thunderbird flew north and landed on Saddleback Mountain near the Columbia River, where it laid a nest full of eggs. The eggs were large — each one the size of a house — and they were laid in a nest woven from whole trees.

The old giantress followed Thunderbird to the mountain. She found the nest and looked into it. She broke one egg and examined it. "Not good," she said, and threw it down the mountainside.

But before the egg reached the valley floor, it changed. The shell cracked open, and from inside emerged a human being — an Indian. He stood up, looked around, and walked down the mountain.

The giantress broke another egg. Another Indian. Another. Another. Each egg became a person, and each person became a member of the Chinook people.

This is how the Chinook were created — from the eggs of Thunderbird, broken by the hands of a giantess, transformed by the same power that had turned a little whale into a being that shook the earth.

The story also explains why the Chinook, and the Indians of the Pacific Northwest generally, never cut the first salmon of the season crossways. They always slit it down the back, following the lesson of South Wind's mistake. To cut a salmon crossways is to risk transforming it into something terrible — something that could shake the world.

title: Blue Jay Visits Ghost Town (Chinook - Ioi and Blue Jay)
summary: Blue Jay's sister Ioi was bought by ghosts as a wife and disappeared to the land of the dead. After a year, Blue Jay went searching for her. He asked all the trees and birds where people go when they die. He journeyed to the ghost town, which appeared to him as a place of bones and decay, but the ghosts saw it as beautiful. Ioi warned Blue Jay not to laugh at the ghosts or behave disrespectfully, but Blue Jay could not control himself. He kicked skulls, laughed at the skeletons, and shouted at the ghost people who were only skeletons to his eyes. When the ghosts went to butcher a whale, Blue Jay saw only a beached skeleton. When they brought in firewood, he saw only bark. Ioi kept explaining that his eyes saw differently because he was alive — the ghosts saw everything as beautiful. He tried to join the ghost dances, but when the ghosts danced gracefully, Blue Jay stood on his head. He died a second time and remained in the ghost world forever. This haunting story explores the boundary between life and death and the dangers of lacking respect for the supernatural world.
source: Chinook Texts, Smithsonian Institution; Chinook oral tradition from Charles Cultee
full_text:
Blue Jay's sister Ioi was gone. She had been bought by ghosts as a wife — purchased with ghost-money, traded like property, taken to the land of the dead. The ghosts had come to the village one night, silent and pale, and they had selected Ioi from among the women, and she had disappeared with them, and the living world was poorer for her absence.

Blue Jay mourned. He mourned loudly, as he did everything, with tears and wailing and dramatic pronouncements of grief. But mourning was not enough. He wanted his sister back.

After a year, Blue Jay went searching for her. He asked everyone he met — the trees, the birds, the animals, the rivers — where people go when they die. The trees told him nothing. The birds told him nothing. The rivers, flowing endlessly toward the sea, told him nothing.

Finally, a salmon — old, wise, its scales worn smooth by years of swimming — told him: "The dead live in a town at the end of the world. Go west, past the last mountain, past the last river, and you will find it."

Blue Jay went west. He walked for days, past mountains that scraped the sky, past rivers that ran black with depth, past forests so old that the trees had forgotten they were trees. And at the end of the world, he found the ghost town.

To Blue Jay's living eyes, the ghost town was a place of bones and decay. The houses were made of ribs and vertebrae, lashed together with sinew. The ground was covered in ash. The sky was the color of old bruises. Everything was broken, hollow, dead.

But Ioi was there. She stood at the entrance to the town, waiting for him, and she was not dead — not entirely. She was translucent, like smoke, and her voice was thin, but she was his sister, and she was glad to see him.

"Do not laugh," she warned him. "Do not behave disrespectfully. The ghosts have their own ways, and you must honor them."

Blue Jay promised. He promised sincerely, with all the sincerity of a being who could not keep a promise if his life depended on it.

He entered the ghost town, and the ghosts welcomed him. They gave him food — or what they called food. To Blue Jay's living eyes, it was rot and decay, maggots and mold. But the ghosts ate it with relish, and their eyes were bright, and they seemed content.

When the ghosts went to butcher a whale that had washed ashore, Blue Jay saw only a beached skeleton. When they brought in firewood, he saw only bark and splinters. When they danced, he saw only bones clicking together in the dim light.

"You see things differently because you are alive," Ioi explained. "To us, everything is beautiful."

Blue Jay could not help himself. He kicked the skulls that lay in the street. He laughed at the skeletons who tried to serve him food. He shouted at the ghost children who had no flesh on their faces.

And when the ghosts danced — gracefully, beautifully, in patterns that represented the seasons and the stars and the turning of the world — Blue Jay stood on his head.

The ghosts were offended. The spirits of the dead do not tolerate disrespect, and Blue Jay had been disrespectful in every way a living being can be. He died a second time and remained in the ghost world forever.

This haunting story explores the boundary between life and death and the dangers of lacking respect for the supernatural world. The living and the dead perceive reality differently, and the gap between their perceptions cannot be bridged by laughter or contempt. Blue Jay, who could not see the beauty of the ghost world, was destroyed by his own blindness.

title: Robin and Blue-Jay (Chinook)
summary: Blue Jay and Robin, two brothers, were hungry. Blue Jay called a large fish (the sleeper) to come ashore through trickery and speared it. When they returned home, Robin asked for the tail, breast, and head, making Blue Jay angry. He said that the Q!têê'nse (a supernatural monster) would eat the fish instead. Robin cried and left. Blue Jay softened and called his brother back, giving him all the choice parts. Later, Blue Jay dreamed that people were sending for him to cure a sick person. Blue Jay and Robin journeyed to cure a duck who was choking, receiving payment of a lake's worth of roots. Next they cured a wolf girl who was choking on an elk's kneecap, receiving two canoes full of meat and grease. But Blue Jay's arrogance and greed in demanding excessive payment led to consequences. The story demonstrates the Chinook trickster cycle's typical structure: Blue Jay is boastful and selfish but ultimately provides for his family through his supernatural curing abilities, while long-suffering Robin represents patience and humility.
source: Franz Boas, Chinook Texts (1894); Chinook oral tradition from Charles Cultee
full_text:
Blue Jay and Robin, two brothers, were hungry. They had not eaten in two days, and their stomachs growled like empty caves. They stood at the edge of the creek, watching the water flow, and Blue Jay said, "I will get us food."

Robin looked at him doubtfully. Blue Jay was always saying he would do things, and he often did them, but he also often got them into trouble.

Blue Jay called to the water. He made a sound — a low, rhythmic pulsing that traveled through the surface of the creek like a heartbeat. It was the sound that the sleeper fish makes when it rests on the bottom, and in time a large fish — fat and slow — rose from the depths and drifted toward the shore.

Blue Jay speared it. It was a good fish, heavy and silver, enough to feed them both.

They carried it home and built a fire. Robin, who was younger and more eager, reached for the fish and asked for the tail. Then he asked for the breast. Then he asked for the head.

Blue Jay's feathers ruffled. "You want everything," he said. "You want the best parts. What about me?"

"I'm hungry," Robin said.

"The Q!təə'nse will eat the fish instead," Blue Jay said, naming the great supernatural monster that lived in the deep forest, the one that ate everything it found. It was a cruel thing to say, and Blue Jay knew it, but he was angry.

Robin cried. He cried loudly, as younger brothers do, and then he left. He walked away from the fire, away from the fish, away from Blue Jay, and disappeared into the forest.

Blue Jay sat by the fire for a long time, eating the fish alone. But as the fire burned low and the night grew cold, his anger cooled too, and his stomach was full, and he began to feel the particular emptiness that comes from having eaten well while someone you love goes hungry.

He called Robin back. "Come eat," he said, and his voice was soft. Robin returned, and Blue Jay gave him all the choice parts — the tail, the breast, the head — everything he had kept for himself.

Later, Blue Jay dreamed that people were sending for him to cure a sick person. He and Robin journeyed to the village where the sick one lay — a duck who was choking on a bone. Blue Jay removed the bone and cured the duck, and the people rewarded him with a lake's worth of roots.

Next they cured a wolf girl who was choking on an elk's kneecap, receiving two canoes full of meat and grease.

But Blue Jay's arrogance and greed in demanding excessive payment led to consequences. The people grew tired of his boasting, his demands, his insistence that he was the greatest healer in the world. They chased him away, and Blue Jay flew off, still boasting, still insisting, still unable to see himself as others saw him.

The Chinook trickster cycle's typical structure is on display here: Blue Jay is boastful and selfish but ultimately provides for his family through his supernatural curing abilities, while long-suffering Robin represents patience and humility. The brothers need each other — Blue Jay's power and Robin's goodness — and neither is complete without the other.

title: Blue Jay Finds a Wife (Chinook)
summary: Ioi decided it was high time for Blue Jay to quit his playful trickery and settle down with a wife. She told him he must select a wife from the land of the dead, from the Supernatural People. Ioi recommended that Blue Jay choose an old woman and suggested the recently deceased wife of a chief. Blue Jay went to the ghost town and courted the ghost woman. True to his nature, he behaved foolishly, misinterpreting the customs of the dead and acting disrespectfully. He made inappropriate jokes and did not understand that the ghosts perceived reality differently than the living. Despite Ioi's warnings, Blue Jay's behavior caused chaos in the ghost village. The story highlights Blue Jay's inability to mature and learn from experience, making him a comic but ultimately tragic figure. It is also one of several Chinook stories that explore the relationship between the living and the dead, suggesting that the boundary between worlds must be approached with humility and respect.
full_text:
Ioi had been patient with her brother for a long time. Too long. Blue Jay was a fool — everyone knew it, including Blue Jay, though he would never admit it — and fools need wives to keep them from getting into trouble. At least, that was Ioi's theory.

"It is high time you settled down," she told him. "You cannot wander the world forever, getting into fights, bragging about things you have not done, and offending everyone you meet."

Blue Jay ruffled his feathers. "I am perfectly capable of taking care of myself."

"You got into a fight with a tree last week," Ioi said.

"The tree started it."

"You set fire to a river."

"It was a small fire."

Ioi sighed. "You must select a wife."

Blue Jay was interested. He had never thought much about wives — they seemed like a lot of work — but the idea of having someone to cook for him and tell him how wonderful he was had a certain appeal.

"Where will I find a wife?" he asked.

Ioi told him: he must go to the land of the dead, to the ghost town at the end of the world, and choose a wife from among the Supernatural People. The ghosts had beautiful women, she said, and they would be willing to trade.

She recommended that Blue Jay choose an old woman — someone experienced, someone who would not be impressed by his nonsense, someone who could keep him in line. Specifically, she suggested the recently deceased wife of a chief, who was said to be wise and patient.

Blue Jay went to the ghost town. He found the old woman, and he began to court her, in his fashion — which is to say, he behaved foolishly, misinterpreted every custom he encountered, and acted with the kind of disrespectful enthusiasm that made the ghosts wish they had stayed dead.

He did not understand that the ghosts perceived reality differently than the living. Where he saw bones, they saw beautiful furniture. Where he saw rot, they saw fine food. Where he saw ash, they saw soft earth. He commented loudly on the ugliness of everything, and the ghosts, who were proud of their town, were offended.

He made jokes about death, which the ghosts did not find funny because death was not an abstraction to them — it was their daily reality. He mocked their ceremonies, which were sacred and ancient and not subject to ridicule. He ate their food and pronounced it terrible, not knowing that to the ghosts it was a feast fit for spirits.

Ioi's warnings echoed in his mind, but Blue Jay could not heed them. He was constitutionally incapable of behaving with decorum, and the ghost town was the one place in the universe where decorum was not optional.

The ghosts drove him out. They chased him with sticks and stones and the fury of beings who had been deeply, personally insulted. Blue Jay fled, squawking and flapping, and he never returned.

The story highlights Blue Jay's inability to mature and learn from experience, making him a comic but ultimately tragic figure. It is also one of several Chinook stories that explore the relationship between the living and the dead, suggesting that the boundary between worlds must be approached with humility and respect — two qualities that Blue Jay possessed in smaller quantities than any being in the Chinook world.

title: Coyote and the Creation of the Tribes (Chinook/Chelan)
summary: Long ago, the Great Chief Above made the world, then the animals and birds. After twelve moons, the animal people gathered. Bluejay, Meadowlark, and Coyote complained about their names, but the Creator declared that names would stay as given. The Creator told Coyote he would be the head of all creatures and given power to keep peace. As the Creator foretold, things became bad — mountains swallowed creatures, winds blew them away. Coyote stopped the mountains and winds, rescued the creatures, and made laws for natural forces. When Coyote's work was done, the Creator told Coyote he would not make the first human. Instead, the four Wolf Brothers took over. The youngest Wolf Brother killed Beaver and cut it into twelve pieces according to the Creator's instructions. The pieces were given to different animal people who carried them to different regions, where each piece became a different Indian tribe: the Nez Perce from the liver, the Spokane, Lake people, Flathead, and others from different organs. The blood became the Blackfeet. This story explains the origin of the twelve tribes of the Columbia Plateau region.
full_text:
Long ago, the Great Chief Above made the world. He made it carefully, thoughtfully, the way a carver makes a canoe — measuring, planning, testing each piece before committing to the next. He made the mountains and the rivers, the forests and the plains, the oceans and the sky. Then he made the animals and the birds, and he gave each one a name and a purpose.

After twelve moons had passed, the animal people gathered for a council. They were restless, dissatisfied. Bluejay complained about his name. Meadowlark complained about her feathers. Coyote — who would later become the most important of them all, though no one knew it yet — complained about everything.

The Creator listened to their complaints and then spoke. "Your names are your names. They were given to you for a reason, and they will not change."

Coyote was not satisfied. He complained louder, and longer, and with more creativity than anyone else. The Creator, recognizing something in Coyote's stubbornness that was necessary for the work ahead, made a decision.

"You," the Creator said to Coyote, "will be the head of all creatures. I give you power to keep peace in the world."

Coyote was pleased. He strutted among the animals, puffing his chest, acting important. But the Creator had spoken truly — things were about to become bad.

As the Creator had foretold, the world began to fall apart. Mountains swallowed creatures whole, opening their rocky mouths and pulling animals into the dark. Winds blew creatures away, lifting them from the ground and carrying them to unknown places. The rivers flooded. The forests burned. The animals cried out for help.

Coyote, to his credit, acted. He stopped the mountains from swallowing. He calmed the winds. He rescued the creatures that had been displaced and returned them to their homes. He made laws for the natural forces — rules that the mountains, the winds, the rivers, and the forests would follow from that day forward.

When Coyote's work was done, the Creator told him something unexpected: "I will not make the first human. That task falls to others."

The four Wolf Brothers took over. They were strong, silent, purposeful — everything Coyote was not. The youngest Wolf Brother killed Beaver, and according to the Creator's instructions, cut it into twelve pieces.

Each piece was given to a different animal person, who carried it to a different region of the world. Where each piece was placed, it became a different Indian tribe.

The liver went to one place and became the Nez Perce. The heart went to another and became the Spokane. The lungs became the Lake people. The stomach became the Flathead. Other pieces became other tribes — the Cayuse, the Umatilla, the Walla Walla, the Yakama, and the others. The blood dripped along the way and became the Blackfeet.

This story of the creation of the twelve tribes of the Columbia Plateau explains not only the origin of the tribes but their relationships to one another. They are all parts of the same animal — the same source — and their differences are differences of organ and function, not of worth. Each tribe has its own role, its own purpose, its own place in the body of the people. And Coyote, who started as a complainer and became a lawgiver, set the world in motion.

title: The Nuxalk Origin of the Sun (Nuxalk)
summary: The Nuxalk people tell that before the sun existed, there was only the dim light of copper-colored darkness. The people prayed constantly to Alhkw'ntam, the Creator, for light. In Nusmata, the house of the gods in the upper world, the Creator's granddaughter Skimina lived. The Four Carpenters created Raven (Qwaxw) from a piece of charcoal to answer the people's prayers. Raven, after being born as Skimina's child, cried persistently for the box containing the globe of light. When Alhkw'ntam finally relented, Raven rolled the globe back and forth until he smashed it against the wall. Light poured out through the smoke hole, flooding the world with brightness. The breaking of the globe created the sun for daytime, the moon for night, and the stars scattered across the sky. The people's sadness ended, and they celebrated the gift of light. This myth emphasizes the cooperative work of the carpenters, Raven's role as mediator between heaven and earth, and the Nuxalk belief that the sun is a living being with whom they maintain a spiritual relationship.
source: Nuxalk oral tradition; Nuxalk Nation; Franz Boas
full_text:
The Nuxalk people tell that before the sun existed, there was only the dim light of copper-colored darkness — a twilight that never brightened, never faded, never changed. The people lived in this permanent dusk, seeing by the faint glow that came from the sky, unable to distinguish friend from foe, day from night.

The people prayed constantly to Alhkw'ntam, the Creator, for light. Their prayers rose from the earth like smoke, filling the sky with a longing that was almost visible. But the Creator held the sun in a box in his longhouse in Nusmata, and he would not release it.

In Nusmata, the house of the gods in the upper world, the Creator's granddaughter Skimina lived. She was young and beautiful, with hair like cedar bark and eyes like polished obsidian. She did not know that the sun was in the box, and she did not know that the people below were praying for light.

The Four Carpenters created Raven — Qwaxw — from a piece of charcoal to answer the people's prayers. They shaped his body from the black carbon, gave him wings from the ash, and eyes from the embers. When they breathed life into him, he opened his eyes and immediately understood his purpose: to bring the light.

Raven, after being born as Skimina's child, cried persistently for the box containing the globe of light. His cries filled the longhouse, shaking the walls, rattling the dishes. Skimina tried to quiet him, but nothing worked.

When Alhkw'ntam finally relented, Raven rolled the globe back and forth until he smashed it against the wall. Light poured out through the smoke hole, flooding the world with brightness. The breaking of the globe created the sun for daytime, the moon for night, and the stars scattered across the sky.

The people's sadness ended, and they celebrated the gift of light. They danced and sang, their voices rising in the new brightness, their faces turned toward the sun.

This myth emphasizes the cooperative work of the carpenters, Raven's role as mediator between heaven and earth, and the Nuxalk belief that the sun is a living being with whom they maintain a spiritual relationship.

title: The Great Flood and the Origin of the Tides (Tlingit)
summary: Raven made a woman under the earth to have charge of the rise and fall of the tides. One time he wanted to explore everything beneath the ocean and commanded the tide woman to raise the water. She made the tide rise very slowly so the people had time to load their canoes and climb to the mountaintops. As the water lifted the canoes between the mountains, bears and other wild animals swam out to them, and those with dogs had good protection. Some people walled the mountaintops and tied their canoes inside. When the tide began to fall, the people followed it down, but the trees were gone and they had nothing for firewood, so they were destroyed by the cold. When Raven returned, he turned all the remaining people and animals into stone. He then made new human beings from leaves, which is why people die off rapidly in autumn when leaves fall. This Tlingit flood narrative explains both the origin of tides and the seasonal cycle of death, reflecting on human fragility and the consequences of curiosity.
source: John R. Swanton, Tlingit Myths and Texts (1909)
full_text:
Raven made a woman under the earth to have charge of the rise and fall of the tides. She was a being of stone and water, her body rooted in the ocean floor, her breath the rhythm of the tides. When she breathed in, the water rose. When she breathed out, the water fell.

One time Raven wanted to explore everything beneath the ocean and commanded the tide woman to raise the water. She made the tide rise very slowly, so the people had time to load their canoes and climb to the mountaintops. The water lifted the canoes between the mountains, and bears and other wild animals swam out to them, and those with dogs had good protection.

Some people walled the mountaintops and tied their canoes inside. They built walls of stone, stacking the rocks with precision and care, sealing the gaps with mud and moss. They pulled their canoes onto the high ground and secured them with ropes, waiting for the water to recede.

When the tide began to fall, the people followed it down. But the trees were gone — drowned by the salt water, stripped of their leaves and bark — and they had nothing for firewood. The nights were cold, the wind was sharp, and without fire, the people were destroyed by the cold.

When Raven returned, he found the people frozen — turned to stone by the cold, their bodies locked in the positions they had held in their final moments. He turned all the remaining people and animals into stone. He then made new human beings from leaves, which is why people die off rapidly in autumn when leaves fall.

This Tlingit flood narrative explains both the origin of tides and the seasonal cycle of death, reflecting on human fragility and the consequences of curiosity. The tides are not simply natural phenomena; they are the breath of a supernatural being, and the death of leaves in autumn is not simply biology — it is the consequence of an ancient event, frozen in stone and memory.

title: Komokwa and the Undersea Kingdom (Haida)
summary: In Haida tradition, the undersea world is ruled by powerful supernatural beings who control the wealth of the sea. The sea chiefs live in houses made of copper and abalone shell, surrounded by supernatural beings including the killer whale people, seal people, and halibut people. Those who drown do not truly die but are taken to live in the undersea kingdom, where they may acquire great supernatural power and wealth. The supernatural killer whales (SGaana) are the most powerful of the undersea beings; they can transform into human form and own houses, territories, and crests. The Haida people take their clan crests from these supernatural beings, copying their likenesses for use on totem poles, blankets, and ceremonial regalia. The relationship between the Haida and the undersea kingdom is reciprocal: humans show respect through proper protocols, and the supernatural beings provide salmon, halibut, seals, and whales for the people's survival.
source: Haida oral tradition; Haida Gwaii Pledge; Terri-Lynn Williams-Davidson
full_text:
In Haida tradition, the undersea world is ruled by powerful supernatural beings who control the wealth of the sea. The sea chiefs live in houses made of copper and abalone shell, surrounded by supernatural beings including the killer whale people, seal people, and halibut people.

The houses are magnificent — their walls glow with the iridescence of abalone, their floors are paved with copper, and their roofs are carved with the images of ancestral spirits. The sea chiefs sit on thrones of carved cedar, wearing robes of sea otter fur, and they preside over a kingdom of abundance.

Those who drown do not truly die but are taken to live in the undersea kingdom, where they may acquire great supernatural power and wealth. The drowning is not an ending but a transition — a passage from the world of air to the world of water, from the world of humans to the world of spirits.

The supernatural killer whales — SGaana — are the most powerful of the undersea beings; they can transform into human form and own houses, territories, and crests. They are the chiefs of the sea, and they govern the salmon, the halibut, the seals, and the whales with the same authority that human chiefs govern their villages.

The Haida people take their clan crests from these supernatural beings, copying their likenesses for use on totem poles, blankets, and ceremonial regalia. The crest is not simply decoration; it is a claim, a connection, a statement of relationship between the human clan and the supernatural being.

The relationship between the Haida and the undersea kingdom is reciprocal: humans show respect through proper protocols, and the supernatural beings provide salmon, halibut, seals, and whales for the people's survival. When the protocols are followed, the sea is generous. When they are broken, the sea withdraws its gifts.

title: The D'Sonoqua Who Became Wealth (Kwakwaka'wakw)
summary: In one Kwakwaka'wakw narrative, a clever boy was captured by D'Sonoqua and carried in her basket to her forest house. While she prepared to cook him, the boy noticed that D'Sonoqua was dim-witted with poor eyesight. He tricked her into showing him her treasures and then pushed her into her own cooking fire. As she burned, her wealth — copper shields, abalone shells, and blankets — spilled out. The boy took the treasures back to his village and became a great chief. But D'Sonoqua's ashes blew into the air and became mosquitoes, which is why mosquitoes bite humans — they carry D'Sonoqua's eternal hunger. This story also has versions where D'Sonoqua cannot truly die; she regenerates from any wound, and the only way to stop her is to burn her completely and scatter the ashes. Her association with wealth makes her a complex figure: she is a terrifying cannibal monster but also a source of great prosperity for those brave and clever enough to defeat her. At potlatches, a chief wearing the D'Sonoqua mask signals the end of the ceremony.
source: Kwakwaka'wakw oral tradition; Audrey Hawthorn, Kwakiutl Art; U'mista Cultural Centre
full_text:
In one Kwakwaka'wakw narrative, a clever boy was captured by D'Sonoqua and carried in her basket to her forest house. The basket was enormous, woven from cedar bark so tightly that nothing could escape, and the boy bounced inside it as D'Sonoqua walked through the forest, her long strides covering the ground in great bounds.

While she prepared to cook him — her fire already burning, her pot already boiling — the boy noticed that D'Sonoqua was dim-witted with poor eyesight. She bumped into things. She reached for objects and missed. She looked at the boy and saw only a模糊.

The boy tricked her into showing him her treasures. He told her that he had treasures of his own, hidden in the forest, and that if she would show him hers, he would show her his. D'Sonoqua, eager for treasure, opened her boxes and displayed her wealth — copper shields, abalone shells, blankets of sea otter fur, necklaces of dentalium shell.

The boy studied the treasures, noting their weight and size, and then he pushed D'Sonoqua into her own cooking fire. She screamed — a sound like the wind howling through cedar trees — and fell into the flames. As she burned, her wealth spilled out. The copper shields gleamed in the firelight. The abalone shells shimmered. The blankets unfurled like wings.

The boy took the treasures back to his village and became a great chief. His wealth was legendary, his potlatches the most generous ever seen, and his name was spoken with respect for generations.

But D'Sonoqua's ashes blew into the air and became mosquitoes, which is why mosquitoes bite humans — they carry D'Sonoqua's eternal hunger. The buzzing of mosquitoes is her voice, and their bite is her reach, extending from the spirit world into the human world.

This story also has versions where D'Sonoqua cannot truly die; she regenerates from any wound, and the only way to stop her is to burn her completely and scatter the ashes. Her association with wealth makes her a complex figure: she is a terrifying cannibal monster but also a source of great prosperity for those brave and clever enough to defeat her.

title: The Transformer Who Became the Mountains (Coast Salish)
summary: The Coast Salish tell of a Transformer (Xe'las) who walked through the land making the world right for the coming humans. Near Lake Chelan, he encountered people who had become corrupted by greed and selfishness. He transformed them into stone, their canoes becoming islands in the lake. Near the Fraser River, he found a woman with a vagina full of teeth who emasculated men — he turned her into a rock formation that still guards the river. In the San Juan Islands, he found two sisters fighting over a man and turned them into a pair of islands called The Sisters. The Transformer also created Mount Rainier (Tacobud) as a refuge during the great flood, and the mountain still bears the scars of the waters. Every rock, island, and mountain in Coast Salish territory has a story of transformation, creating a landscape that serves as a permanent record of moral teachings. The land itself is a library of stories that instruct people in proper behavior and remind them of the consequences of their actions.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; Hibulb Cultural Center; Brian Thom
full_text:
The Transformer — Xe'las — walked through the land making the world right for the coming humans. He moved with purpose, his eyes seeing not what the world was but what it needed to become. And everywhere he went, he found things that needed changing.

Near Lake Chelan, he encountered people who had become corrupted by greed. They hoarded food while their neighbors starved. They took more than their share of salmon from the river. They filled their houses with possessions while others slept in the cold. Xe'las looked at them and shook his head.

"You have forgotten the old agreements," he said. "You have forgotten that the world belongs to everyone."

He turned them to stone. Their bodies became the rocky shoreline of Lake Chelan, their arms reaching out toward the water they had once exploited. Their canoes, still loaded with stolen food, became islands in the lake, visible even today — dark shapes floating on the blue water, reminders of the consequences of greed.

Near the Fraser River, Xe'las found a woman who was something other than human. She had a vagina full of teeth, and she used it to emasculate men who came too close. She was a danger to anyone who traveled the river, and the people who lived nearby were terrified of her.

Xe'las confronted her and transformed her into a rock formation that still guards the river — a jagged outcropping of stone, visible from the water, warning travelers to keep their distance.

In the San Juan Islands, Xe'las found two sisters fighting over a man. They pulled each other's hair, scratched each other's faces, screamed at each other with voices that carried across the water. They had forgotten that they were sisters, that their bond was older and deeper than any romantic attachment.

Xe'las turned them into a pair of islands called The Sisters — two rocky formations that sit close together in the water, visible from the shore, a permanent reminder that the bond between siblings should never be broken by jealousy or competition.

The Transformer also created Mount Rainier — Tacobud — as a refuge during the great flood that he himself would later send to cleanse the earth. The mountain still bears the scars of the waters, visible in the striations of rock and the way the tree line breaks at certain elevations, marking the height to which the flood rose.

Every rock, island, and mountain in Coast Salish territory has a story of transformation. The land itself is a library of stories — a permanent record of moral teachings carved into the earth by a being of immense power and infinite patience. The stories teach people in proper behavior and remind them of the consequences of their actions. To walk through Coast Salish territory is to walk through a textbook of ethics, geology, and spiritual wisdom, written in stone and water and the shapes of mountains.

title: The Bluejay Cycle (Coast Salish)
summary: Bluejay is a prominent trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly among the Chemainus, Cowichan, and other Salish communities. He is generally a benevolent being who helps people, but he is also extremely foolish and careless, and stories about him are often humorous or slapstick. In one classic story, Bluejay boasted that he could steal the sun, but his lies got him into trouble when the people took him seriously and he had to deliver on his impossible promise. In another, he tried to imitate the skills of other animals and birds, with disastrously funny results. Bluejay often interacts with his long-suffering sister Ioi, who tries to keep him out of trouble but fails because Bluejay refuses to listen to good advice. Unlike Raven, who possesses genuine supernatural power, Bluejay's adventures typically stem from his foolishness rather than malice. The Bluejay stories serve as comic relief in the storytelling tradition while also teaching lessons about humility, honesty, and the dangers of boastfulness.
source: Coast Salish oral tradition; Salish Myths and Legends (University of Nebraska Press)
full_text:
Bluejay is a prominent trickster figure in Coast Salish mythology, particularly among the Chemainus, Cowichan, and other Salish communities along the Strait of Georgia and the Fraser River. He is not like Raven — not powerful, not wise, not possessed of genuine supernatural gifts. Bluejay is, above all, foolish. And it is his foolishness, not his cleverness, that drives his stories.

In one classic tale, Bluejay boasted that he could steal the sun. He announced this at a feast, standing on a cedar plank and squawking his declaration to the assembled people. Everyone laughed, but Bluejay took their laughter as encouragement. He flew up into the sky, flapping his blue wings, squawking louder and louder, getting closer and closer to the sun.

The sun, unimpressed, simply grew hotter. Bluejay's feathers began to smolder. His beak started to melt. He squawked in panic and tumbled back to earth, landing in a creek where the water sizzled and steamed around him. He emerged singed, humiliated, and hungry — which was, in many ways, his natural state.

In another story, Bluejay tried to imitate the skills of other animals and birds. He watched Eagle catch a salmon and tried to do the same, but he could not dive fast enough and hit the water face-first. He watched Owl hunt mice and tried to do the same, but his eyes were too bright and the mice saw him coming. He watched Bear catch berries and tried to do the same, but he fell out of the berry bush and landed in a thorn patch.

Bluejay often interacts with his long-suffering sister Ioi, who tries to keep him out of trouble. Ioi is the voice of reason, the voice of caution, the voice of "please stop talking and think about what you are doing for once in your life." But Bluejay refuses to listen to good advice, and his adventures inevitably end in disaster — for himself, and often for anyone unlucky enough to be nearby.

Unlike Raven, who possesses genuine supernatural power and uses it to reshape the world, Bluejay's adventures typically stem from his foolishness rather than malice. He does not set out to harm anyone; he simply cannot help being himself. He is loud where he should be quiet, brave where he should be cautious, and certain where he should be doubtful.

The Bluejay stories serve as comic relief in the storytelling tradition while also teaching lessons about humility, honesty, and the dangers of boastfulness. Every community has its Bluejays — the ones who talk too much, who promise too much, who believe their own press releases — and the stories about Bluejay remind listeners that the gap between what you say you can do and what you can actually do is a dangerous place to live.

title: Kwatyat the Transformer (Nuu-chah-nulth)
summary: Kwatyat is one of the most important transformer figures in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology. After his adventures with his brother Tihtipihin rescuing their mother from the monster, Kwatyat traveled the land transforming the world and making it ready for human beings. He changed dangerous beings into harmless animals, taught people how to fish and hunt, and established the proper relationship between humans and the supernatural world. Kwatyat also had a trickster aspect — he could be foolish and greedy, and many stories tell of his failed attempts to imitate others or his schemes backfiring. In one story, he tried to catch salmon by building a weir but was too impatient and it collapsed. In another, he tried to fly like an eagle and fell into the ocean. Despite his flaws, Kwatyat's transformations established the fundamental order of Nuu-chah-nulth life. He is sometimes paired with or compared to Raven, sharing the role of culture hero and trickster in a complementary way.
full_text:
Kwatyat is one of the most important transformer figures in Nuu-chah-nulth mythology — a being who walked the land correcting what was wrong, shaping the world for the people who would come after. His story begins with the rescue of his mother from the monster, when he was still a young man with a knife of sharpened bone and a heart full of courage. But it does not end there.

After the rescue, Kwatyat traveled the land. He walked the coast from one end to the other, from the rocky shores of the north to the sandy beaches of the south, and everywhere he went, he transformed the world.

He found dangerous beings — monsters, spirits, creatures that preyed on humans — and he changed them. Some he turned into harmless animals: bears became deer, wolves became foxes, giant birds became songbirds. Some he turned into landmarks: a monster that had terrorized a village became a distinctive rock formation; a spirit that had haunted a river became a waterfall.

He taught people how to fish — where to find the salmon, when to cast the net, how to read the tides. He showed them how to hunt — which plants attracted deer, which trails the bears used, which mountain passes were safe in winter. He established the proper relationship between humans and the supernatural world, teaching the people which spirits to honor, which to avoid, and which to appease with offerings.

But Kwatyat was not all power and wisdom. He had a trickster aspect — a foolish, greedy, impulsive side that got him into trouble as often as his courage got him out of it.

In one story, he tried to catch salmon by building a weir across a river. He was impatient — he wanted the fish now, not tomorrow, not next week — and he did not wait for the structure to be properly completed. The current overwhelmed the unfinished weir, and the salmon swam through the gaps, laughing at him (or so Kwatyat believed). He spent the rest of the day hungry and wet, sitting on the riverbank, muttering about ungrateful fish.

In another story, he tried to fly like an eagle. He tied feathers to his arms, climbed to the top of a cliff, and jumped. He did not fly. He fell into the ocean, and the waves tossed him about like a piece of driftwood until a passing whale pushed him to shore, gasping and spitting saltwater.

Despite his flaws, Kwatyat's transformations established the fundamental order of Nuu-chah-nulth life. The world as the Nuu-chah-nulth knew it was Kwatyat's creation — every rock, every island, every bend in the river bore the mark of his passing. He is sometimes paired with or compared to Raven, who shares the role of culture hero and trickster in a complementary way. Where Raven brought light, Kwatyat brought order. Where Raven was clever, Kwatyat was brave. Together, they made the world habitable for the people.

title: One Who Walks All Over the Sky (Tsimshian)
summary: This Tsimshian myth explains the origin of the sun, moon, and night sky. After Weeget (Giant/Raven) brought light from heaven, there was still the question of who would carry the sun across the sky each day and what the patterns of stars meant. The One Who Walks All Over the Sky is a supernatural being assigned to carry the sun on his daily journey from east to west. He walks across the dome of the sky, and his path determines the seasons. When he walks high, it is summer; when low, winter. The stars are his footprints or the campfires of other sky beings. This story is part of the larger Tsimshian astronomical tradition that interprets the night sky as a map of supernatural activities. The movements of celestial bodies are guided by the same social and spiritual principles that govern Tsimshian life on earth — chiefs, potlatches, journeys, and encounters with supernatural beings all have their counterparts in the sky world.
source: Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology; Tsimshian oral tradition
full_text:
This Tsimshian myth explains the origin of the sun, moon, and night sky. After Weeget — Giant/Raven — brought light from heaven, there was still the question of who would carry the sun across the sky each day and what the patterns of stars meant.

The One Who Walks All Over the Sky is a supernatural being assigned to carry the sun on his daily journey from east to west. He walks across the dome of the sky, his feet leaving no prints, his passage leaving only the light that warms the earth. His path determines the seasons: when he walks high, it is summer; when low, winter.

The stars are his footprints or the campfires of other sky beings. Some say the stars are the marks left by his feet as he walks, each one a point of light where his sole touched the sky. Others say the stars are the campfires of sky beings who live along his path, lighting their longhouses and warming themselves against the cold of the upper world.

This story is part of the larger Tsimshian astronomical tradition that interprets the night sky as a map of supernatural activities. The movements of celestial bodies are guided by the same social and spiritual principles that govern Tsimshian life on earth — chiefs, potlatches, journeys, and encounters with supernatural beings all have their counterparts in the sky world.

The sky is not empty; it is full — full of beings who live their own lives, pursue their own purposes, and watch the human world with an attention that is both encouraging and admonishing. To look up at the stars is to look into the spirit world, and to understand the stars is to understand the forces that shape human destiny.

title: The Bear Who Married a Woman (Tsimshian)
summary: A Tsimshian woman gathering berries in the forest encountered a bear who removed his bearskin and revealed himself as a handsome man. He took her to his village, where the bear people lived just like humans inside their lodges but appeared as bears to outsiders. The woman married him, learned the ways of the bear people, and gave birth to children who were half-human, half-bear. Her husband provided abundantly for her, bringing salmon and berries. She grew content with her bear husband, but when her human brothers came searching for her, she was forced to choose between her two families. The brothers killed the bear husband in a hunt, but the woman begged them not to harm her children. The children grew up with special powers of communication between humans and bears. Their descendants became the Bear Clan. This cross-cultural marriage story, found throughout the Northwest Coast, establishes the bear as a relative rather than an animal, requiring respect and proper protocol in hunting.
source: Tsimshian oral tradition; Franz Boas, Tsimshian Mythology; native-languages.org
full_text:
A Tsimshian woman gathering berries in the forest encountered a bear who removed his bearskin and revealed himself as a handsome man. He stood before her in the forest clearing, his human body pale and strong, his eyes dark with an intelligence that was more than animal.

He took her to his village, where the bear people lived just like humans inside their lodges but appeared as bears to outsiders. The village was hidden in the deep forest, invisible to those who did not know where to look. Inside the lodges, the bear people cooked, carved, and told stories. Outside, they were bears — large, powerful, and solitary.

The woman married him, learned the ways of the bear people, and gave birth to children who were half-human, half-bear. Her husband provided abundantly for her, bringing salmon and berries, his bear strength making the hunt easy.

She grew content with her bear husband, but when her human brothers came searching for her, she was forced to choose between her two families. The brothers killed the bear husband in a hunt, their spears flashing in the dim light of the forest. But the woman begged them not to harm her children.

The children grew up with special powers of communication between humans and bears. They could speak both languages, understand both worlds, and move between them with ease. Their descendants became the Bear Clan.

This cross-cultural marriage story, found throughout the Northwest Coast, establishes the bear as a relative rather than an animal, requiring respect and proper protocol in hunting. To hunt a bear is not simply to take game; it is to take a relative, and the proper ceremonies must be observed.

title: The Wonderful Tar-Baby
summary: Brer Fox fashions a doll made of tar and turpentine and sets it in the road to trap Brer Rabbit. When Brer Rabbit greets the silent Tar-Baby and receives no reply, he grows angry and strikes it, getting his paw stuck. He strikes with the other paw, then kicks, and finally butts with his head—each limb becoming hopelessly ensnared in the sticky tar. Brer Fox emerges from hiding, delighted at his capture, but Brer Rabbit's clever pleading ultimately allows him to escape when he begs not to be thrown into the briar patch—the one place he was born and bred to thrive.
source: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881)
full_text:
Brer Fox had been watching Brer Rabbit for weeks, cataloguing his tricks, noting his habits, building a case file of grievances that grew thicker every day. Brer Rabbit had outwitted him at the fishing hole, humiliated him at the barn dance, and stolen the best persimmons from the tree that Brer Fox considered his own. Something had to be done.

So Brer Fox went to work. He mixed tar and turpentine with the patience of a craftsman, shaping the mixture into a doll — a small, round figure with stubby arms and a flat face. He set it in the road where Brer Rabbit was sure to pass, propped it against a fence post, and hid in the bushes to watch.

Brer Rabbit came along, swinging his arms, whistling a tune, not a care in the world. He saw the Tar-Baby sitting in the road and stopped.

"Good morning," said Brer Rabbit. "Nice day, isn't it?"

The Tar-Baby said nothing.

"I said, good morning," Brer Rabbit repeated, louder. "How do you do?"

The Tar-Baby said nothing.

Brer Rabbit frowned. He was not accustomed to being ignored. He spoke to everyone — trees, rocks, people, animals — and they all spoke back, if only to tell him to go away. But this creature simply sat there, staring with its flat tar face, and said nothing.

"What's the matter with you?" Brer Rabbit demanded. "Cat got your tongue?"

The Tar-Baby said nothing.

Brer Rabbit was angry now. He struck the Tar-Baby with his right paw. His paw stuck. He struck it with his left paw. That paw stuck too. He kicked it with his right foot. His foot stuck. He kicked it with his left foot. His foot stuck. He butt the Tar-Baby with his head, and his head stuck fast.

Now Brer Rabbit was trapped, pinned to the Tar-Baby by all four limbs and his head, and Brer Fox emerged from the bushes, grinning from ear to ear.

"Well, well, well," said Brer Fox. "Look what we have here."

Brer Fox was delighted. He had Brer Rabbit exactly where he wanted him, and he intended to make the most of it. He danced around Brer Rabbit, mocking him, recounting every trick Brer Rabbit had ever played, building a case for his execution with the thoroughness of a prosecutor.

But Brer Rabbit was not finished. He was never finished. Even pinned to a Tar-Baby in the middle of the road, with Brer Fox dancing around him and planning his demise, Brer Rabbit had a trick left.

"Go ahead and kill me, Brer Fox," he said. "Roast me, drown me, skin me — I don't care. Just don't throw me in that briar patch."

Brer Fox paused. A briar patch? That sounded like a fine idea.

"Please, Brer Fox, not the briar patch!" Brer Rabbit begged, his voice rising with what sounded like genuine terror. "Anything but the briar patch!"

Brer Fox grabbed Brer Rabbit by the hind legs and flung him deep into the briar patch.

To Brer Fox's astonishment, Brer Rabbit appeared on a hillside, picking burrs from his fur, and shouted back: 'Bred en bawn in a brier-patch, Brer Fox — bred en bawn in a brier-patch!' The briar patch, which would tear the skin of any other creature, was Brer Rabbit's ancestral home.

title: Brer Rabbit and the Briar Patch (Bred and Bawn)
summary: After Brer Fox captures Brer Rabbit using the Tar-Baby, he declares his intent to kill and eat him. Brer Rabbit pleads for his life, begging not to be thrown into the briar patch, suggesting instead that he be roasted, hanged, drowned, or skinned. The more Brer Rabbit begs to avoid the briar patch, the more determined Brer Fox becomes to throw him there. Finally, Brer Fox snatches Brer Rabbit by the hind legs and flings him deep into the briar patch. To Brer Fox's astonishment, Brer Rabbit appears on a hillside, picking burrs from his fur, and shouts back: 'Bred en bawn in a brier-patch, Brer Fox—bred en bawn in a brier-patch!' The briar patch, which would tear the skin of any other creature, was Brer Rabbit's ancestral home.
source: Uncle Remus: His Songs and His Sayings (Joel Chandler Harris, 1881)
full_text:
After Brer Fox captured Brer Rabbit using the Tar-Baby, he declared his intent to kill and eat him. This was not idle talk — Brer Fox had been planning this moment for weeks, and he had brought a rope.

But Brer Rabbit was not ready to die. He was never ready to die. He began to plead — not for his life, exactly, but for the manner of his death, because Brer Rabbit understood that the right words at the right time could change anything.

"Roast me over a slow fire," he said. "That's the worst thing you can do to me. I can't stand a slow fire."

Brer Fox considered this. A slow fire did sound like a lot of work. He'd have to gather wood, build a fire, watch it burn down to coals, and then tend it while Brer Rabbit roasted. That would take all afternoon.

"How about I drown you?" Brer Fox offered.

"Please, Brer Fox, not drowning!" Brer Rabbit cried. "I have a fear of water. I'd rather be hanged."

"Hanged?" Brer Fox considered this. Hanging required a tree with a sturdy branch, a rope, and time. It was simpler than a slow fire, but still involved effort.

"I tell you what," Brer Fox said. "I'll throw you in the briar patch."

Brer Rabbit's eyes went wide. "Not the briar patch!" he begged. "Please, Brer Fox, anything but the briar patch! Those thorns will tear me to pieces! I'll be skinned alive! Just kill me quick — roast me, drown me, hang me — but don't throw me in the briar patch!"
